2- The importance of purity and chastity for the married.
3- This law declares that God knows all hidden things, and so it makes a person keep away from every sin even if no one sees him.
4- Showing the right of the innocent, so that she is not wearied by false accusations.

entries.section: (4) The law of jealousy and suspicion

paragraphs.text: Lie with seed: that is, complete adultery, or adultery that resulted in pregnancy.
Kept close: that is, she was able to hide her deed and her sin from people.
Taken: not caught in the sin.
The spirit of jealousy: a spirit of suspicion and anger.

God goes into the detailed description of the case should it occur, and says that if a woman committed complete adultery that resulted in pregnancy, and even if she was able to hide everything from people, but her husband was seized by jealousy and suspicion, whether his suspicion was well founded and his jealousy true, or the woman was innocent of what her husband accused her of and did nothing of the foregoing, then in order to be sure of his course of action he does what will be mentioned in the following verses:

entries.section: (4) The law of jealousy and suspicion

paragraphs.text: The tenth part of an ephah: the ephah is a measure of grain, and its tenth is 2.3 liters.

The man brings his wife to the tent of meeting and meets the priest, and takes with him an offering of barley meal, which is cheap and available to all. Because this offering relates to sin, suspicion and unfaithfulness, and is not like the other offerings, God forbade adding to it the oil and frankincense usually added, because oil is a symbol of the Holy Spirit and His gladdening work, and frankincense (incense) points to pure prayers, and this does not apply at all to what is before us.

entries.section: (4) The law of jealousy and suspicion

paragraphs.text: The priest takes the woman who is suspected and makes her stand at the door of the tent of meeting "before the Lord," and takes holy water from the water of the laver, as most interpreters think, though there are other opinions that it is living running water, or water taken from the law of the red heifer (ch. 19). He puts this water in one of the earthen vessels of the service that were in the Tent, and takes a little of the dust, which points to the shameful position in which this woman stands, and the dust also points to being broken down before God, as Abraham said when he began his speech with God, "I am but dust and ashes" (Gen 18:27). The aim of this rite is to encourage the sinning wife to repent.

entries.section: (4) The law of jealousy and suspicion

paragraphs.text: Uncover the woman's head: he removes her head covering as a sign of her being accused and her innocence not yet being proved.

The bitter water that causeth the curse: it is the same holy water, and it was called the water of the curse because it brings the curse on the woman if she has sinned, and it was called bitter as a reference to the bitterness of sin and its consequences. It is said that the priest used to add to it a bitter plant or a very bitter substance such as myrrh or wormwood.
Under thy husband: that is, married and joined to your husband, and then you went aside from him.

The priest brings the accused woman and reminds her that she stands before the Lord, holding in her hands the offering of ground barley after her head has been uncovered, while the water of the curse is in the priest's hand. The priest begins to question her with a clear and direct question after she swears that she will tell the truth, and he makes clear to her that if she did not commit the sin or become defiled by it with another man, God will declare her innocence and the bitter water of the curse will do her no harm.

entries.section: (4) The law of jealousy and suspicion

paragraphs.text: The priest continues his speech with the woman, telling her that if she has fallen into sin and wronged her husband and committed adultery with another man than her husband.

entries.section: (4) The law of jealousy and suspicion

paragraphs.text: The priest charges the woman with an oath of cursing: he declares that the curse must come upon her.
A curse among thy people: that is, you will become an example among women and a byword that they speak about you.

The priest invokes the curse on the woman. The curse will not come upon her unless she is guilty, and he says to her that you will be a curse instead of a blessing and become a mockery among your people. As for her bodily punishment, it is the sagging of her belly together with its visible swelling, and likewise her thigh, which was defiled by sin, will be afflicted with slackness and inability to walk (like paralysis ...). All this will be because of the water that she is now going to drink, which brings these curses upon her, and the woman answers affirming, "Amen, amen," or "truly, I know."
Let us notice together how harsh are the consequences of sin ...
1- Spiritual consequences, for because of it a person becomes a curse instead of a blessing, that is, cursed by God until he repents.
2- Social and moral consequences, for he becomes an example and a reproach by whom people swear: "[the quotation is garbled in the source and cannot be translated]"
3- Bodily consequences, in that the body is struck by illnesses that weary it as a direct result of this sin.
So take heed, my brother, and do not make light of sin, for it is exceedingly sinful and calls for repentance and confession so that you may obtain the mercies of God.

entries.section: (4) The law of jealousy and suspicion

paragraphs.text: The priest writes what he said orally to the woman on a piece of skin or a wooden tablet, and he may also write the woman's name with the curses, and puts what he wrote into the water in the earthen vessel, and the writing is blotted out. The meaning intended here is that the water the woman will drink has become the bearer of the curse that the priest pronounced, so that when the woman drinks of this water it enters her inwards to cause her the bitter consequences of sin if she has in fact sinned.

entries.section: (4) The law of jealousy and suspicion

paragraphs.text: It is understood from these two verses that before the woman drank of the water, the priest would take a handful of the offering of ground barley and present it on the outer, ever-burning altar of burnt offering to burn it before the Lord, as was the custom with the other offerings (Lev 2:2), while the rest of the quantity of barley was the portion of the priest and his house; and when the priest had completed that, the woman drank of the water.

entries.section: (4) The law of jealousy and suspicion

paragraphs.text: If the woman has committed adultery, then when she drinks the water her belly swells and her thigh falls away.

entries.section: (4) The law of jealousy and suspicion

paragraphs.text: But if the woman is innocent, the result is God's declaration of her innocence, so no sign of sickness appears on her; on the contrary, as Jewish tradition says, she would increase in beauty, and her life would be blessed, and God would lift up her head before her people, and her pregnancy would be completed to its end, and she would rejoice in her child.

The teachers of the Jews say that if the man had fallen into adultery and accused his wife of adultery, and she was in fact an adulteress and drank of the water of the curse, no symptoms appeared on her because of her husband's adultery. For this reason, when corruption and adultery spread among the children of Israel, they neglected to carry out this law, as in the days of Hosea the prophet (Hos 4:13, 14).

entries.section: (4) The law of jealousy and suspicion

paragraphs.text: These two verses are a summary of all that came in the law of jealousy, with which Moses ends his discourse about its procedures, steps and results.

entries.section: (4) The law of jealousy and suspicion

paragraphs.text: When this law is completed the husband is cleared of guilt, even if his wife is innocent, because he did not hasten to condemn her or kill her or divorce her, but left the whole matter to the judgment of God.
As for the woman, she bears her guilt if she is at fault and is exposed to God's punishment as He said.
Notes on the law of jealousy: from Jewish tradition we can add some matters connected with this law.
1- If the woman confessed before drinking the water, she was divorced from her husband and was given no compensation in anything.
2- If the woman refused to drink, they would force her to.
3- But if she tried to vomit this water, she was driven out and considered unclean.

May we all learn not to pass judgment on anyone but to leave matters to God, for He alone is the One who knows and He is also just ... Prayer and committing matters to Him is the best counsel and teaching we can receive from the law of jealousy in this chapter.
The law of vows and the priestly blessing, the introduction of the chapter:

After God declared His care for His people and they were counted and numbered, and each of them had a name (a standard) by which he was known to God, and a dwelling around His house (the Tent) or a work within it, God brings us through this chapter into a more special relationship, as we shall see.

entries.section: (1) The obligations of the Nazirite during his vow

paragraphs.text: Separate themselves: to be set apart and distinguished by special conduct and behavior from the rest of the congregation.

God defined for Moses the duties of the person, man or woman, for there is no spiritual difference between them, who offers himself as a vow to the Lord. The Nazirite was either by the choice of the Lord, like Samson and John the Baptist, or a person vowed his son, like Samuel, or a person vowed himself to the Lord for a period of time, which the Talmud says is not less than a month, like Paul the Apostle. The spiritual concept of the Nazirite is that he withdraws from the pleasures of the world, lives as an ascetic and devotes himself entirely to the service of God, and it is an optional law for whoever wishes.

entries.section: (1) The obligations of the Nazirite during his vow

paragraphs.text: Vine tree: the grapevine or grape tree.
Kernels: the seed of the grape.
Wine: the product of the vine is meant.
Strong drink: old (aged) wine, or one in which the proportion of alcohol has increased so that it became stronger in effect.

Vinegar of wine or of strong drink: wine, if exposed to certain weather conditions, may spoil and its taste become close to vinegar, but it does not lose its effect ... and the poor used to drink this vinegar because of its cheap price. The first obligation that the Nazirite takes on is not to go near wine and everything connected with it at all. For wine points to the joys of the world and the lusts of the flesh, and whoever is consecrated must therefore wean his heart from the pleasures and lusts of the world; and this is the state in which every Christian ought to be, for we died to the world by Baptism and became consecrated, that is, Nazirites for Christ. The prohibition also came upon moist grapes, that is, fresh, or raisins, that is, dried grapes, although they are natural fruit, but because they are the source from which wine comes, God forbade them to the Nazirite, as a clear reference to the spiritual man: it is not enough that a person not sin, but he must also keep away from the sources of evil or sin.
To convey this concept God adds in His speech to Moses that the Nazirite must also not eat of the vine itself, that is, the fruit of the grape or its seed.

Let us notice together how careful God is of those consecrated to Him and who love His holy name, for He keeps them from approaching the roots or origins of evil, because God who formed us knows perfectly that we are all under warfare and liable to be influenced and enticed ... So flee, beloved, from everything that hinders the salvation of your soul.

entries.section: (1) The obligations of the Nazirite during his vow

paragraphs.text: The second obligation on the Nazirite was that he should not shave his hair throughout the period of his vow, as a clear sign before everyone that he is consecrated and set apart for the Lord during the period of his vow. Since cutting the hair was a sign of a man's adornment, letting the hair grow comes as a sign of self-denial and of not caring about personal appearance.

entries.section: (1) The obligations of the Nazirite during his vow

paragraphs.text: The third obligation is not to touch a dead person, because it is a symbol of touching sin and its consequences, as came in (ch. 5:2), and this includes even close relatives such as father and mother, brothers and sisters ... This obligation also includes not entering the tent of the deceased and not taking part in escorting his funeral. The meaning intended, as with the prohibition of wine, is to keep away from everything connected with sin.
Because the consecration of his God is upon his head: that is, his loosened hair is a testimony and sign of his total consecration to God. So he must not forget that.

entries.section: (1) The obligations of the Nazirite during his vow

paragraphs.text: The consecrated person must remain on guard like this throughout the period of his vow and not forget that he is holy, that is, set apart for the Lord, and that this vow has obligations by which he must live ... The subject includes us also, for the Myron with which we were anointed has made us a dwelling place of the Holy Spirit, that is, we were set apart for God, and for this reason we must be on guard and keep away from evil and the appearance of evil, even if its source is those nearest to us, so there is no laxity or flattery toward sin at all.

entries.section: (1) The obligations of the Nazirite during his vow

paragraphs.text: Verses (9-12) speak about the remedy required of the Nazirite if he becomes defiled accidentally and without intention. If someone dies suddenly by him in his tent, without previous signs of death, so that he was not on guard and did not keep away, he becomes unclean, and so does his vow, "the head of his consecration," and he must complete the law of purification on the seventh day, which applies to everyone who touched a dead person, except that he must shave the hair of his head, as an indication that the previous days of his vow are not counted.

entries.section: (1) The obligations of the Nazirite during his vow

paragraphs.text: Although his uncleanness came as an accidental thing, God obligated him to come to the priest the day after shaving his hair, that is, on the eighth day, with two young pigeons or two turtledoves, which are the cheapest sacrifices, so that the priest offers one of the two as a sin offering and the other as a burnt offering, because without shedding of blood there is no forgiveness for the sin of his uncleanness and the breaking of his vow. The burnt offering is a sweet savor and the appeasing of God, and thus his unintentional sin is pardoned.
And shall hallow his head that same day: that is, he becomes ready to let his hair grow again and to begin his vow from the beginning on that eighth day.

entries.section: (1) The obligations of the Nazirite during his vow

paragraphs.text: A lamb of the first year: a lamb one year old.

The days in which he was defiled because of the dead all fall away from his vow, and he must begin his vow anew, and on the first day of renewing his vow he brings a lamb one year old and offers it as a trespass offering on the first day of his new vow ... It is known that the trespass offering was offered for sins done unwittingly by a person, and after this offering God accepts his new vow from him.

May we learn two important things from the law of the Nazirite: the first is to flee from sin so that we are sheltered from its consequences, and the other is the necessity of apologizing to God and to people for our accidental or unwitting errors, for this teaches us humility on the one hand and comforts the hearts of those we have wronged on the other.

entries.section: (2) What happens when the vow is fulfilled

paragraphs.text: When the days of the vow are fulfilled, the Nazirite comes before God and the priest at the door of the Tent and offers to God an offering, "his offering," which includes more than one thing:
First: a burnt offering, that is, one burned entirely on the outer altar, of which no one eats because it is a sweet savor to the Lord, and this sacrifice is a male lamb one year old.
Second: a ewe lamb, also one year old, offered as a sin offering for the unwitting sins and the sins of the Nazirite.
Third: he also offers "a ram," that is, a sheep, with no age required for it, as a thank offering to God for accepting the vow and for the Nazirite's completing his full period.

Fourth: the sacrifices are accompanied by a basket of cakes of unleavened bread well kneaded "mingled," but not leavened, and with the cakes other unleavened wafers anointed, that is, smeared with oil.

Fifth: with their meat offering and their drink offerings: it was customary and known that burnt offerings and peace offerings were accompanied by other offerings and drink offerings such as oil and wine (Num 15:1-7). One may refer to the interpretation of these sacrifices and offerings in what came in the interpretation of the Book of Leviticus.

entries.section: (2) What happens when the vow is fulfilled

paragraphs.text: The priest begins by offering the sin offering and its detailed rite in (Lev 4:27-35), then the burnt offering as came in (Lev 1, 2), and likewise the peace offering (Lev 3). As for the basket of unleavened bread, he would take one of them, that is, one cake and one wafer, to be burned on the altar also, while the rest of the basket is the portion of the priests, and the same applies to the oil and the wine: a part of it was poured on the altar and the priests kept another part.

entries.section: (2) What happens when the vow is fulfilled

paragraphs.text: The head of his separation: his head, on which he let the hair grow and hang loose.

The loosened hair was the visible sign of the vow, and for this reason at the end of the period of the vow the Nazirite had to shave his hair and throw the hair into the fire of the altar to consume it. God linked the burning of the hair with the peace offering (the thank offering) as evidence of the Lord's acceptance of the vow and His approval and the delight of His heart in it.

entries.section: (2) What happens when the vow is fulfilled

paragraphs.text: Wave them: the priest makes the Nazirite move his hands in the four directions and then raise them upward and lower them downward, for he offers his sacrifice to God who is in every place and dwells in heaven and has mercy on and blesses His children on earth.

After the peace offering is boiled, the priest takes the right front leg, called the shoulder of the heave offering, with a cake and a wafer from the basket of unleavened bread, and makes the Nazirite hold them after he has shaved his hair, and the priest holds the Nazirite's hand that grasps what was mentioned and waves them before God, that is, these offerings are presented before the face of God. Everything the Nazirite waves before God is God's portion, so it is given to the priests, who are themselves the portion of the Lord. As a sign of the end of the vow the Nazirite drinks wine, which had been forbidden to him throughout the period of his vow, and thus he returns to his normal life.

entries.section: (2) What happens when the vow is fulfilled

paragraphs.text: This verse comes as the conclusion of everything that came in the law of the Nazirite up to the end of the time of his vow.

Beside that that his hand shall get: that is, the other things and offerings that he may have vowed to God, which are apart from and in addition to the essential sacrifices and offerings that came in the Law.
The Nazirite must fulfill all that he said and pronounced in his vow, for everything he vowed is regarded as a covenant that came out of him and must be fulfilled.

The idea of the offering has become absent from many of us. Despite the abundant good that God gives His children, they often turn away from the offering or, at best, offer nothing but tithes ... Although God reminds us not to appear before Him empty (Deut 16:16), we forget that we have brothers in Christ who are in need while bread is abundant with us. So remember that God has rights over you, and remember also that everything you offer with joy gladdens the heart of God as well.

entries.section: (3) The priestly blessing

paragraphs.text: The discourse moves to another subject, and God directs His speech to Moses and through him to the priests, "Aaron and his sons," that they must bless the people. This puts before us another work of the priesthood besides offering sacrifices, which is intercession for the people: the priest conveys the offerings and petitions of his people to God and conveys the blessing of God to his people. The blessing was recited with the priest turning toward the people and raising his hands upward above the level of the people's heads, as a sign that graces and blessing have God Himself as their source.

entries.section: (3) The priestly blessing

paragraphs.text: The blessing had the following text and content:

(1) Blessing and keeping: that is, the priest asks God for spiritual and material blessings for His people, and asks also for His care, shepherding and guarding of His people from anything or any harm.

(2) Light and mercy: he also asks that God enlighten the mind of His people so that they are filled with all understanding, guidance, knowledge, insight and spiritual wisdom, and have mercy on their weakness and accept their repentance of their sins.

(3) Lift up His countenance: that is, God looks with a special look on His people, the look of a father on his children, and the look of very special care like the shepherd whose eyes do not neglect his sheep.
(4) Give His peace: for God is the King of peace and its only source, and it is a peace that includes the mind (thought), the heart (feelings) and the whole life of man.
The repetition of the name of the Lord three times in the three verses is to affirm that the source of all blessings is God alone, the Three Hypostases, and none other.

entries.section: (3) The priestly blessing

paragraphs.text: By this blessing with which the priests bless the people, they make the name of God exalted and holy always in the hearts and minds of the children of Israel, and likewise God answers the petitions and prayers of the priests for the people, so that the people themselves feel the effectiveness of these requests through God's blessing on them and on their possessions and their whole life.

It is good that you enjoy the blessing of the priests and ask for their prayers for you, for they hold the greatest thing in existence, the Body and Blood of the Lord. So kissing their hands and asking for their prayers pours out upon you blessings from God whom they serve.
The offering of gifts and sacrifices to the house of the Lord

entries.section: (1) The offering of the wagons and oxen and their distribution

paragraphs.text: Anointed it: that is, poured on it and anointed it with the holy oil (Ex 30:31). Sanctified it: that is, set it apart and consecrated it for the service of the Lord.
The vessels thereof: the implements and appurtenances of the service.

This verse comes as an introduction to the whole chapter, making clear that the events that follow took place after Moses the prophet finished setting up the tent of meeting and anointing it and consecrating it with all its contents to the Lord.

entries.section: (1) The offering of the wagons and oxen and their distribution

paragraphs.text: Offered: presented.
Covered wagons: carts to keep the implements of the tent of meeting when journeying, and they were covered to protect what was in them from rain and sun.

The princes of the tribes came, the same ones who numbered and counted all the people (ch. 1), and offered their gifts and offerings before the Lord "before the tabernacle." These offerings consisted of twelve oxen to draw the wagons, one ox for each tribe, with every two oxen sharing in drawing a wagon, and also "six covered wagons," that is, every two tribes share in one wagon.

entries.section: (1) The offering of the wagons and oxen and their distribution

paragraphs.text: God's command to Moses was that he accept these offerings from the princes of the tribes, and He also charged him to use them in the service, especially at the time of journeying. Since the Levites were the ones charged with this service, Moses distributed them to them with wisdom and according to need, to each group according to the kind of their service.

entries.section: (1) The offering of the wagons and oxen and their distribution

paragraphs.text: The distribution was as follows: Moses the prophet gave two wagons with four oxen to draw them to the sons of Gershon, since their service, as mentioned in (ch. 4:21-28), was the curtains and coverings of the Tent and the inner pins and cords.

entries.section: (1) The offering of the wagons and oxen and their distribution

paragraphs.text: As for the sons of Merari, whose work and burdens were heavier, Moses gave them four wagons drawn by eight oxen, since they had to carry the boards of wood, the pillars, the bars, the metal sockets and the outer pins and their cords (ch. 4:29, 30).

entries.section: (1) The offering of the wagons and oxen and their distribution

paragraphs.text: But the sons of Kohath did not take any of the wagons or oxen, because their loads were the lightest and all of them were carried on the shoulders, and they include the contents of the sanctuary and the Holy of Holies.

My beloved brother, there was divine wisdom in the distribution of the wagons and oxen, for the offerings were distributed according to need. As an application to our spiritual life, never compare yourself with others in their gifts or talents and say to yourself, why did the Lord not give me this or that? ... Accept your talents and trade with them, and do not look around you, and trust in the wisdom of God ... for you will be asked only for what you were given, so be careful to be faithful in it.

entries.section: (2) The other offerings and gifts

paragraphs.text: Dedication: setting apart and consecrating for the service of God.

The altar: what is meant is the tent of meeting with the bronze altar and the altar of incense it contains and everything in it. Each prince of the tribes of the people came to the Tent after the anointing and sanctifying, offering his offerings and gifts of wagons and oxen and other gifts, as we shall learn, but God's command to Moses was that they should not all come forward on one day, but that a day be assigned to each prince of a tribe on which to offer his offerings. In this way the celebrations of the dedication of the altar continued for twelve days, which were regarded as feasts in their gladness. The expression dedication of the altar does not mean that the dedication was repeated every day, but the celebrations of the dedication are meant.

entries.section: (2) The other offerings and gifts

paragraphs.text: The tribe of Judah and its prince Nahshon the son of Amminadab was the first to offer his offerings, that is, his gifts, on the first day, and the following is noted regarding the order of the days of the offerings:

1- Presenting the offerings was in the order of the places of encampment around the Tent and for no other consideration, so that there would be no competition or quarrel over who should offer his offerings first. Perhaps he began with the tribe of Judah because from it Christ would come (Gen 49:8-12).

2- It mentioned that Nahshon was of the tribe of Judah and not the prince of Judah, although he was a prince, to teach us that leadership is a position for the service of God and not for pride or for controlling others; then in the rest of the tribes it mentioned that the one who offered the offerings was the prince of the tribe.

3- This order proceeded in one direction: the first three tribes were encamped on the east side, the next three tribes were encamped on the south side, and so the tribes of the west side, and finally the north side.

4- The offering of all the princes of the tribes was alike and exactly identical, so explaining the offering of one tribe spares us repetition in explaining the rest of the tribes and their offerings.

entries.section: (2) The other offerings and gifts

paragraphs.text: The details of the offering that the tribe of Judah and its prince presented, and which all the tribes repeated, were as follows:
1- A broad, flat dish of silver weighing one hundred and thirty shekels, that is, about 1.950 kilograms of silver (the shekel = 15 grams).
2- One silver bowl: a deeper dish (hollow) weighing about one kilogram of silver.
Both the dish and the bowl were filled with fine flour mingled with oil, to be offered as came in the Book of Leviticus (ch. 2).
3- One golden spoon: its weight was about 150 grams, and sweet incense was offered on it.

4- A burnt offering: this sacrifice consisted of one young bullock, one ram and one lamb of the first year. The difference between the ram and the lamb of the first year is a difference in the age of the two: the ram is the male of the sheep with fully grown horns and is known as the stud of the flock, while the lamb of the first year is a lamb one year of age, that is, ripe for eating but smaller in size and age. All of this was burned on the altar of burnt offering (see Lev 1).
5- A sin offering: it was of a male goat, offered for the sins or unwitting errors in which the prince of the tribe may have sinned, and the priest takes a part of it.

6- A peace offering: this consisted of two oxen, five rams, five he-goats (male goats) and five lambs, each of the first year. These are offerings from which the priests take a portion, and so does the one who offers them, according to what came in the laws of the Book of Leviticus.

entries.section: (2) The other offerings and gifts

paragraphs.text: The same offerings as before were repeated with each tribe, mentioning the name of the prince of the fathers of each tribe before mentioning his offerings or the offerings of his tribe.

entries.section: (2) The other offerings and gifts

paragraphs.text: As for these verses, before the end of the chapter, they came as a summary of all the previous offerings, but in a collective form.
The tally was twelve dishes and bowls of silver, the total of their weights being two thousand four hundred shekels, which is equivalent to 36 kilograms of silver.
Likewise the total of the golden spoons was twelve spoons weighing one hundred and twenty shekels, which is close to 1.8 kilograms of gold.

Likewise the total of the oxen was counted and came to twelve oxen, the total of the rams came to twelve rams, and the total of the he-goats came to twelve he-goats. All of these were offered as sin offerings.
As for what was offered as peace offerings, the total number was twenty-four oxen, sixty rams, sixty he-goats, and the lambs of the first year were also sixty.

Perhaps the purpose of this final summary of all the offerings is that God wished us to know that nothing is forgotten before Him, but everything we offer Him of vows and offerings is a lasting memorial for us before Him, for God in His justice and love never forgets the labor of love of His children.

entries.section: (3) The manner of the Lord's speaking with Moses

paragraphs.text: The place of the lampstand was the sanctuary, and it consisted of a base and a shaft bearing seven lamps, that is, lights for illumination.

When thou lightest the lamps: that is, when you have cleaned them, filled them with oil and put them in their place on the lampstand. Over against the candlestick: the lampstand here means the middle shaft, and the meaning is that at the lighting the three right-hand lamps face toward the left and the three left-hand lamps face toward the right, so that all six lamps face toward the middle shaft.

The Lord commanded Moses that after he prepares the lampstand for lighting, Aaron is to light it, because the priests alone are permitted to light the lamps of the lampstand, since it is inside the sanctuary which only the priests enter, and the lampstand was lit from the holy fire that came down from heaven upon the altar of burnt offering. See also what was said about the lampstand and its lighting in (Ex 25:31-40).

entries.section: (3) The manner of the Lord's speaking with Moses

paragraphs.text: This verse shows Aaron's complete commitment to carrying out all that God commanded.

entries.section: (3) The manner of the Lord's speaking with Moses

paragraphs.text: As for the workmanship of the lampstand and the material it was made of, it was as follows:

Beaten work: that is, it was made of gold by hammering and carving, since God forbade that it be made cast (Ex 32). The specifications of the lampstand were exactly like the pattern the Lord showed Moses on the mountain (Ex 25), with its seven lamps. It was made of gold not cast but beaten, so that God might keep the people away from the memory of the cast gods that the Egyptians worshiped.

The lampstand was a symbol of Christ, "the light of the world ..." and Christ gave His children to be a light of the world also, to bear witness to His name ... Are we truly so? Grant us, O Lord, to be so for the glory of Your holy name.

(2) The ordination and consecration of the Levites (vv. 5-15:) 5 And the LORD spake unto Moses, saying, 6 "Take the Levites from among the children of Israel, and cleanse them. 7 And thus shalt thou do unto them, to cleanse them: Sprinkle water of purifying upon them, and let them shave all their flesh, and let them wash their clothes, and so make themselves clean. 8 Then let them take a young bullock with his meat offering, even fine flour mingled with oil, and another young bullock shalt thou take for a sin offering. 9 And thou shalt bring the Levites before the tabernacle of the congregation: and thou shalt gather the whole assembly of the children of Israel together: 10 And thou shalt bring the Levites before the LORD: and the children of Israel shall put their hands upon the Levites: 11 And Aaron shall offer the Levites before the LORD for an offering of the children of Israel, that they may execute the service of the LORD. 12 And the Levites shall lay their hands upon the heads of the bullocks: and thou shalt offer the one for a sin offering, and the other for a burnt offering, unto the LORD, to make an atonement for the Levites. 13 And thou shalt set the Levites before Aaron, and before his sons, and offer them for an offering unto the LORD. 14 Thus shalt thou separate the Levites from among the children of Israel: and the Levites shall be mine. 15 And after that shall the Levites go in to do the service of the tabernacle of the congregation: and thou shalt cleanse them, and offer them for an offering." The discourse moves us, through a new divine command, to the consecration and setting apart of the Levites for service, and this included four stages:
1- Their cleansing (vv. 5-9) 2- The laying on of hands upon them (v. 10)
3- Their waving before the Lord (v. 11) 4- The offering of sacrifices for them (vv. 12-15)

entries.section: (3) The manner of the Lord's speaking with Moses

paragraphs.text: The Lord commanded Moses to take the Levites prepared for the service from among the tribes of the children of Israel and begin to cleanse them. The bodily cleansing that Moses will perform for them also points to the purity of the spirit, and the counterpart of the Levites in the New Testament are the deacons who help the priests in the service.

entries.section: (3) The manner of the Lord's speaking with Moses

paragraphs.text: The steps of the cleansing itself were as follows:

1- Sprinkling water of purifying: that is, the water made for purification from sin. There are two opinions: either it was water from the laver from whose water the priests washed, or it was other water mixed with the ashes of a sin offering, as was done in the law of the water of separation (ch. 19). The Levites were sprinkled with it; and this rite points to cleansing from sin.
2- Letting a razor pass over their flesh: this is the second step, which means shaving all the hair of their skin with the razor, as a reference to removing sin from all its roots.

3- Washing the clothes: also as a reference that a person's outward conduct, which the clothes point to, must be in keeping with inner purity, so that a person behaves with purity and righteousness toward all those around him.

entries.section: (3) The manner of the Lord's speaking with Moses

paragraphs.text: The Levites, of course, had to prepare the sacrifices that they would offer at their consecration, and they were two bullocks offered as a sacrifice, one of them a burnt offering of delight to the Lord, and the other a sin offering, with an offering of flour mingled with oil.

The spiritual meaning in this is that when a person comes forward to the service of the Lord he must come first with repentance, that is, with a sin offering, and offer his whole life for the delight of God's heart as a burnt offering. All the men of God and His holy servants throughout the ages of the Church were daily sacrifices poured out on the altar of service.

entries.section: (3) The manner of the Lord's speaking with Moses

paragraphs.text: The discourse here is to Moses the prophet, that he bring all the Levites before the door of the Tent and the people gather around them for the beginning of the celebrations and rites of consecration.

entries.section: (3) The manner of the Lord's speaking with Moses

paragraphs.text: Before the Lord: before the door of the tent of meeting.

Because the Levites are chosen basically from the people, the children of Israel lay their hands on them as a sign that they are the sacrifices offered by the people to God and to the service. The laying on of hands also carries the meaning of calling and consecration for the one on whom the hand is laid, and likewise the people's declaration that they are their deputies for the service of God. Of course the whole people would not lay hands on the Levites, but only the elders and the heads of the people.

entries.section: (3) The manner of the Lord's speaking with Moses

paragraphs.text: The sacrifices or offerings were "waved" before the Lord, that is, some pieces of them were taken and the priest moved them with his hands in all directions and raised and lowered them as a sign that this sacrifice belongs to the Lord and is presented to Him. The waving of the Levites has the same spiritual meaning: Aaron, and whoever succeeds him in the headship of the priesthood, comes and gently moves the Levites to declare that they belong to the Lord and are living sacrifices presented to Him on behalf of all the people of the children of Israel, so that by this rite the Levite becomes a servant of the Lord.

entries.section: (3) The manner of the Lord's speaking with Moses

paragraphs.text: Then the sacrifices are offered by the usual rite, both the burnt offering and the sin offering, with the Levite laying his hand on the head of the sacrifice before it is slain (see Lev 1, 2). Just as the people appointed the Levites in their place for the service and as a redemption of the firstborn of the people, so the sacrifices redeem the Levites by their blood before God, as a clear sign and symbol of Christ's redemption by His blood of all His people. He is the true living sacrifice who was offered once on the Cross and has been extended to us with every Divine Liturgy until His second coming.

entries.section: (3) The manner of the Lord's speaking with Moses

paragraphs.text: This verse came as a repetition of what came in (v. 11), and the purpose is not to repeat the waving after the sacrifices but to stress the spiritual meaning, that they were fully set apart for the service of God. We notice also that God will repeat this command a third time in (v. 15).

entries.section: (3) The manner of the Lord's speaking with Moses

paragraphs.text: Thou shalt separate: that is, set apart and bring out.

The inspired text affirms what is known and practiced, that the Levites are separated from the people and set apart for the service only, and God declares clearly His ownership of them: "the Levites shall be mine." Thus, after the rite of ordination and setting apart, the work of the Levites becomes the service of the tent of meeting according to all that has been explained, and the last words of the inspired text in this section are an affirmation of the necessity of inner and outer purity and the declaration of ownership belonging to God alone.
Care for the consecration of your heart to God by driving out evil thoughts through repeating the Psalms and prayers, and keep your goal clear before your eyes always, which is the love of God.

entries.section: (3) The Levites instead of the firstborn of the children of Israel

paragraphs.text: Although it is God who chose and set apart the Levites for His service, He also regards them as a gift and present from the people to Him, giving His people the honor of presenting the tribe of their brother Levi to Him and to His service. Besides this being humility from God and great fatherly love, it also teaches us that when a father and mother accept God's choice of one of their sons as a priest or a monk, God regards this acceptance as a gift that He receives and values very highly from the father and mother.

entries.section: (3) The Levites instead of the firstborn of the children of Israel

paragraphs.text: God again reminds the people that His choice of the Levites was a substitute and redemption for offering every firstborn of the people, and this takes us back to the events of the tenth plague when God smote the firstborn of the Egyptians and put them to death, and in return He sanctified, that is, set apart for Himself, all the firstborn of the children of Israel, and silver was offered for them to the Lord ... But after the crossing of the Red Sea, and the people's need of the Tent for servants to serve God and His dwelling, God substituted the Levites for the firstborn of the people.

entries.section: (3) The Levites instead of the firstborn of the children of Israel

paragraphs.text: After God set the Levites apart for Himself instead of the firstborn, He put them under the authority of the priests, that is, Aaron and his sons, and their task is as follows:
1- Serving the house of the Lord, that is, the Tent, under the supervision of the priests, taking it down when journeying and setting it up when settling.

2- Making atonement for the children of Israel: the Levites had to alert the people and warn them against transgressing the commandments or touching or defiling the Tent and its appurtenances. By this they averted the wrath of God against His people, so that no plague would strike them when they draw near to God in worship or in offering sacrifices.

entries.section: (3) The Levites instead of the firstborn of the children of Israel

paragraphs.text: Aaron made an atonement for them to cleanse them: he offered sacrifices for them.

These three verses come as a summary of all that the Lord commanded Moses concerning the sanctification and cleansing of the Levites, the offering of sacrifices for them and their waving before the Lord to begin their service; and the words "Moses did, thus did the children of Israel unto them, so did they unto them" are mentioned to stress that everything God commanded was carried out with all precision.

Moses was exact in fulfilling all that the Lord commanded with all faithfulness; may we, beloved, learn to be faithful to the rites of the Church and to learn them, for whoever preserves the rite and order of the Church preserves the Church herself.

entries.section: (4) The age of the Levites' service

paragraphs.text: God defined for Moses the age at which the Levites begin the service of the Lord, which is from the age of twenty-five, although at the beginning of the fourth chapter He set the age of the Levites who perform the service at thirty. From this it is understood that the Levites actually began from the age of twenty-five as assistant servants and as a period of preparation and training for them, so as to carry the full responsibilities at the age of thirty.

entries.section: (4) The age of the Levites' service

paragraphs.text: From the age of thirty to fifty the Levites perform the full and arduous service, but after the age of fifty, with the beginning of the weakness of their bodies, they perform a light service and leave the carrying of what is difficult, and are content with guarding, direction and guidance.

Whatever your age, you have a role in the Church, so offer what you can, and let no one despise your youth, and do not be lazy because of your old age, for your service, however small it may seem, has great value in the eyes of God, especially if it is out of your need, that is, if you offer to God whatever your weakness.
The reminder of the keeping of the Passover and the pillar of cloud and fire

entries.section: (1) Keeping the Passover at its appointed time

paragraphs.text: The Lord spoke to Moses: the speech of God to Moses here does not follow the order of the events of the previous chapters, for the time here is clear and specific, the first month of the second year of the Exodus, whereas the numbering and counting of the people was in the second month of the same year; that is, God's speaking with Moses in this chapter about keeping the Passover preceded what came in the first chapter about the numbering of the people.

entries.section: (1) Keeping the Passover at its appointed time

paragraphs.text: Because of the importance of the Passover sacrifice, which redeemed the firstborn of the people and is a type of Christ's redemption of us, God required the people to keep it at its appointed time and without postponement. Its date was set in (Ex 12) as the evening of the fourteenth day of Nisan, which is the first month of the religious year and the seventh in the civil year. The words "in its appointed season" include not only the day but the time of eating it, which is between the two evenings, which now corresponds in the time known to us to between the afternoon and before sunset.

entries.section: (1) Keeping the Passover at its appointed time

paragraphs.text: According to all the rites of it shall ye keep it: that is, according to all that God explained before of slaying, cleaning, roasting and eating, which are the ordinances that the people kept well and which were explained before in (Ex 12), and are also referred to in (Lev 23).

entries.section: (1) Keeping the Passover at its appointed time

paragraphs.text: As the Lord spoke to Moses and commanded him, so the people did and obeyed with all exactness, and they ate the Passover between the two evenings exactly as its ordinances prescribe.

The children of Israel kept the first Passover in Egypt, and this is the second Passover, at the beginning of the second year of their departure from Egypt, and unfortunately they were afterward occupied with their sins and murmurings, so they did not keep the Passover until after they entered the Promised Land under Joshua. In the New Testament, however, the Church is careful to celebrate the sacrament of Communion of the Body and Blood of the Lord, of which the Passover was a type, because this sacrament is the food and strength of Christians.

Christ our Passover is present on the altar every day, and the times of the prayers are known to all, so are you careful to attend the Divine Liturgy early, and do you teach your children such care? My brother, a small word in your ear: "care means respect," so what do laziness, laxity and lateness mean?!

entries.section: (2) Rulings concerning one who refrained from eating the Passover

paragraphs.text: A case appeared here that needed guidance and clarification from Moses the prophet and Aaron his brother the priest. This exceptional case was that when the children of Israel kept the Passover at its appointed time, a relative of some of the people died, and they were defiled by touching him and burying him, and according to the provisions of the Law they could not approach the Passover or practice its rites. This pained them, the feeling that they would be separated from the people and miss this grace, which is the eating of the Passover that is kept only once a year, so they came forward to Moses and Aaron and asked them, sorrowful at their being separated.

entries.section: (2) Rulings concerning one who refrained from eating the Passover

paragraphs.text: But Moses the faithful servant did not come with an opinion of his own, but asked them to wait until he heard the opinion and command of the Lord on this matter, and he entered the Tent and God spoke with him as usual from above the ark of the testimony and from between the cherubim.
If only you would learn, when you answer a person who asked you for guidance or advice, to lift your heart toward God, asking Him for opinion and help before you answer his question.

entries.section: (2) Rulings concerning one who refrained from eating the Passover

paragraphs.text: The Lord's answer to those who asked was comforting and reassuring, and the Lord made His answer a law binding on all generations: whoever was defiled by a dead person, or whose circumstances of travel to a distant place prevented him from keeping the law of the Passover at its appointed time, must keep the Passover on the same day, that is, the fourteenth of the following month, which is the second of the religious year, and must observe in keeping it all that came in the Law: eating it between the two evenings, and eating it with unleavened bread and not with leavened bread, and also with bitter herbs, and leaving none of it until the morning ... see all that was said about the Passover in (Ex 12). We see from this God's mercy and flexibility in carrying out His commandments, for He seeks an excuse for those in special circumstances. This responsibility is carried out in the Church of the New Testament by the father of confession in guiding those in special circumstances.

entries.section: (2) Rulings concerning one who refrained from eating the Passover

paragraphs.text: But whoever was lax without any of the previous excuses that God mentioned, and did not take part in keeping and eating the Passover, that person will bear the result of his neglect and carelessness and is thereby exposed to the punishment of God, while the congregation of the people must cut him off and separate him, that is, put him away from itself, so that he is not of it any longer.

entries.section: (2) Rulings concerning one who refrained from eating the Passover

paragraphs.text: The stranger: the incomer who became a Jew, that is, not of the offspring of the tribes but who joined the people and was circumcised.
Born in the land: that is, a Hebrew Jew of the offspring of Abraham and Isaac.

God allowed every person who joined the people to share in the Passover offering with all its laws, even if he was a stranger who had joined, but he must first be circumcised ... for God in His love receives all, but faith and circumcision are required, as we say now that faith and Baptism are required.

Make allowance for those around you and do not be harsh in your judgments of them, and encourage them to live with God and to correct their errors, so that they come to love the spiritual life and love you.

entries.section: (3) The pillar of cloud and fire, and the journeying

paragraphs.text: The day that the tabernacle was reared up: when the tent of meeting was set up for the first time. The names are used interchangeably for the same thing: the tent of meeting is the tent of the testimony, and it is the tabernacle.

As one of the signs of God's love for His people and His tender care, the cloud, that is, the pillar of cloud, accompanied the people from their departure from Egypt until they reached the Promised Land. It guided them and shaded them, keeping the scorching sun from them, and when night came the pillar of cloud turned into a pillar of fire to give them light and guide them also.

On the day the Tent was first set up, God descended upon the Tent with His glory and blessing, and the cloud thickened and grew until it covered the whole Tent, and likewise at night the sight was awesome, for the pillar of fire enwrapped the Tent and went up from it and above it in the form of great glory (Ex 40). The pillar of cloud and the pillar of fire declare the presence of God in the midst of His people and His care for them, and they are a symbol of the mystery of the Incarnation and the union of divinity with humanity: the fire and the cloud signify divinity, and the material Tent signifies humanity.

entries.section: (3) The pillar of cloud and fire, and the journeying

paragraphs.text: Abode: came down.

God alone determined when the people would depart and when they would encamp, because He is their leader: "at the commandment of the Lord." The sign for that was the lifting of the cloud or its descending. If the cloud was lifted, the Levites began to take down the Tent for the journey and all the people followed them, and if the cloud abode again, the people also followed it and pitched their tents around the house of the Lord.

entries.section: (3) The pillar of cloud and fire, and the journeying

paragraphs.text: These five verses came as a confirmation and detailing of what was mentioned before in (vv. 19, 20), affirming in sum that whether the days were few or many, there was no journeying and no encamping except at the command of the Lord ... And in verses (21-23) it affirms again that even if the cloud was lifted for one day and then came down, the journeying would be for one day and the encamping for one day, and in all cases it was God who set the timetable and the people obeyed Him.

They kept the charge of the Lord: that is, as soon as they encamped they began to set up the Tent and begin worship at once, to complete the rites and offer the sacrifices as God had spoken before and made clear to Moses.

May we learn to commit all the affairs of our life to God, and leave to Him the ordering and the leading, and receive the blessing of obedience ... For all of man's problems begin when his will is separated from the will of God ... Be careful to pray and ask for God's good counsel before you begin any work.
The two silver trumpets and the people's departure from Sinai

entries.section: (1) The two silver trumpets and their use

paragraphs.text: In continuation of God's care for His people and His concern for the organization of their affairs, the Lord commanded Moses to make two trumpets of silver, and they were to be made by hammering and carving and not by casting, "of a whole piece." God made clear the first and basic purpose of making these two trumpets, which is communicating with the people and calling them and summoning them to journey or for other matters, as we shall see in the coming verses. It is also noted that the trumpets were spoken of earlier in (Lev 23). God commanded Moses to make two trumpets because there were only two priests, Eleazar and Ithamar the sons of Aaron. But later the number of priests increased greatly, so there were many trumpets: in the days of David there were seven trumpets (1 Chr 15:24) and in the days of Solomon there were a hundred and twenty trumpets (2 Chr 5:12).

entries.section: (1) The two silver trumpets and their use

paragraphs.text: If the priests blew both trumpets together, this was a sign summoning all the congregation of Israel to assemble before the door of the Tent for the announcement of something important.

entries.section: (1) The two silver trumpets and their use

paragraphs.text: But if they blew with one trumpet, this was a summons to the heads of thousands only, who are of course the chiefs supervising the heads of hundreds, the heads of fifties and the heads of tens, who were appointed to settle the people's problems as judges for them.

entries.section: (1) The two silver trumpets and their use

paragraphs.text: If the blowing of the trumpet was for the purpose of journeying, then at the first sound this was the signal for the three tribes of the east side to begin journeying, which are the tribes of Judah, Issachar and Zebulun.

entries.section: (1) The two silver trumpets and their use

paragraphs.text: The second sound was for the departure of the camps encamped south of the Tent, which are the camps of the tribes of Reuben, Simeon and Gad. Although the third and fourth sounds for the departure of the rest of the camps are not mentioned afterward, it is implicitly understood and the order of the journeying is known: the camps of the west were the third, then the camps of the north.

entries.section: (1) The two silver trumpets and their use

paragraphs.text: You shall blow (strike): that is, blowing the two trumpets with an ordinary, broken blast.
You shall shout: that is, blowing with a continuous, loud blast.

God distinguished between two ways of using the trumpets, each way used in a specific manner for a specific purpose. At the time of journeying the sound of the two trumpets is continuous, unbroken and very loud, so that everyone is alerted to the event of departure, and this method was called shouting. But if the sound was ordinary and broken, it was understood from it that it was to summon the congregation without their journeying, and this method was called blowing (striking) the trumpets.

entries.section: (1) The two silver trumpets and their use

paragraphs.text: The blowing was limited to the priests, who are the sons of Aaron and their offspring only, but at the feasts, such as the Feast of Shouting, the Levites proclaimed the feast by shouting with the trumpets among the people (Lev 23:23).

entries.section: (1) The two silver trumpets and their use

paragraphs.text: In your land: that is, the land of Canaan.
That oppresseth you: that attacks you.

God also commanded the use of the trumpets in a state of war. If circumstances compelled the people to war and to defend their promised land against their enemies, they were also to use the trumpets, and the purpose of this, besides alerting the soldiers and the people to war, was that it be a sign of prayer and of taking refuge in God, as shown by His saying "and ye shall be remembered before the Lord," meaning that when the Lord sees the people's recourse to Him He gives them victory over their enemies. And indeed the trumpets were used afterward in all the wars of the people, as happened with the walls of Jericho in the days of Joshua, and likewise the war with the Midianites in the days of Gideon (Judg 7:19).

entries.section: (1) The two silver trumpets and their use

paragraphs.text: The beginnings of your months: the start of the months.

The last of the matters in which the Lord asked Moses and the people to use the trumpets is the joyful announcement of the feasts and of the beginnings of the months of the religious year, which were also celebrated, and the trumpets were also blown at the offering of the sacrifices of the feasts and of the spiritual occasions.

They shall be to you for a memorial before your God: that is, these feasts and celebrations bear witness for you that you have kept the commandments of the Lord and done as He commanded, so that His heart is pleased with you and He blesses your feasts and your spiritual seasons.
The sound of the trumpets signifies the word of God that the Church teaches her people.

The trumpets have disappeared and have no use in Christianity any more, but in their place have come what is stronger than they, the prayers of the Church's Midnight Praise (Tasbeha), which the heart shouts before the mouth ... Have you ever taken part in the Church's Tasbeha prayers ... and have you meditated on the power of their spiritual meanings and the peace of heart they give to whoever repeats them and shouts them ... Do not let this matter pass you by, and try to begin with the simple, especially since they have become available on tapes and in the Arabic language as well.

entries.section: (2) The departure from the wilderness of Sinai

paragraphs.text: After eleven months and nineteen days that the people spent in the wilderness of Sinai, for their coming down to the wilderness was at the beginning of the third month of the first year (Ex 19:1) and their departure from it on the twentieth day of the second month of the second year, the cloud, that is, the pillar of cloud, was taken up from over the Tent, as a clear sign from God for the beginning of the people's movement.
As a summary of the events of this period we can say that the most important of its events were:
1- Seeing the glory of God when Moses and the chiefs went up to the mountain.
2- Receiving the Ten Commandments.
3- The numbering of the people, the firstborn and the Levites.
4- The setting up of the tent of meeting.
5- Receiving the rite of the sacrifices and the feasts.
6- The ordination of the priests and the setting up and consecration of the Levites for the service.

entries.section: (2) The departure from the wilderness of Sinai

paragraphs.text: The children of Israel left the wilderness of Sinai heading north, and after a journey of three days they reached the wide wilderness of Paran, in which they afterward spent 38 years. The wilderness of Paran is a wide wilderness that includes the middle of present-day Sinai and extends to the west of the city of El-Arish in the north, and passes beyond the Gulf of Aqaba, and merges with the wilderness of Zin ... See the map at the end of the book.

entries.section: (2) The departure from the wilderness of Sinai

paragraphs.text: They first took their journey: that is, they journeyed for the first time.

The first journey of the people began as the Lord commanded Moses and made clear to him the order of this journey in the second chapter (ch. 2:9 ...). The inspired text has shown us here the people's commitment and obedience to the order that God set, and has given us the detail of this journey in the following verses (vv. 14-28).

entries.section: (2) The departure from the wilderness of Sinai

paragraphs.text: In the first place went the standard of the camp: a figure for the journeying of the company bearing its standard (its flag). Host – hosts: that is, the strong men counted for war.
Rereward: the rear.
According to their hosts: according to the order of their company.
God already announced the order of this journey (ch. 2), so we shall summarize this journey here.

1- The journeying of the first group, which is the group of Judah and includes the three eastern tribes. The names of the tribes are mentioned, "Judah, Issachar and Zebulun," as are the names of the chiefs of these tribes.
2- The second group was of the clans of the Levites, the sons of Gershon and the sons of Merari, who carried the outer Tent without its inner contents and followed directly after the group of Judah.
3- The third group: this was of the southern tribes and included the camp or tribe of Reuben, then Simeon and Gad under the standard of Reuben.

4- The fourth group: this was of the third division of the divisions of the Levites, which is the division of the Kohathites, who carried on their shoulders, without wagons, the contents, furnishings and implements of the inner tabernacle such as the ark, the table of the showbread and the lampstand.
5- The fifth group: this is the camp of Ephraim, and it included the tribes "Ephraim, Manasseh and Benjamin," which were situated on the west side of the tent of meeting.
6- The last group: this is the group of the sons of Dan, and its three tribes are "Dan, Asher and Naphtali," which are the northern tribes, and this group was the rear of all the people.

Note: observe God's wisdom in the journeying of the Levites, in that He made them journey in two stages. The first stage (v. 17) is the journeying of the Gershonites and the Merarites, who carried the tabernacle and the heavy things (using the wagons), after the journeying of the tribes of Judah, and after their journeying comes the group of the tribes of Reuben before the group of the Kohathites who carried the light contents of the sanctuary (v. 21). This was so that God might give a span of time to the first group of the Levites to take down the Tent and set it up, so that when the others came they put its contents inside it.

entries.section: (3) Moses' conversation with Hobab

paragraphs.text: Hobab: he is the son of Reuel, that is, the brother of Zipporah the wife of Moses, and Reuel is the father-in-law of Moses; and likewise in the custom of the Arabs Hobab, the brother of Zipporah the wife of Moses, is also regarded as the father-in-law of Moses. The name Hobab means beloved.

Moses asked Hobab to accompany them on their journey in the wilderness so that he might receive the good things of God that He had promised them, since they were going to move from the wilderness of Sinai to the wilderness of Paran on their way to the Promised Land.

entries.section: (3) Moses' conversation with Hobab

paragraphs.text: Hobab's reply was an excuse because of the difficulty of leaving his land and his kindred, as is the case with many people who do not leave their homes for the unknown.

entries.section: (3) Moses' conversation with Hobab

paragraphs.text: Moses repeated his request, making clear this time his need for Hobab as a helper who knew the desert and the wilderness better than anyone, so that he would be to the people like the eye that sees and guides a man to his way. Hobab of course knew the terrain of the region better than anyone, that is, he knew the pastures and the springs of water, so he would be a guide for them in the wilderness.

This does not cancel Moses' faith that God is the true leader of His people by means of the pillar of cloud and the pillar of fire, but he encourages Hobab that he has a work and a service with them, which is guiding them to some springs of water on their way, although the basis is the water that flows from the rock and that the Lord God gives them.

entries.section: (3) Moses' conversation with Hobab

paragraphs.text: A repetition of the same offer that Moses made to Hobab in (v. 29), to share in the good things that God promised the people. No answer from Hobab is mentioned here, nor whether he went with them or not, although there is a reference to the going of the family of Moses' wife to the Promised Land in (Judg 4:11), and therefore it is most likely that he went with Moses.

Some saw in Moses a loving heart that does not forget a kindness, and, as the heart of a zealous servant, he wished to repay the favor to his wife's family by their sharing with him in the journey and then in the good things that God would give His people, and as a zealous servant he pressed his request more than once ...; do we too have this heart that calls and preaches to distant souls to share in the good things of Christ and the Church!!?

entries.section: (4) The ark goes before the journey

paragraphs.text: The mount of the Lord: that is, Mount Horeb in the wilderness of Sinai.
To search out a resting place for them: an expression meaning that God would guide them where to encamp.

Was the ark going before the people?...! According to the order that God set, the ark was carried by the Kohathites, who are the fourth group of the journeying groups, and consequently the ark would be in the middle, and this agrees with providing the greatest protection for the ark in case they met enemies on their way, so that the ark would not fall into their hands ... Consequently one can say that the expression "the ark before them" is a figurative expression like the prophet's saying "The Lord is before me" ... "The Lord is at my right hand," or we say the Lord is before us in this matter or the Lord is in our midst, and in all these linguistic expressions the intent is to bring out God's leadership and the people's following.
Note: some interpreters see that only in the first journey, and as an exception, the ark did actually go before them as an encouragement to the people and to reassure them.

entries.section: (4) The ark goes before the journey

paragraphs.text: As for the pillar of cloud, which signifies God's leadership, it went before the people to guide, and shaded them in divine care from the burning sun of the desert.

entries.section: (4) The ark goes before the journey

paragraphs.text: Ten thousands: ten thousand.

These two verses mention a prayer of praise that Moses used to repeat when the ark was lifted onto the shoulders, saying as the ark was lifted: Rise up, O Lord, and let all the enemies of Your people, spiritual or human, flee and vanish from before Your divine glory, for there is no place for whoever hates Your holy name and there is no one who can stand before You or challenge Your people who carry Your ark and Your holy name.

And when the ark was set down and rested in its place in the Holy of Holies, he used to repeat another prayer, also of praise to God, in which he says: Return, O Lord, and dwell in the midst of Your people, and bless the ten thousands and thousands of Your people Israel ... The Church took these words and prays them in the Litany of the Assemblies. As the priest turns toward the east he says "Rise up, O Lord" and let all Your enemies be scattered, and then the priest turns toward the west, that is, toward the people, and completes his prayer saying, "As for Your people, may they be, by blessing, thousands of thousands and ten thousands of ten thousands."

The ark went before the people, and it signifies God's dwelling in the midst of His people ... Do you let God go before your steps ... your thoughts ... your feelings ... your decisions ... If only you would do this with a praying heart, then God will always be with you as a guide and a close friend.
The punishment of murmuring - the manna and the quails

entries.section: (1) The first murmuring

paragraphs.text: Complaining evilly: that is, murmuring, and their murmuring was plain in their words or deeds.

The ears of the Lord: a rhetorical expression meaning that everything they complained of in a spirit of murmuring was before the Lord. We do not know here, and the cause of the murmuring is not mentioned ... perhaps it was because of exhaustion or some troubles from the hardship of life in the wilderness, but it meant that the people had forgotten all that God had done with them, and therefore this murmuring was evil, so the wrath of God came upon this people who denied all the good, and He allowed a fire to be kindled, regardless of its causes, and it burned the outer parts of the camp. We do not know the number of people it destroyed or the amount of the loss of animals or tents. We note that the murmuring began at the edge of the camp, that is, among those dwelling far from the tent of meeting, that is, nearness to the Church protects us from many sins.

entries.section: (1) The first murmuring

paragraphs.text: The people understood and felt that what happened was a divine punishment that came upon them, and therefore they went to Moses crying out and asking his intercession with God that He might lift His wrath from them. And indeed Moses went before God and entreated Him, asking Him to remove the punishment, and God answered and quenched the fires.

entries.section: (1) The first murmuring

paragraphs.text: So that what happened might become a memorial throughout the generations, Moses and the people called the name of this place "Taberah," which means burning, so that they might remember that murmuring angers the Giver of good things, and perhaps a person is punished for his murmuring with a punishment he cannot bear and cries out afterward for its removal from him.

Beloved, the life of true thanksgiving is what saves a person from falling into murmuring and spares him many punishments ... Thank your God every day for what He has done with you, and thank Him also for the evil He has kept from you.

entries.section: (2) The murmuring against the manna

paragraphs.text: The mixt multitude: they are the incomers (foreigners) among the people, and most of them were Egyptians who went out with them from Egypt.

The source of the murmuring this time was the Egyptian few who accompanied the people on their journey, but soon the rebellion and murmuring spread through all the people of Israel, and they declared their longing to eat various foods such as meat, fish and vegetables, like leeks, onions and garlic, and fruit such as melons, and in this they fell into a great fallacy, since they said "freely" although they were slaves forced into the service of Pharaoh ... This is what lust does to a person when it takes possession of him ... it makes him forget God entirely and all His kindnesses, and he no longer remembers anything but his need and what he lacks of fleshly desires.

entries.section: (2) The murmuring against the manna

paragraphs.text: The people expressed their murmuring by saying "our soul is dried away," that is, our bodies have grown weak and our freshness has gone, and we have become weary of the repeated eating of the manna, which we loathe and our eyes see nothing but it.

If you long one day for something, why do you not ask for it gently from your heavenly Father who gives to all and upbraids not!! ... But beware of murmuring against the divine graces poured out on you ... for there are many in the world who hope for the crumbs of bread left over from you. Beware of arrogance ... beware of murmuring ... lest God's grace be taken from you, for there is no gift without increase except that which is without thanksgiving, as St. Isaac the Syrian said.

entries.section: (3) The description of the manna

paragraphs.text: Coriander seed: small grains whose color is between yellow and slightly green. Bdellium: a kind of yellow gum inclining to white, with a pleasant smell, used like incense, and in the form of flakes.

So that the divine inspiration may show us how wrong the people of the children of Israel were in their murmuring, it makes clear to us what the manna is: it is the free divine gift from God who loves His people, and its appearance was like small yellow grains resembling coriander seeds and flakes of bdellium.

entries.section: (3) The description of the manna

paragraphs.text: Cakes: that is, bread baked on a flat stone, which is unleavened bread made on the hot stone in the desert (Gen 18:6). God sent it down at night with the dew, that is, before dawn, and the people did not sow it or toil for it, but all they did was gather it early, and they ground it and it became like flour and could be cooked or made into bread. Its taste was sweet, resembling the taste of cakes kneaded with oil, and its taste also like wafers made with honey (Ex 16:31), and the meaning is that because of the blessing of God the food was free and its taste was as though oil and honey had been put on it.

entries.section: (4) Moses' complaint and God's reply to it

paragraphs.text: As the people's murmuring increased and the lust for food took possession of them, it reached the point of weeping like children at the doors of their tents, that is, openly, and the murmuring spread from one person to another until it included all. As for Moses the servant and shepherd, his soul was greatly wearied and embittered by the state of the people, for he felt with his spiritual sense that what the people were doing greatly angered God and wounded Him. And when the soul of Moses overflowed and his pains increased, he turned to the Lord, raising his complaint and reproaching Him, saying "Wherefore have You dealt ill with Your servant," which is an unbecoming expression, because God never does ill to any of His children, but He who searches the hearts understood well what Moses wanted to say, and Moses' expression meant that the weight of the responsibility of shepherding this murmuring people was beyond his endurance.
I have not found favour in thy sight: You have not relieved me of the responsibility of leading the people and have not given me anyone to help me.

entries.section: (4) Moses' complaint and God's reply to it

paragraphs.text: Moses continues in his complaining prayer to God, going on in his groaning, expressing his weariness with his people, and he reproaches God, saying: why do You oblige me with the burden of the father and mother responsible for carrying their son to the Promised Land, when I did not give birth to this people.

entries.section: (4) Moses' complaint and God's reply to it

paragraphs.text: They murmur and weep to me asking me for meat, so from where can I provide them meat enough for them? This people has become a heavy load that I cannot bear alone.

entries.section: (4) Moses' complaint and God's reply to it

paragraphs.text: As the weariness of Moses the prophet increased, his soul became very distressed, so that he reached a degree of despair and depression in which he wished for death, and he expressed that by asking God "Kill me out of hand," and Moses regarded his death as a favor that God would do him, for by his death he would put an end to his misery and unbearable weariness.
We can draw some spiritual lessons from the position of Moses (vv. 10-15:)

1- Moses was the meekest of men by the testimony of God, but the hardness of the people and their murmuring together with the greatness of the responsibility made him weak and shaken, and the lesson learned here is that every person is liable to human weakness, however great his holiness.
2- Moses' recourse to God teaches us that there is no way to solve our psychological and spiritual problems except by prayer to God.

3- Despite the weaknesses and unexpected words that Moses' prayer carried, we also learn that he spoke with God frankly and his prayer carried all his true inner feelings, and for this reason God answered his prayer at once, as we shall see.
Take refuge in God in all your problems, however hard, and trust in His love, for He is able to give you rest and guide you, so that you walk assured and successful by His strength.

entries.section: (4) Moses' complaint and God's reply to it

paragraphs.text: The Lord did not reproach Moses and was not angry with him, for God knows perfectly the background of matters and appreciates what came from human weakness, especially since God Himself testified of Moses that he was meeker than all men (ch. 12:3), and this means that if any other person had been the leader of this people, he would not have endured, and his weariness and anger would have been many times more than Moses'.

But we find that God wanted to solve the problem for Moses positively by appointing helpers and counselors to help him in leading the people, so He asked him to choose seventy men and come to the tent of meeting. We note that God left the choice to Moses, but He also specified for him that these seventy be of the wise elders known to the people; and we note also that this tradition remained with the Jews after their settlement, so we know that the Sanhedrin council consisted of seventy men, and Christ also chose, with the twelve disciples, seventy apostles ...

entries.section: (4) Moses' complaint and God's reply to it
