paragraphs.text: I will come down: a human expression that God used to indicate that the events that will come are God's own will.

God continues His speech to Moses and says to him, when you gather with the seventy before the tent of meeting I will speak with you before them and I will give them of My Holy Spirit as I gave you, so that they too may be qualified to share with you in leading this heavy people.

If you are a servant or a person in charge, be careful to involve others with you, for distributing responsibilities lightens many burdens on you and raises up a generation of leaders after you, but you must choose the best, as the Lord commanded Moses.

entries.section: (5) The promise of meat and the coming of the Spirit of God upon the elders

paragraphs.text: God commanded Moses to command the people to sanctify themselves, and the sanctification was spiritual by repentance and bodily by washing their clothes and their bodies, and this sanctification always preceded standing before the Lord or receiving something great from Him.

The event that followed the sanctification was that God would give them meat to eat, for He had heard their murmuring, "ye have wept in the ears of the Lord," and their belief that slavery in Egypt had been better for them, and therefore God will give them what they asked, which is the eating of meat.

entries.section: (5) The promise of meat and the coming of the Spirit of God upon the elders

paragraphs.text: The eating of meat will be not for one day or several days but for a whole month, and they will eat of it greedily until it comes out at their nostrils, that is, its smell comes out of their noses as a result of the filling of the belly with this meat, and after that they will loathe it and abhor it from their eating too much of it, because of their rejection of the manna and their murmuring against God and their lust for eating meat.

entries.section: (5) The promise of meat and the coming of the Spirit of God upon the elders

paragraphs.text: Moses wondered at God's words, which seemed strange to him and hard to carry out, and he also expressed his astonishment in a manner that seems to us unexpected from Moses ... for he addressed God, saying: from where? and how? The number of footmen counted for war is six hundred thousand, apart from the rest of the people, so the total number of the people is more than two million. Would all the fish of the sea and all the sheep and cattle available suffice for them, and how can that be for a whole month?!!

entries.section: (5) The promise of meat and the coming of the Spirit of God upon the elders

paragraphs.text: God bore Moses' human weakness and the weariness of his soul, but He also rebuked him, that perhaps he might awake and examine himself: had he forgotten all that the Lord had done before in Egypt and during the crossing and at the receiving of the tables of the Law?! So He asks him "Is the Lord's hand waxed short?" that is, is there anything I am not able to do ... is My power unable to do anything?! But you will see soon My great power, and then you will realize whether My promises come to pass or not ...!

How long is Your patience, my God, with Your children ... What Moses said is unreasonable, and yet You humble Yourself and condescend to speak with him and converse with him and reproach him and rebuke him, but with patience and love. So You do with us also in many cases ... Forgive us, my God, our ignorance and continue Your mercies upon us.

entries.section: (5) The promise of meat and the coming of the Spirit of God upon the elders

paragraphs.text: The first scene ended, which was the speech and complaint of Moses to the Lord, and here we are before a new scene from which we understand that Moses had indeed chosen the seventy elders and they gathered around the Tent. When they gathered, the glory of the Lord was manifested in the form of a pillar of cloud and He began His speech with Moses, and the Lord God gave the seventy elders holy gifts, and as a sign of the coming of the Spirit of God upon them they prophesied. Prophesying here means that they uttered words and things they had had no knowledge of before, whether future matters or teachings and preaching to the people that they had not been able to do before.
But they did no more: that is, other gifts were not given to them, like the miracles that Moses performed, but the gift was limited to showing God's choice of them, so they only prophesied.

entries.section: (5) The promise of meat and the coming of the Spirit of God upon the elders

paragraphs.text: Two elders called "Eldad and Medad" of the seventy stayed behind and did not come before the Tent with the rest of the elders. We do not know the reason for their not coming, but perhaps it was their feeling of unworthiness. Despite their not coming and their remaining in the camp among the people, the Spirit of the Lord came upon them, and the sign of that was that they prophesied like the rest of the seventy.

entries.section: (5) The promise of meat and the coming of the Spirit of God upon the elders

paragraphs.text: Their news spread, and a young man came informing Moses that they were prophesying in the camp like the rest of the seventy. When "Joshua the son of Nun," Moses' first servant and closest disciple, heard, he was seized by jealousy for the honor of Moses, and felt that what happened with "Eldad and Medad" should not have happened to them, as they were the ones who stayed behind from God's and Moses' calling to them; so Joshua asked Moses whether he should go to them to prevent them, even by force, from prophesying.

entries.section: (5) The promise of meat and the coming of the Spirit of God upon the elders

paragraphs.text: The heart of Moses was different, and he reproached his disciple Joshua, "Are you jealous for my honor because these two elders did not listen to my word?! ... I (Moses) wished that the Spirit of the Lord would come upon all the people and they would all become prophets. This position shows us the breadth of the heart of Moses, which was distinguished from the narrower heart of his disciple, for the truly spiritual man rejoices in the filling of the Church of God with gifts and does not oppose them with a war of mistaken jealousy.

entries.section: (6) The sending of the quails and the punishment of murmuring and lust

paragraphs.text: After the end of God's speech with Moses, he and the elders returned to the camp, and afterward a strong wind blew from the south, that is, from the direction of the Red Sea, and this wind brought huge numbers of the "quail" bird and cast them upon the people sitting in the camp ... To know the size of the flocks of these birds that God sent to His people, the inspired text used the expression "as it were a day's journey on this side, and as it were a day's journey on the other side," and a day's journey is about 35 kilometers, because a person walks about 5 km an hour and walks about 7 hours a day, so a day's journey = 5 × 7 = 35 km, that is, an area 35 km in breadth around the camp on all sides, and this area is very large, so it contained flocks of quail enough and overflowing, far more than the need of the people.

It was also of God's care that He made the height of these flocks no more than one meter above the surface of the ground, "two cubits," so that the people could catch them and hunt them ... Most likely the quail bird is the migratory quail, which does indeed pass over the desert of Sinai.

entries.section: (6) The sending of the quails and the punishment of murmuring and lust

paragraphs.text: The people sinned greatly, for although God promised the people that meat would not fail for a month and that there would be more than enough for their need ... the people, driven by their lust and their lack of reliance on God's promises, continued all day and night and until the morning of the second day in hunting and gathering the quail with an eagerness and lust that were greatly exaggerated ... so that even the one who gathered least gathered of the birds what equals the load of ten donkeys, so they did not take only enough but took more for storing, and they "spread them out," that is, salted them and spread them around the camp.
Ten homers: the homer is a measure estimated at about 230 liters, and they used to estimate the homer by a donkey's load, that is, what a single donkey can carry.

entries.section: (6) The sending of the quails and the punishment of murmuring and lust

paragraphs.text: Greed, gluttony, unbelief of God's words and haste to store in large quantities were behind God's great wrath against His people, for instead of praying and thanking God for what He had done for them, they opened their greedy mouths to eat and fill their bellies.

God's stroke came strong, for before they finished their eating, that is, while the remains of the meat were still between their teeth, God punished them with a very great stroke, which most interpreters see as a painful plague of which many of the people became victims ... And since the people knew that this punishment was just and knew that its cause was the evil lust that had taken possession of them and made them murmur against God, they called the place where they buried their victims "Kibroth-hattaavah," that is, the graves of lust.

How evil is the sin of lust and what it brings upon a person, for it brought down David and destroyed the strength of Samson, and how great also was God's punishment of them ... Beware, beloved, of the lust of the flesh, which has humbled many.

entries.section: (6) The sending of the quails and the punishment of murmuring and lust

paragraphs.text: And from the place of burial of the victims of the lust of the flesh the cloud was lifted again, as a divine sign that it was necessary to journey again, and the pillar stood in a place called Hazeroth north of Mount Sinai, so the people encamped there and pitched their tents.
The leprosy of Miriam

entries.section: (1) Miriam's talk with Aaron

paragraphs.text: The Cushite woman: Cush was the firstborn son of Ham, and many tribes branched off from him, the most famous of which settled in Ethiopia, which was called by the name of Cush.

Gossip arose between Miriam, the sister of Moses, and her brother Aaron. The subject of the gossip was the person of the prophet Moses and the event of his marriage to a Cushite woman. It appears that they condemned him for marrying a woman after Zipporah, his first wife. The first reason for the condemnation was that she was of a race foreign to the people, and perhaps also because she was dark-skinned, like the descendants of Cush, whose complexion inclines from brown to black. This woman may have been one of the mixed multitude who came out of Egypt with the people, or from the tribes that met the people in the land of Sinai. From the context of the verse we find that Miriam, driven by the jealousy of women, was the one who began the conversation with Aaron.

Thus Moses was exposed many times to the murmuring of the people against him, and even those nearest to him, his own brothers, also murmured. But he endured with patience and calm, as Christ endured and was wounded in the house of those He loved, when those nearest to Him abandoned Him and His disciple betrayed Him.

entries.section: (1) Miriam's talk with Aaron

paragraphs.text: In this verse the divine inspiration shows us that the feeling of Miriam and Aaron was not pure, but that human jealousy lay behind it. In pride they claimed to be equal to Moses in standing, because the Lord had earlier spoken with Aaron, calling him to meet Moses at Sinai. They forgot that Moses was the one who held the calling, that he alone had received the Law, and that he had not cast a golden calf, as Aaron did, out of fear of the people.

And the LORD heard it: God hears everything and watches all our deeds, hidden and open. The expression “the LORD heard it” here is a prelude to the punishment the Lord was about to carry out afterward.

entries.section: (1) Miriam's talk with Aaron

paragraphs.text: Meek: calm, humble and long-suffering.

We conclude from this verse that the talk spread from one to another and reached many ears among the people, until it reached Moses himself, whom God describes as meek and calm above all the men that were upon the face of the earth. The meaning is that Moses was not disturbed and did not become angry at what his brother and sister said against him, but in largeness of heart he punished neither of them for what they had said.

Beware of condemning others, or even of listening to condemnation, for it is evil and the pride of the heart, and it brings you to account before God, so that He condemns you for all your faults and shows you no mercy. Cover the faults of others, make excuses for them and have compassion on them, and God will have compassion on you.

entries.section: (2) God's intervention

paragraphs.text: In the face of Moses' silence, humility and meekness, and his not answering the offense, God intervened and commanded that the three be brought to the tabernacle of the congregation. When they came, the glory of God descended in the form of a pillar of cloud at the door of the tabernacle, and the Lord called Aaron and Miriam, and they came forward before Him.

We notice God's swift intervention to defend His children. Although Moses was silent and endured, God hastened to declare his right and to rebuke his brother and sister, so that they might feel their sin and hasten to repentance.

entries.section: (2) God's intervention

paragraphs.text: The Lord began His speech to Aaron and Miriam by answering the talk that had passed between them, namely that they were equal to Moses in speaking with God! He proved to them that there is a great difference between any other human being and Moses, who was entrusted fully with the people of God and His house. God made this difference clear in the following:
1- When God speaks to any other prophet, whether from the people or one of the two of them, or wishes to convey something to him, visions or dreams are the means of dealing with him.

2- As for Moses, when God speaks with him, his position is higher than that of anyone else. He speaks with him mouth to mouth, as happened at the bush and on the mountain for many days, and now also from the Holy of Holies, from above the ark, so that he hears His voice like the voice of a man speaking with his friend. Indeed he also sees Him “apparently.” What is meant is seeing the phenomena that accompany the manifestation of the Lord and His speaking with him; see (Ex 33:10). God hides nothing from him, no “dark speeches,” and he saw things such as the fire and the light: “the similitude of the LORD shall he behold.”
It is as if God wished to say to them: Consider where you stand in all this. After this, do you dare to speak against My servant Moses, when you know how dear he is to Me?!

entries.section: (2) God's intervention

paragraphs.text: Departed: an expression meaning the end of the speech and the lifting of the cloud.

God's speaking with them at this meeting ended in a sad way, for the tone of the speech was one of rebuke. The greatest shock was that after the cloud was lifted and the speech ended, Miriam found herself leprous, white as snow, and the color of her skin was gone, and Aaron was astonished when he found her so. Perhaps God did not punish Aaron with the same punishment because he was not the one who began the talk, but only listened to his sister's gossip, and perhaps so that he could continue his priestly service.

Be at peace when many stand against you and wrong you, because your God looks at your endurance and your love for them, and defends you and shows forth your righteousness. Then you become a true image of God, and He blesses you and rewards you, even if after a while.

entries.section: (3) Moses' intercession for Miriam

paragraphs.text: Confusion and fear appeared on Aaron, and he besought Moses with contrition, addressing him as “my lord,” and entreated him to forgive them their fault, which was ignorance and folly, and to pardon them, so that God might remove His anger from them.

entries.section: (3) Moses' intercession for Miriam

paragraphs.text: Aaron likened his sister Miriam to one dead, not only because of the change in the color of her body and the possible loss of parts of it, but because she had become unclean and would be shut out of the camp and no one would touch her, like the dead whom no one touches. He also likened her to a child that has died in its mother's womb and has lost some of its members, so that it comes out dead and incomplete.
These comparisons show us two things:
1- Aaron's distress and fear at the situation.
2- The bad state of Miriam, with her leprous body.

entries.section: (3) Moses' intercession for Miriam

paragraphs.text: The loving, interceding heart of Moses could not bear the sight of his sister and Aaron's pleading. With overflowing feelings of love and fatherhood he stood before God, asking Him for pardon and healing. The expression “cried” shows the intensity and persistence of his prayer.

entries.section: (3) Moses' intercession for Miriam

paragraphs.text: The Lord answered Moses at once, in a swift response to his prayer, but He wished to make Moses understand His fatherly divine plan in disciplining and teaching His children, and so He explained it to him by a parable.
Any son feels great shame if his father punishes him by spitting in his face, and in his great shame he does not want to go out and be seen by people.
So I, God the Holy One, if I punish her, ought she not to be shut out from the people for seven days and then return to her normal life?

God in His perfect fatherhood also cares to discipline and chasten His children, “for whom the LORD loveth he correcteth” (Prov 3:12). God does not punish His children for all their sins, but only the very least of them, which, if God left it, might become a chronic illness in them. So accept God's chastening if you feel it, consider it a sign of love and care, and repent of your sin.

entries.section: (3) Moses' intercession for Miriam

paragraphs.text: After the punishment ended, which was her being shut out of the camp for seven days, Miriam returned to her place among the people, was healed, and God's forgiveness of her was declared. After that the people journeyed and left Hazeroth and went to the wilderness of Paran according to the command of the Lord, as was customary and as has already been explained, by the movement of the pillar of cloud and then its coming down in the new place.

Spying out the Promised Land (1) God commands Moses to send the spies (vv. 1-20) 1 And the LORD spake unto Moses, saying, 2 “Send thou men, that they may search the land of Canaan, which I give unto the children of Israel: of every tribe of their fathers shall ye send a man, every one a ruler among them.” 3 And Moses by the commandment of the LORD sent them from the wilderness of Paran: all those men were heads of the children of Israel. 4 And these were their names: of the tribe of Reuben, Shammua the son of Zaccur. 5 Of the tribe of Simeon, Shaphat the son of Hori. 6 Of the tribe of Judah, Caleb the son of Jephunneh. 7 Of the tribe of Issachar, Igal the son of Joseph. 8 Of the tribe of Ephraim, Oshea the son of Nun. 9 Of the tribe of Benjamin, Palti the son of Raphu. 10 Of the tribe of Zebulun, Gaddiel the son of Sodi. 11 Of the tribe of Joseph, namely, of the tribe of Manasseh, Gaddi the son of Susi. 12 Of the tribe of Dan, Ammiel the son of Gemalli. 13 Of the tribe of Asher, Sethur the son of Michael. 14 Of the tribe of Naphtali, Nahbi the son of Vophsi. 15 Of the tribe of Gad, Geuel the son of Machi. 16 These are the names of the men which Moses sent to spy out the land. And Moses called Oshea the son of Nun Jehoshua. 17 And Moses sent them to spy out the land of Canaan, and said unto them, “Get you up this way southward, and go up into the mountain: 18 And see the land, what it is; and the people that dwelleth therein, whether they be strong or weak, few or many; 19 And what the land is that they dwell in, whether it be good or bad; and what cities they be that they dwell in, whether in tents, or in strong holds; 20 And what the land is, whether it be fat or lean, whether there be wood therein, or not. And be ye of good courage, and bring of the fruit of the land.” Now the time was the time of the firstripe grapes. Introduction: The following section cannot be separated from what is in the book of Deuteronomy (Deut 1:21). God's command to the people was that they go up to the land and possess it, but the people asked Moses to send spies first, and Moses agreed with them. As a result of what the spies said and reported, the people murmured, even though they were on the border of Canaan, and the Lord was angry at their murmuring. Their punishment was that that whole generation was deprived of entering the land, and God allowed them to wander about thirty-eight years in the wilderness.

entries.section: (3) Moses' intercession for Miriam

paragraphs.text: A ruler: a man among the prominent and courageous of his tribe.

God commanded Moses to spy out the Promised Land by sending one man from each tribe, that is, twelve men, and this one was to be one of the rulers. This is of course different from the head of the tribe mentioned earlier during the numbering of the children of Israel (ch. 1). We understand from the book of Deuteronomy (Deut 1:22) that it was the people who asked God to spy out the land, and He allowed them to do so, so that they might know how good the land was and how strong its inhabitants were. God agreed to their request out of respect for their freedom, although this request was harmful to them, for they were deprived of entering, God was angry with them, and He made them wander in the wilderness for about 40 years.

entries.section: (3) Moses' intercession for Miriam

paragraphs.text: Moses sent them, as the Lord commanded, from the wilderness of Paran, which lies north of the wilderness of Sinai, while the place of the camp, that is, where the people were, was at Kadesh, which is part of the wilderness of Paran. The divine inspiration confirms that the most prominent men of the tribes were chosen, “heads of the children of Israel” (Map 1). Midian. Map (1)

entries.section: (3) Moses' intercession for Miriam

paragraphs.text: In the following verses (vv. 4-16) the man chosen for this great task from each tribe is mentioned by his name and the name of his tribe, as a record of the history of the children of Israel, and because God also remembers and does not forget anyone who has a work. We notice the following:
1- No one was chosen from the tribe of the Levites, since their work was limited to consecration for worship and guarding the house of the Lord.
2- The tribes are not mentioned here in the familiar order; perhaps God wished to indicate the equality of all before Him.
3- The first to be mentioned was “Shammua the son of Zaccur, of the tribe of Reuben.”

Caleb the son of Jephunneh (v. 6): one of the most famous figures. He is the only one, with “Joshua the son of Nun,” who encouraged the people, unlike the other ten spies. He is mentioned often afterward in the Holy Bible for his courage and strength, and he is also the only one, with Joshua the son of Nun, who remained of all the people to inherit in the new land.

Oshea the son of Nun (v. 8): he is “Joshua the son of Nun.” He was the closest disciple of Moses and the one who led the people after the death of Moses. Moses changed his name (v. 16) from Hoshea, meaning salvation, to Joshua, meaning Jehovah is salvation. He was of the tribe of Ephraim the son of Joseph, for it is known that Ephraim and Manasseh were counted as two tribes in place of Joseph their father. Joshua is the one who led the war against Amalek in the days of Moses (ch. 17:9).

entries.section: (3) Moses' intercession for Miriam

paragraphs.text: Returning to the mission, we find that Moses guides the spies in the routes they should take to reach the land of Canaan. He pointed with his hands, “Get you up this way,” southward. The south meant is the south of the Promised Land, that is, the south of Palestine. The phrase “go up into the mountain” means that they should not take the open road that everyone takes, so as not to expose themselves to discovery of their identity, but climb and then slip in. As for this mountain, its name is not mentioned; perhaps it was one of the mountains known to the people, or a high plateau in the south of Palestine.

entries.section: (3) Moses' intercession for Miriam

paragraphs.text: The task of the spying was to learn:
First: the nature of the land, meaning its terrain, roads, valleys and hills.
Second: the quality and number of the people. The concern was how strong the people were physically and militarily.
Third: how good and fertile the land was.
Fourth: the kind of dwellings, whether they were buildings and cities fortified with walls, or tents in the open.
Fifth: the goodness of the land, that is, the quality of its fruits.

Verse 20 indicates that it was the season when the grape harvest appears, and Moses charged them to bring some of the fruit of the land to the people, so that it might be an incentive for them to see the good things God had prepared for them. The three preceding verses show the wisdom of Moses as leader and manager of the people, and also show his instructions to the spies in defining their tasks.
When you meet any situation, ask God's help, organize your thoughts, and determine the steps required for the work, guided by those with experience, and you will reach the greatest success.

(2) The spying (vv. 21-25) 21 So they went up, and searched the land from the wilderness of Zin unto Rehob, as men come to Hamath. 22 And they ascended by the south, and came unto Hebron; where Ahiman, Sheshai, and Talmai, the children of Anak, were. (Now Hebron was built seven years before Zoan in Egypt.) 23 And they came unto the brook of Eshcol, and cut down from thence a branch with one cluster of grapes, and they bare it between two upon a staff; and they brought of the pomegranates, and of the figs. 24 The place was called the brook Eshcol, because of the cluster of grapes which the children of Israel cut down from thence. 25 And they returned from searching of the land after forty days.

entries.section: (3) Moses' intercession for Miriam

paragraphs.text: The spying journey took forty days (v. 25). Most likely the spies divided themselves into small groups, each group going to a different place and in a different direction, so as to keep suspicion away from themselves. The divine inspiration explains to us that they began their spying from the wilderness of Zin, which is north of the wilderness of Paran and is considered the southern entrance to the land of Palestine. They went north along the length of the land until they reached the farthest point in the north, the city of Rehob, which lies before the city of Hamath, a Syrian city; Rehob is considered the farthest northern border of Palestine (Map 2). The Dead Sea. Wilderness of Sinai. Map (2): The journey of the spies in Canaan.

entries.section: (3) Moses' intercession for Miriam

paragraphs.text: The spies crossed the south of Palestine and came to Hebron, which is Kirjath-arba, where Sarah, the wife of Abraham, died (Gen 13:18, 23:2, 35:27). They also passed by the tribes of Ahiman, Sheshai and Talmai, all of them tribes ascribed to the children of Anak. The children of Anak were tall in stature and among the strongest and most famous men of Canaan. As a historical note, the building of Hebron preceded the Egyptian city of Zoan by seven years (Ps 78:12, 13).

entries.section: (3) Moses' intercession for Miriam

paragraphs.text: Eshcol: a Hebrew word meaning a cluster.
Staff: a rod of wood or a pole.
Branch: a shoot or twig of the vine bearing a cluster.

The spies advanced north after Hebron, where they came to the brook of Eshcol, north of the village of Hebron. There, when they saw the goodness of the land and its fruit, they cut from its fruits a branch from a vine bearing a large cluster of grapes, and they also took some fruitful branches of pomegranates and figs. So that these fruits would not fall apart, they were carried on a wooden staff between two men.

entries.section: (3) Moses' intercession for Miriam

paragraphs.text: This verse mentions the reason the brook of Eshcol was given this name. The word Eshcol means a cluster, and because the spies took the cluster from this place, it was so called.

entries.section: (3) Moses' intercession for Miriam

paragraphs.text: The time of the spying was forty days, from the day they left Kadesh until their return a second time.

The spies were faithful in all that Moses charged them with. They went to the farthest border of the land in the north, examined everything, and brought Moses the fruit of the land. So be faithful in every work you are charged with, for the faithfulness of the children of God is a witness to Christ Himself in the midst of generations that do not walk in faithfulness.

(3) The spies' report to Moses and the people (vv. 26-33) 26 And they went and came to Moses, and to Aaron, and to all the congregation of the children of Israel, unto the wilderness of Paran, to Kadesh; and brought back word unto them, and unto all the congregation, and shewed them the fruit of the land. 27 And they told him, and said, “We came unto the land whither thou sentest us, and surely it floweth with milk and honey; and this is the fruit of it. 28 Nevertheless the people be strong that dwell in the land, and the cities are walled, and very great: and moreover we saw the children of Anak there. 29 The Amalekites dwell in the land of the south: and the Hittites, and the Jebusites, and the Amorites, dwell in the mountains: and the Canaanites dwell by the sea, and by the coast of Jordan.” 30 And Caleb stilled the people before Moses, and said, “Let us go up at once, and possess it; for we are well able to overcome it.” 31 But the men that went up with him said, “We be not able to go up against the people; for they are stronger than we.”

32 And they brought up an evil report of the land which they had searched unto the children of Israel, saying, “The land, through which we have gone to search it, is a land that eateth up the inhabitants thereof; and all the people that we saw in it are men of a great stature. 33 And there we saw the giants, the sons of Anak, which come of the giants: and we were in our own sight as grasshoppers, and so were we in their sight.”

entries.section: (3) Moses' intercession for Miriam

paragraphs.text: Brought back word unto them: presented a report.

Kadesh: its meaning is holy. It is Kadesh-barnea, and it was called in the book of Genesis En-mishpat (Gen 14:7). It lies in the south of Palestine, 50 miles south of Beersheba, and is an eleven-day journey from Mount Horeb. The tabernacle of the congregation was set up there, then they moved about in Sinai and returned to it at the end of the forty years, before entering the Promised Land.

The spies returned once more to Kadesh in the wilderness of Paran and presented a report to Moses, Aaron and all the people. This report included the accounts they told of the things they had encountered, and also a sample of the fruit of the land, represented by what they brought of grapes, pomegranates and figs.

entries.section: (3) Moses' intercession for Miriam

paragraphs.text: As for the oral report, its first part was reassuring and encouraging to the people, for the shortest and most eloquent description was that this land overflows with goodness, and this goodness is:
Milk: that is, an abundance of pastures and a plenty of cattle, so that milk was in very large quantities.
Honey: bees and their honey are found only in gardens and in vineyards fruitful with fruit, so the land is full of produce and fruit.
This expression the spies used, “floweth with milk and honey,” has become an expression used throughout all generations to describe any place in which goodness abounds and overflows.

entries.section: (3) Moses' intercession for Miriam

paragraphs.text: The second part of the report was terrifying to the people dwelling in the wilderness, for the spies described the cities as fortified with their walls, and the addition of the words “very great” gives a feeling of helplessness at storming them. As for the peoples, they are very strong, “strong.” The spies concentrated on mentioning the children of Anak, of terrible appearance, for they are men of war and all of them tall in stature. They then mentioned the number of peoples who would have to be defeated if they wished to possess the land, as if they were frightening the people by what they mentioned: in the south of Palestine the Amalekites, of the descendants of Esau, while the men of the mountains, who are usually fierce because of the mountain terrain, had these tribes:
The Hittites: the children of Heth, the second son of Canaan the son of Ham the son of Noah.
The Jebusites: they are also of the descendants of Canaan, and their place was present-day Jerusalem.

The Amorites: of the descendants of Canaan, and they were the strongest tribes of the region, so that at times they became a state and a people. The Canaanites: of the descendants of Canaan, who kept the name of the “forefather” of all the preceding lines, but they dwelt as a broad strip extending from the river Jordan in the east to the Mediterranean Sea in the west.
Because most of the inhabitants of Palestine were of the descendants of Canaan, it was anciently called the land of Canaan.

entries.section: (3) Moses' intercession for Miriam

paragraphs.text: Stilled the people: that is, he quieted the people and made them listen.
Before Moses: in another translation, “concerning Moses,” that is, he quieted the people in place of Moses.

The features of “Caleb the son of Jephunneh” as a leading figure began to become clear. He quieted the people and silenced them before Moses, and offered a positive opinion, that the people should go up with their hosts to this land because they were able to do so. He trusts in the power of God, so he did not fear the new land, its fortresses or its inhabitants.

It is noticed that he did not mention the name of Joshua here, although in (ch. 14:5-9) it is declared that Caleb and Joshua tried to persuade the people to trust in God, obey Him and enter the Promised Land. But only the name of Caleb is mentioned because he was the foremost in speaking. Joshua may have joined him a little later, or Joshua did not begin to speak lest it be said that he was partial to Moses because he was his disciple, and not out of conviction and faith in obedience to God.

entries.section: (3) Moses' intercession for Miriam

paragraphs.text: A land that eateth up the inhabitants thereof: a land in which war and plagues are frequent.

The opinion of the other ten spies was contrary to this, for we understand from ch. 14 that Joshua the son of Nun was with Caleb in his opinion and in quieting the people. They feared to go up to the new land and felt that the peoples there were stronger and mightier than they, and they began to speak of the evils of the new land, an “evil report,” among the children of Israel, so that they described it to the people as “a land that eateth up the inhabitants thereof...” Likewise most of its inhabitants and men were tall in stature, an indication that they were mighty and strong and that the Israelites could not fight them, so their destruction was certain.

entries.section: (3) Moses' intercession for Miriam

paragraphs.text: The spies continued to terrify the people, saying that they had seen the giants, the sons of Anak, who also come of the giants, so that their souls became very small, until they looked at themselves as grasshoppers before them... and they too, that is, the sons of Anak, looked at them as grasshoppers and as nothing.
By such words and others the spies went on frightening the people.

If we look at Satan and his armies and his wars, our strength and spiritual resolve would collapse... May we be like Caleb and Joshua, who put their hope in God and His power and not in the enemy and his might, for however great the forces of the enemy, the Lion that came out of the tribe of Judah, our Lord Jesus Christ, has overcome them by the power of His life-giving Cross. God's punishment of the fearful, murmuring people

entries.section: (1) The fear of the people and the encouragement of Joshua and Caleb

paragraphs.text: As a result of the bad report that the ten spies brought to the people, great fear, regret and anguish arose. Most of the people did not sleep that night, but came out of their tents in weeping, crying and wailing, and as usual they murmured and put all the blame on Moses and Aaron. This shows us how fickle this people was and how quickly evil spreads. Although they stood on the threshold of the land God had promised, in their great despair they wished that they had died in the land of Egypt or in the wilderness of Sinai, which would be better than facing these mighty enemies, the inhabitants of the land of Canaan.

v. 3 (with): Their murmuring and their lack of faith increased, despite the great miracles God had worked among them. They raised their murmuring to a level higher than Moses and Aaron, for they murmured against God Himself, and in a regrettable manner they criticized the wisdom of God and His plan. In their distress they said brazenly: Would it not be better for us to return and be enslaved in Egypt?! For obeying God, they said, means that we die at the hands of our enemies, who will take our children and our women captive.

entries.section: (1) The fear of the people and the encouragement of Joshua and Caleb

paragraphs.text: As the weeping, crying and murmuring spread and grew, some of them called out with a strange idea, which was to depose Moses and Aaron and appoint a new head over the people to lead them in their return to Egypt, forgetting that the true leader is God, who leads them through the pillar of cloud and guides them through His speaking with Moses. But this is how anger blinds a man from seeing the facts and the obvious.

entries.section: (1) The fear of the people and the encouragement of Joshua and Caleb

paragraphs.text: As for Moses and Aaron, they fell on the ground before God. This means their helplessness with the people and their taking refuge in God, so they humbled themselves before Him that He might bring them and this people through this critical situation.

Let us all beware of anger, its results, and the rising of agitation within us, for the wrath of man does not work the righteousness of God, but usually leads him to a folly of which he repents afterward. So let us take refuge in God by prayer when distress comes upon us, and leave the matter in His hand, confident that He always gives and does for us what is best.

entries.section: (1) The fear of the people and the encouragement of Joshua and Caleb

paragraphs.text: Rent their clothes: an act expressing grief, sorrow and severe distress.

Here we see another face and a positive direction of thinking. Joshua the son of Nun, together with Caleb the son of Jephunneh, stood facing the people, declaring their objection and their grief at what they had seen of the people, and they rent their clothes in grief and anger at and over this people who had forgotten all of God's previous work.

entries.section: (1) The fear of the people and the encouragement of Joshua and Caleb

paragraphs.text: Both of them began to speak and tried to persuade and encourage the people that this land, that is, the land of Canaan, is a good and wonderful land which cannot be left or given up. It is a land whose goodness overflows with milk and honey, as they had told the people before (ch. 13:27), and if God is pleased with them, He will give them this land as an inheritance for them and for their children.

entries.section: (1) The fear of the people and the encouragement of Joshua and Caleb

paragraphs.text: For they are bread for us: we shall defeat them, take their spoil and eat it as we eat bread.
This land will become ours and we shall defeat its peoples, because the Lord our God is with us and has delivered them to us, so do not fear anything.
Their defence is departed from them: an expression meaning that God has removed His protection from these peoples, and therefore it is easy to defeat them.

entries.section: (2) God's anger and Moses' intercession

paragraphs.text: The insolence and murmuring reached their height, and instead of listening to Joshua and Caleb, the faithful witnesses, the people turned the more against them and even demanded that they be stoned to death. When God saw all this murmuring, and even the attempt to kill Joshua and Caleb, He intervened swiftly and appeared in His glory in the tabernacle to all the people.

entries.section: (2) God's anger and Moses' intercession

paragraphs.text: The Lord began His speech with Moses, declaring His anger at the people and showing Moses the great evil into which they had fallen. The Lord showed His anger by using a hard expression, for He regarded what the people had done as an insult to His holy person. Their murmuring was unbelief in the power of God, or disbelief of His holy promises, and a lack of acknowledgment and thanks for all that He had previously done for them.

entries.section: (2) God's anger and Moses' intercession

paragraphs.text: God declared to Moses the punishment He was about to carry out, namely a plague He would send to destroy the people, and He would make of Moses and Aaron and the faithful among the people a new beginning for a new people, greater and larger in number, as He did with Noah before at the renewal of creation. For God in His justice does not include all in His punishment, but the sinners alone. As for those who were faithful and kept His covenants, God preserves them from the hard trial and does not punish them.

entries.section: (2) God's anger and Moses' intercession

paragraphs.text: Moses, the loving one, the intercessor and advocate for his people, began to plead and defend them, for it greatly troubled him that the people should be destroyed. Overcome by his love for his people, he spoke with God, saying: You have brought up, O my God, by Your strong arm this people from the land of Egypt, and You taught all peoples that You have become our leader and king and that You dwell in our midst. We, Your people, have seen You face to face, and we saw Your glory on Mount Horeb; You overshadowed us with Your cloud and led us by the pillar of cloud and the pillar of fire by day and by night.

entries.section: (2) God's anger and Moses' intercession

paragraphs.text: If it should happen that You carry out Your punishment by the destruction of this people, will not the Egyptians, and with them all the peoples who heard of Your previous works with us and then of Your chastisement of Your people, say that their God did not fulfill for them His promise, which He had promised, to bring them into the land, but on the contrary destroyed them and got rid of them in the desert?!

entries.section: (2) God's anger and Moses' intercession

paragraphs.text: Let the power of my Lord be great: an expression of praise and glorification of God and an introduction to what Moses is about to ask of God.

Moses gives God the glory, for He alone is almighty and in His hand are all judgments, and he reminds Him of His previous promises which He made with His people on the mountain and which are recorded in (Ex 34:6, 7).

entries.section: (2) God's anger and Moses' intercession

paragraphs.text: These words, which God had spoken before and which Moses uses here, are, as we have said, a review of what God said, namely:

The LORD is longsuffering: You have already declared, O God, Your mercies and Your long-suffering toward Your people, and we hold fast to this as a promise from You to us, and we now ask that it be fulfilled in us.
Forgiving iniquity: that is, You pardon Your people and forget their sin if they come to You repentant, which accords and agrees with the Master who is gracious and generous to His servants.

And by no means clearing the guilty, but visiting...: that is, God is also just in the case of the impenitence of His servants, for His wide and abundant mercies go side by side with His justice. The expression “the iniquity of the fathers upon the children” means that in many cases the children reap the result of the bad conduct of the fathers, like spendthrift fathers who squander their inheritance and leave their children in poverty, or hereditary diseases of which the wayward fathers are the cause for their children. But this saying is not absolute, as evidenced by the fact that God punished the people who sinned by not letting them enter the land, yet those under twenty years of age did not suffer the punishment but entered the land of promise. In sum, God declares the breadth of His mercies toward repentant sinners and the severity of His justice toward the refusing and the disobedient. What is meant also by visiting the iniquity of the fathers upon the children is the children's walking in evil like their fathers, so that He punishes them in His justice for their evils, which they acquired from their fathers and which extended through the generations.

entries.section: (2) God's anger and Moses' intercession

paragraphs.text: Moses continues in his entreaty and intercession with God for the people, and asks Him to have mercy on them and forgive their sin as His grace and divine salvation, regardless of whether this people deserves this forgiveness or not!! He also reminds God that this is nothing new to His fatherly heart, for He had already forgiven His people many times since their departure from the land of Egypt.

May we all possess this loving heart of the prophet Moses, so that we learn to pray for everyone, especially those who do wrong and those who are far away, and ask God's mercies for all. For one of the things that most rejoices the heart of God is that we pray for those who do wrong and those who are far away before we pray for ourselves.

entries.section: (3) The Lord's speech to Moses and the answer to his intercession

paragraphs.text: God's answer comes as very joyful to Moses, for He declares His forgiveness and pardon of His people. In His wonderful humility and His exalting of the accepted intercession of Moses, God says to him, “according to thy word.” What honor, then, belongs to the holy men of God! God forgives the people here for the sake of Moses' request, and again He shuts up the heaven so that it does not rain, as Elijah asked?!

entries.section: (3) The Lord's speech to Moses and the answer to his intercession

paragraphs.text: As I live: a form of oath and affirmation equal to the expression “I have sworn by Myself.”

God continues His speech with Moses, saying: Although I have answered your request for forgiveness, My glory, which fills the whole earth, also requires that I execute My justice. This verse is considered an introduction to God's sentence in the coming verses.

entries.section: (3) The Lord's speech to Moses and the answer to his intercession

paragraphs.text: As for God's justice, His judgment was as follows: the whole generation that had seen God's power and His lofty arm and how He brought them out of the land of Egypt would be punished by not seeing the land that God promised to their fathers, and they would not enter it and possess it. God gives as the reason this generation did not deserve this grace that they insulted Him greatly, having tempted Him ten times, and yet they murmured against Him. “Ten times” means many times, but literally also they tried Him in the ten plagues in the land of Egypt, and also ten times in different places, which we show here by mentioning ten occasions on which the people tried God and His power, though the meaning intended is that they tempted Me many times.
1- The killing of the firstborn of the Egyptians and the preservation of their own firstborn.
2- When they crossed the Red Sea and Pharaoh and all his armies pursued them (Ex 14:10-12).
3- Their murmuring because of the bitterness of the water at Marah and what the Lord did for them (Ex 15:24).
4- The worship of the golden calf when Moses went up the mountain and delayed coming back to them, and their punishment (Ex 32:1).
5- Their murmuring for food in the wilderness of Sin (Ex 16:2, 3).
6- Their murmuring again for meat (ch. 11:4-6).
7- Their murmuring at Taberah and their punishment by the burning of the camp at its outskirts (ch. 11:1-3).
8- The people's disobedience in keeping the manna until the second day (Ex 16:20).
9- The people's disobedience in gathering manna on the Sabbath day (Ex 16:27, 28).
10- And finally, their murmuring because of the words of the spies at Kadesh, the lofty (ch. 14:1-4).

entries.section: (3) The Lord's speech to Moses and the answer to his intercession

paragraphs.text: God excepts Caleb from these punishments, and of course Joshua the son of Nun, but Caleb was the foremost in speaking. God is just and does not forget here the stand of Caleb the son of Jephunneh, whose conduct and faith differed from the conduct of the people, “another spirit,” and because he followed God fully, He will bring him into the land and give him a portion in it and an inheritance for his descendants after him.

entries.section: (3) The Lord's speech to Moses and the answer to his intercession

paragraphs.text: The Amalekites dwell in the mountains and the Canaanites dwell beside the shores of the Mediterranean Sea. When the two, the Amalekites and the Canaanites, heard of the people of the children of Israel and their approach and the power of their God, they gathered in the valley in a state of preparation for war. Here God, in His love and fatherhood, warns the people against war and against meeting their enemies in the valley, and commands them to depart the next day into the wilderness, southward, in the direction of the Red Sea. Of course this command also agrees with God's punishment of the people and His intention that they not enter at this time.

If you refuse to obey God, you will deprive yourself of many blessings, and if you lose them you may not be able to make up for them. So seize every opportunity to draw near to God and enjoy His fellowship... Today is an opportunity to repent, to ask His mercies and to put away from you every evil.

entries.section: (4) The Lord's speech about His punishment and the death of the ten spies

paragraphs.text: The previous speech was directed to Moses alone, but here God directs the words to Moses and Aaron together. The words in the coming verses come as a confirmation of God's justice and judgment, and they make clear to Moses and Aaron the reasons for this judgment. He begins His speech in an interrogative form, in disapproval of what the people had done, and says “How long,” an expression that indicates the abundance of His previous forgiveness and His long-suffering toward them, and also indicates the necessity of disciplining them because of their many murmurings.

entries.section: (4) The Lord's speech about His punishment and the death of the ten spies

paragraphs.text: God affirms here, in the form of an oath, “As I live,” that He will punish them with the very punishment they brought on themselves when in the revolt of their murmuring they said, “would God we had died in this wilderness” (v. 2). “In mine ears”: an expression God used, from which we all understand that everything a man says and utters with his tongue, or everything he thinks in his heart, is heard in the ears of God.

Take heed, beloved, and ask yourself: is everything you say, and God hears, pleasing before Him? And if it is not, you must take care and be precise, lest you bring wrath and anger upon yourself. Habit in words of thanksgiving keeps a man away from the circle of murmuring.

entries.section: (4) The Lord's speech about His punishment and the death of the ten spies

paragraphs.text: I lifted up my hand: an expression of the promise or oath that God promised to His people.

God's judgment was that everyone of the people over twenty years of age, that is, an adult and aware of what he says, would not enter this land but would die in the wilderness. God exempted from this punishment the two courageous spies, Joshua the disciple of Moses and Caleb, who spoke before the people to strengthen their resolve.

entries.section: (4) The Lord's speech about His punishment and the death of the ten spies

paragraphs.text: Likewise God also exempts those under 20 years of age, of whom the children of Israel had said that they would be a prey, captives and slaves to the Canaanites... They alone will enter this land and inherit it, know its goodness and excellence, and enjoy what the children of Israel despised. As for the rest, they will not be able to do any of this, for they will die in the wilderness.

entries.section: (4) The Lord's speech about His punishment and the death of the ten spies

paragraphs.text: Your whoredoms: your rebellion, your revolt and your murmuring.

However, the punishment will include your children also, in a measure, for because of your murmuring and your revolt your children will go on wandering in the wilderness for forty years instead of enjoying it now, until the whole present generation, those over twenty years of age, is consumed. God fixed the forty years on the ground that, since the days of their spying out the land came to forty days, the punishment for each day would be a whole year in which the people pay the price of their murmuring and know God's anger against them and His not walking with them and His distance from them. The exile of the children for 40 years in Sinai teaches them the heinousness of the sin of rebellion and its evil results, so that they obey God all their life.

entries.section: (4) The Lord's speech about His punishment and the death of the ten spies

paragraphs.text: The Lord affirms in this verse that everything He has spoken is irrevocable, describing His people, whom He regarded as a son and firstborn, as an evil people and a sinful congregation that conspired against its King and Father, “gathered together against” Him, rejecting His authority and not trusting in the power of His arm, which is able to destroy their enemies.

entries.section: (4) The Lord's speech about His punishment and the death of the ten spies

paragraphs.text: Made all the congregation to murmur: they made the people doubt and shook their faith in God.

As for the ten spies who caused the people to stumble, made them doubt and terrified them out of entering the land, God's judgment on them was swift and collective, for a plague struck them and the ten spies died because of their stumbling-block. As for Caleb the son of Jephunneh and Joshua the son of Nun, the punishment did not include them, for the just God gives every man according to his deserving.

There are people who are a source of stumbling, who weary the simple by their talk and gossip, perhaps about the Church or various matters, and there are also people who are a source of blessing and peace. Their words are few, but effective and useful for edification. So which of the two groups are you?!

entries.section: (5) The people's regret and defeat

paragraphs.text: The people listened to the words of Moses and felt their grave fault, for which they deserved God's punishment, and the people expressed their regret by their weeping. They wanted to atone for their fault by going up and fighting the Amalekites and the Canaanites, but they did not understand the Lord's purpose in their punishment and did not heed His warning about their enemies (v. 25).

entries.section: (5) The people's regret and defeat

paragraphs.text: Moses, the faithful shepherd and spiritual man experienced in the wisdom and purpose of God, warned the people not to do anything without God's command, for everyone who relies on his own thought and understanding without the divine plan will not succeed in it. In his warning he added that God was not with them and not in their midst in this war, and therefore they would not be victorious. He added that their enemies the Amalekites and the Canaanites were on alert and prepared for them, carrying their swords, that God would not intervene and would not protect His people from their enemies, and that their fate would be to be killed by the sword because of their fault and their turning back from God.

entries.section: (5) The people's regret and defeat

paragraphs.text: In pride and stubbornness the people did not listen to their leader and went up to meet their enemies without Moses, the guide, and without the ark of the covenant, which represents the presence of God. Since the people acted with folly and rashness and did not listen to the voice of their spiritual father, the Canaanites and the Amalekites, who were lying in wait for them on the mountain, came down on them, fought the people and inflicted on them the worst defeat and rout.

And discomfited them, even unto Hormah: Hormah is a place in the south of Palestine on the border of Edom, and it was called Hormah because there the Amalekites devoted them to destruction, that is, killed them.

Obedience to the spiritual father in the sacrament of confession is a duty, for the One speaking in the sacrament is the Holy Spirit. So do not be stubborn and harden your heart, lest you lose the blessing of obedience and the blessing of God Himself.
On the offerings of sacrifices, sins of ignorance and of presumption, and other laws

entries.section: (1) Offerings of sacrifices

paragraphs.text: The land of your habitations: that is, the land of Canaan, which will be given to the people.

After the punishment of the people and their turning once again toward the wilderness and the Red Sea, God begins His speech with Moses anew, renewing to them His promise to bring them into this land, and He affirms that He will give it to them in the end despite the many peoples who dwell in it. After punishing them, He returns and encourages them that He will bring them in, that is, will bring their children, into the land of Canaan. These are the laws which they will fulfill there, where they will sow the land and have wheat, oil and wine in abundance, since in the wilderness they had been living on manna and did not sow.

entries.section: (1) Offerings of sacrifices

paragraphs.text: Make an offering by fire unto the LORD: an expression meaning “offer your sacrifices to the Lord.”
Freewill offering: a voluntary sacrifice offered as an expression of love for God.

This verse is an introduction to verses 4-11. In this verse He begins by mentioning the kinds of animals offered in the various sacrifices, as a preparation for the accompanying offerings that would be required of them with these sacrifices.

entries.section: (1) Offerings of sacrifices

paragraphs.text: A tenth deal: 2.3 liters.
The fourth part of an hin: 0.950 liter.

Everyone who offers the animal of the sacrifice, his “offering,” to God before the tabernacle must also offer a “tenth deal” of flour mingled with oil, and the amount of oil with which the flour is mingled is the fourth part of an hin. As for the wine that was poured on the sacrifice or the altar, its measure is also the fourth part of an hin.
Note: the purpose of these offerings was to teach the people the following:
1- That everything we offer to God is from the good with which He has blessed us.
2- The pouring out of wine signifies joy, and God accepts nothing from a man unless he offers it to God with joy of heart.
3- Wine also signifies the blood of Christ, which was shed on the wood of the Cross and gave salvation to the whole world.
4- The pouring out of wine also signifies the giving of sweat and blood and striving in order to enjoy salvation and the Kingdom of Heaven.

entries.section: (1) Offerings of sacrifices

paragraphs.text: The previous offering accompanied the ordinary lamb. As for the ram, which is the large male sheep distinguished by its large horns, the offerings accompanying it, of fine flour mingled with oil and wine poured out, were somewhat more: the flour became double and the drink offering became a third part instead of a fourth.

entries.section: (1) Offerings of sacrifices

paragraphs.text: If the sacrifice is a bullock, that is, a son of the herd, the flour offering is increased to three tenth deals and the wine offering to half an hin.
Offering made by fire: an indication that these offerings are offered on the altar.
A sweet savour: that is, what a man offers to the Lord with pleasure, God also accepts with pleasure and favor.

entries.section: (1) Offerings of sacrifices

paragraphs.text: These two verses come as a review of all the preceding verses concerning the earlier offerings. He returns and mentions the names of the animals again and affirms that each sacrifice has its own offerings, which usually correspond to its size.

entries.section: (1) Offerings of sacrifices

paragraphs.text: God makes the native, that is, the one of Hebrew origin, equal to the stranger in the offering, for the offering to God is not tied to nationality or color but to the sacrifice, and this is a type of Christ, in whom all are equal. The stranger meant here is of two kinds:
1) The mixed multitude: that is, the Egyptians who came out with the people from Egypt.

2) “Among you”: that is, the peoples who lived among them, such as the Gibeonites in the days of Joshua the son of Nun, with whom peace treaties were made, and who intermarried with the people and became part of them.

entries.section: (1) Offerings of sacrifices

paragraphs.text: These two verses are a review and confirmation of what preceded, that the law of the preceding offerings is an everlasting and eternal law, from which neither the stranger nor the guest is excepted.

The idea of offerings and gifts to God has been dwindling in people's minds, since everyone is content with tithes only. But when we offer more than the tithes with joy, what we offer is a sweet savour presented to God, and He accepts it with joy... And do not forget that everything we offer is from the gifts of God to us.

entries.section: (2) The offering of dough

paragraphs.text: God renews His speech to the people, as He did in (v. 2), about the laws that follow after their dwelling in the land which He will give them. The expression “when ye eat of the bread of the land” means that they had settled, sown the land and reaped it, and had wheat and flour from which they made their own bread, and therefore they had to heave, that is, to offer to the Lord, a “heave” offering.

entries.section: (2) The offering of dough

paragraphs.text: This offering was that a man should offer to God the first cake of dough that he had leavened for making wine.
The threshingfloor: the place where the wheat is separated from the ears.

What is meant is that the first quantity of wheat to come out of the threshingfloor, enough to make a cake of bread, a man must take, grind and knead, and offer as a firstfruit directly from the floor to God before taking bread for himself.

entries.section: (2) The offering of dough

paragraphs.text: Here He affirms the importance of offering firstfruits. In this verse God repeats to them the necessity of offering the first of the dough to the Lord, and the priests and their households used to eat it (Neh 10:37).

If you feel that everything you receive in life is a gift from God, it is natural that you should share with God in enjoying these gifts by offering Him their firstfruits, so that His needy brethren may rejoice with you.

entries.section: (3) The offering of sacrifices for sins of ignorance and of presumption

paragraphs.text: Ye have erred: you have forgotten, or your failure was unintentional.

God speaks to the people through Moses, telling them that if a failure should occur on the part of the whole people in any of the commandments or laws of worship that God gave to the people, and this was because of forgetfulness and not on purpose, then they must hold to everything that follows, throughout all their generations, to atone for this error (see Lev 4). From the day that the LORD commanded: that is, since you received the commandments and the laws.

entries.section: (3) The offering of sacrifices for sins of ignorance and of presumption

paragraphs.text: Ignorantly: without the knowledge of the congregation.

Of course the people had to make amends for this error, even if it was by oversight or unintentional, so the people offer from their possessions two sacrifices, one of them a sin offering, which is a he-goat, that is, a male goat. When the sin offering is offered and God accepts their amends, they then offer a burnt offering, which is a bullock, for a sweet savour to God, as a collective gift from the people to the Lord.
Note: the bullock is mentioned before the he-goat, perhaps because of its higher price than the goat, but the goat was offered first, for the due apology comes before the gift of reconciliation.

When we sin it is not enough to offer our apology to God only in words, or merely to abstain from sin, but we must also grow in virtue and the spiritual life, such as prayer and reading the Holy Bible.

entries.section: (3) The offering of sacrifices for sins of ignorance and of presumption

paragraphs.text: When the people did this, that is, offered the sin offering and the burnt offering, God forgave them their sin and made allowance for them because this sin was by oversight. The compassionate God has pity on and takes account of human weakness, but man must offer repentance and apology in all cases. God makes clear that His forgiveness and pardon include all the people, the Hebrews and also the rebellious strangers who dwell with them or who came out with them from the land of Egypt.
An offering made by fire unto the LORD: the expression “made by fire” is used with the burnt offering only because it was burned entirely as a sweet savour to the Lord.
Second: the sin of ignorance of the individual:

entries.section: (3) The offering of sacrifices for sins of ignorance and of presumption

paragraphs.text: A she goat of the first year: that is, a year old.

But if one person falls into a sin of ignorance, and not the whole people, he too must draw near to God with repentance in order to atone for his sin, so he offers a sacrifice of redemption for himself from the mature goats (a year old). The atonement took place by taking the blood of the sacrifice and pouring it out at the bottom of the altar to be burned, which is a clear indication of the blood of Christ shed on the Cross, without which no atonement for man's sins takes place (see Lev 4). God did not except the stranger sojourning among the people from this law, and there is a beautiful spiritual meaning in this: when a guest comes to stay with one of us, we should not indulge him at God's expense, but rather he should submit to our order, our prayers and our fasts, and we should encourage him to do so, instead of our being led along with him.
Third: sins of presumption:

entries.section: (3) The offering of sacrifices for sins of ignorance and of presumption

paragraphs.text: Doeth ought with an high hand: that is, commits its sin deliberately.

God in His justice distinguishes between what a man does by oversight or from human weakness, on the one hand, and the evil he commits with audacity, full will and prior planning, that is, premeditation, on the other. God regards deliberate sins as a direct contempt of His holy person and of His word and commandments, and therefore the punishment here is proportionate to the offense and also severe: the punishment was cutting off. Cutting off here means that this person is set apart and driven out from the congregation of the people, and his fate is in the hand of God according to His wisdom and judgment. To show the gravity of the offense, God affirms a second time, “shall utterly be cut off,” and that the iniquity of this soul is upon him, the one who committed his sin with awareness and full planning.

We do not know what happened afterward, whether this soul was received again if it repented or not, but the story of the prophet David assures us that God does not reject a repentant heart forever but receives it with His wide mercies. There is no sin without forgiveness except the one without repentance. But we must also guard with all care against despising the dignity of the holy God by doing evil with indifference or deliberately.

entries.section: (4) The Sabbath-breaker

paragraphs.text: Right after the speech about sins of presumption and what they represent of contempt for God and disdain or disregard of His commandment, an incident comes here that confirms that God does not tolerate the deliberate sinner. The divine inspiration here tells us the story of a man who broke the commandment of the Sabbath and did not sanctify it, for he went out of his tent and began gathering and breaking up some sticks on the Sabbath day.

entries.section: (4) The Sabbath-breaker

paragraphs.text: Ward: confinement.

When some of the people saw that, they took him and brought him to Moses and Aaron before all the people. Since Moses and Aaron did not know what to do with him, because this was the first time a man had broken a Sabbath, they put him in confinement so that Moses might have the opportunity to ask the Lord about him.

Ask God's counsel before any work, however great your experience or position, as Moses did not rely on his own understanding but asked God. Then God will guide you, bless you and protect you from many troubles.

entries.section: (4) The Sabbath-breaker

paragraphs.text: When Moses asked the Lord, the punishment came decisive and deterrent. The sentence was that he be put to death by stoning outside the camp, and that all the people take part in stoning him.
In this incident the following is noticed:
1- There was no injustice in the punishment, for the man broke one of the important Ten Commandments and so deserved the punishment.
2- This man insulted the dignity of God, did not care about obeying Him, and departed from the custom of all the people of his nation.
3- He did not learn from the previous punishments that God brought on His people when they disobeyed.
4- He did not heed the previous warning that every soul that commits sin deliberately is cut off from its people.
5- He was extremely brazen and impudent, for he dared to commit this sin in the middle of the day.
6- The punishment had to be a deterrent so that all the people would fear and such an event would not be repeated, and the people would learn that God is jealous for His glory.

entries.section: (4) The Sabbath-breaker

paragraphs.text: In great fear and awe the people obeyed God's command and carried out the punishment on this man. It was a lesson no one forgets and a practical teaching that the days do not erase, that God's commandments must be respected, and that despising them means death and destruction.

entries.section: (5) Making fringes and ribbons for garments

paragraphs.text: After one of the people dared to despise God and broke the Sabbath, forgetting His commandment, God asked Moses to command the people to make a memorial set before their eyes that would make them always remember the divine commandments. This memorial was as follows:
Fringes: a group of threads forming a tuft, like the button of a tarboosh, or what is called in colloquial speech (tassels). Borders: ends.
Ribband: a band placed above the fringes, blue in color, one of whose purposes is to fasten these fringes.

God asked the people to be committed to making fringes on the borders of their garments, and these fringes hang from a piece of cloth of the color sky-blue, that is, blue, as a symbol that the various laws and commandments, “the fringes,” have their source in the blue heaven and that the whole Law is heavenly.

entries.section: (5) Making fringes and ribbons for garments

paragraphs.text: The purpose on seeing these fringes is to remember the heavenly Law and that a man's eyes should stay on God's commandments, so that his heart does not stray after its desires to the right and to the left, and likewise the eyes are fixed on the divine commandments and see nothing but God and His judgments.

God uses material memorials so that we do not forget His teachings. He reminds His children of the pot of manna and the Passover and many things so that they do not forget His work with them, and He still reminds us in the New Testament through the rites of the Church so that we abide in His love. But unfortunately some are occupied with appearance rather than essence, like the Pharisees, who cared for these ribbons and fringes and left the love of God and mercy, and Christ rebuked them (Mt 23:4, 5).

entries.section: (5) Making fringes and ribbons for garments

paragraphs.text: As a result of a man's eyes being fixed on the commandments and his zeal to fulfill them and to please the heart of God, he becomes holy and set apart for God.

entries.section: (5) Making fringes and ribbons for garments

paragraphs.text: At the end of God's speech with His people, He reminds them that He is their only God, who loosed their captivity and brought them out of the land of Egypt with a strong arm to be a God to them and that they be a people to Him, but on condition of their holiness and their remembering His commandments.

Note: Jews in many parts of the world still wear these fringes, whether on religious occasions or in their daily life. They wrap their waists (their loins) with a piece of light blue cloth ending in these fringes, to declare their adherence to the commandments of their God.

My beloved brother, the Cross has become for us a memorial set before our eyes that reminds us not only of God's commandments but of His love and redemption of us all... Set your eyes on the Cross and you will receive help and strength from your remembering the love of Christ for you, so that sin will not prevail over you and will have no authority over you, but you will tread it down with the authority of the children of God.
The murmuring of Korah, Dathan and Abiram

entries.section: (1) The rebellion against Moses and Aaron

paragraphs.text: Korah was the son of Izhar, and Izhar was the brother of Amram, the father of Moses and Aaron; therefore Korah was the cousin of Moses and Aaron. He was the ringleader of the rebellion and the sad events that followed. There shared with him in this rebellion, from the tribe of Reuben, Dathan, Abiram and On. However, On is not mentioned afterward in the events of the rebellion and murmuring, and so it is likely that he withdrew, turned back and repented after first taking part in the revolt. The tents of the Kohathites were beside the tents of the Reubenites, and perhaps this helped them to agree on the revolt against Moses and Aaron. Korah demanded the priesthood because he was of the tribe of Levi and a cousin of Moses, while the Reubenites, who were the descendants of the firstborn, demanded the leadership of the people in place of Moses, in addition to making the priesthood general among all the tribes. They were followed by two hundred and fifty men (v. 2) of the princes or leaders in the various tribes. All demanded the priesthood, and perhaps they were demanding the return of the priesthood to every family, so that its head would be the priest, as it was before the age of Moses.

entries.section: (1) The rebellion against Moses and Aaron

paragraphs.text: Princes of the assembly: that is, among the most famous people at the level of the nation.

Famous in the congregation: that is, men of standing, who are summoned to attend the important assemblies of the people. Korah and those with him (v. 1) gathered with two hundred and fifty of the most famous personalities of the people and men of standing, “men of renown.” This verse makes clear that this alliance had only one purpose, which was to resist Moses and Aaron.

entries.section: (1) The rebellion against Moses and Aaron

paragraphs.text: The motive of this murmuring was jealousy, malice and envy, and therefore Korah and those with him could not hide their feelings, and they confronted Moses and Aaron with the words “.. Ye take too much upon you.” What is meant is: enough of this distinction and this exaltedness and this position that belongs to you two. God is available to the whole people, and He is the One who dwells in the midst of the congregation and sanctifies it, and we have no need of a mediator or a priest. Any one of us can do the work that you two are doing.

entries.section: (1) The rebellion against Moses and Aaron

paragraphs.text: Moses was grieved and greatly disturbed by what he heard, and he prostrated himself before the Lord, “fell upon his face,” taking refuge, complaining and humbling himself that God might intervene in this grave matter, which was liable to divide the people and scatter their unity.

entries.section: (1) The rebellion against Moses and Aaron

paragraphs.text: After this submissive and humble prayer and prostration before God, Moses spoke with Korah and his company, saying that the judgment and the choice belong to God alone. He is the One who decides whom He chooses for His service, and the one whom God chooses He brings near as priest to Himself. Moses also asked Korah and all his company to come the next day before the Lord carrying their censers, imitating the priests who carry censers of incense before God. Perhaps they had censers that they used in their family worship before the descent of the law of Moses, when the head of the family was its priest.

entries.section: (1) The rebellion against Moses and Aaron

paragraphs.text: Moses also asked them to light their censers when they came the next day and put incense in them to offer before God, and God is the One who decides whether He accepts their offering of incense or not. The expression “Ye take too much upon you,” ye sons of Levi, expresses Moses' displeasure at their stand, and he knows that they are deceived by Satan and are asking for what is not theirs and what God did not allow. By sons of Levi he means Korah and those of the tribe of Levi who follow him.
Among the important spiritual lessons we draw from the preceding verses:
1- The enemy of good may use the nearest of relatives, “the cousin,” to fight a man, and then the war is dangerous and very embarrassing.
2- We also learn that the war of jealousy, if it is not suppressed in its cradle, takes control of a man and his feelings, and his later actions expose him.
3- The spiritual man, facing a fierce war, finds no solution except to prostrate himself before God, humbling himself that He may deliver him.
4- How sweet it is for a man to empty himself and leave judgment and retribution to God the Almighty.

entries.section: (2) Moses' attempt to calm the rebellion

paragraphs.text: Moses spoke first with Korah and his followers of the tribe of Levi, trying to contain the crisis and give them counsel. He addressed them, saying: Why this rebellion? Did God not choose you apart from the other tribes, distinguish you, and give you the honor of serving His house and its contents apart from the others? This is a very high honor, and yet with all this you were not content, but dared to ask for the service of the priesthood which God assigned to Aaron and his sons alone.
