What you are doing now is a transgression of the divine order and purpose.

entries.section: (2) Moses' attempt to calm the rebellion

paragraphs.text: Moses here draws the attention of Korah and his followers and warns him that what he is doing is murmuring, objection and revolt against God Himself, and not against Aaron, who has nothing in his hand except that he carries out the divine ordinance that God had already declared.

entries.section: (2) Moses' attempt to calm the rebellion

paragraphs.text: After speaking with Korah and the Levites, Moses, the faithful servant, wished to do the same and counsel Dathan and Abiram of the tribe of Reuben, so he called them to meet him. But they proudly refused to meet him, declaring strongly their hatred and malice and their insistence on demanding the priesthood.

entries.section: (2) Moses' attempt to calm the rebellion

paragraphs.text: Their reply was devoid of all decency and courtesy, and went beyond this to sheer impudence. Their reply to Moses was: Have you forgotten that you are the cause of our coming out of a land of good things, “Egypt,” and have brought us to the barren wilderness of Sinai in order to lord it over us as a ruler instead of Pharaoh? Of course their words were pure slander, for Egypt was a land of humiliation, slavery and forced labor. Their words also show their rebellion and their forgetting of the strong hand of God in the ten plagues and the parting of the sea. This was also blasphemy, because God did not bring them out to make them die but that they might inherit the land of promise, which flows with milk and honey; but because of their many murmurings God punished them by postponing their entry into this land.

entries.section: (2) Moses' attempt to calm the rebellion

paragraphs.text: Dathan and Abiram continue their objection to answering Moses' invitation to speak with him, saying, in the form of an accusation against Moses, that he had not fulfilled what he promised either: where is the land with its fields, its goods and its vineyards...? They put a question to Moses, “wilt thou put out the eyes of these men?!” The meaning is: can you blind this people so that it does not see the truth of the bad state we are in in the wilderness? You, then, are the cause and the one responsible for all this, and therefore we will not come up to talk with you about anything.

entries.section: (2) Moses' attempt to calm the rebellion

paragraphs.text: Moses was very displeased at the words of Dathan and Abiram, and instead of entering with them into a fruitless argument, he lifted his heart to God and prayed, asking that God not regard the offering of these rebels. He addressed God, saying: You know, O my God, that I am innocent of all their false accusations, that I have not wronged any of my people, and that I have not taken from these rebels anything, not even one ass.

entries.section: (2) Moses' attempt to calm the rebellion

paragraphs.text: Since Moses found no benefit in this last attempt at counsel, he asked Korah and all those with him in his revolt to gather the next day, with Aaron also, before the Lord, and that every man take his censer lit and carry incense to offer before God. He specifies that the number of men taking part in this rebellion was two hundred and fifty men.

We take from Moses a wonderful example in facing problems. Moses was wronged in all the false accusations directed at him, which no man could bear, but in all his affairs he turned to God in prayer. We too may be wronged, and an unexpected war may face us that shakes our being, but we have nothing but the closet on which to rely and from which to receive our help. God, who hears our prayer in secret, rewards us openly, shows forth the truth and gives us comfort.

entries.section: (3) Standing before God and the divine retribution

paragraphs.text: In pride and incitement, Korah did not gather only the two hundred and fifty, but gathered with them very many of the people, “all the congregation.” The two hundred and fifty stood carrying strange fire and incense in their censers, while the fire of Aaron's censer was holy. When all the congregation gathered, the glory of the Lord appeared to all, most probably in the form of the pillar of cloud.

entries.section: (3) Standing before God and the divine retribution

paragraphs.text: The Lord spoke with Moses and Aaron and commanded them not to stand in the midst of the congregation but to get away from it, because God was determined to destroy them. Despite the disobedience of Korah, we find the heart of Moses, the intercessor for his people, speaking with God again and asking Him to forgive them, asking God not to take the sin of one man and repay all the people for it, because the evil of the people was far less than the evil of the one who incited them.

entries.section: (3) Standing before God and the divine retribution

paragraphs.text: After this intercessory prayer of Moses, we find that the Lord answered him and commanded him to counsel the people to move away from the crowd and the gathering around Korah, Dathan and Abiram, and that the congregation not even approach their dwellings.

entries.section: (3) Standing before God and the divine retribution

paragraphs.text: Wicked men: the unjust or the tyrants.

In (v. 12) Moses asked Dathan and Abiram to come up to him and speak with him, and despite their refusal he here goes himself to the place where they lived and takes with him some of the elders of the people as witnesses. At the command of the Lord he addressed all the congregation dwelling beside the tents of Dathan and Abiram, calling on them to leave the whole area and not to mingle with them or touch anything of the belongings of Dathan and Abiram, so that they might escape the divine anger and the retribution that would come swiftly.

entries.section: (3) Standing before God and the divine retribution

paragraphs.text: The people responded to the call of Moses and moved away, and all the household of Dathan and Abiram also came out of their tents, from the greatest to the least, and each stood outside his tent at its door.

entries.section: (3) Standing before God and the divine retribution

paragraphs.text: In the strength of a servant confident in his God, Moses began to speak, saying to all the congregation: If these men, that is, Dathan and Abiram and all who belong to them, live a natural life and also die a natural death, then I am not a prophet or one sent from God to you. But if the Lord makes a new thing and the earth opens and swallows up all these into it, this will be the strong sign of their wickedness and the fitting punishment for what these men did in despising the Lord and exalting themselves against Him.

entries.section: (3) Standing before God and the divine retribution

paragraphs.text: Moses had hardly finished speaking when the earth indeed split as he had said, in a frightening and terrifying scene, and swallowed up Dathan and Abiram and all their households, as well as all the possessions of Korah and his family. However, Korah was not among those who perished in this scene, as we shall see later in (v. 35).

entries.section: (3) Standing before God and the divine retribution

paragraphs.text: Closed: shut.

When they went down into the depths of the earth alive and it closed again, and as the cries of their voices rose when they went down, the whole congregation of the people was afraid and fled far away, as a kind of psychological reaction to this very terrifying scene, and they said to themselves: Let us flee far away, lest the earth swallow us up also.

entries.section: (3) Standing before God and the divine retribution

paragraphs.text: As for the second scene, which was before the tabernacle of the congregation, where Korah and the two hundred and fifty men were gathered with their censers, who wanted to seize the priesthood for themselves in foolish jealousy, the punishment of the Lord was also severe on them, for a fire came out from the Lord and burned them alive. Of course there was also a great fear among the people, like the earlier fear when the earth opened and swallowed up the living. Korah was burned with these men, as is mentioned in (ch. 26:10), but the sons of Korah feared God and did not walk in the disobedience of their father, so they escaped the divine punishment, as is mentioned in (ch. 26:11). Holy men appeared from the sons of Korah, such as the prophet Samuel (1 Chr 6:28) and Heman the psalmist (Job 6:33), and this confirms that whoever obeys God escapes His wrath and is even blessed by Him with many blessings.

Moses combined the loving heart that intercedes for its people with the decisive leader in the face of wrong, especially wrong directed at God and His worship. So is the faithful servant and priest: his heart is wide with love and sympathy for all his people, but in what concerns the rights of God, the faith of the Church and the order of its worship and rite, he neither yields nor neglects, because he is entrusted by God with all these.

entries.section: (4) Beating out the censers

paragraphs.text: The Lord gave Moses a new command, which was to tell Eleazar the priest, the son of Aaron, to gather the censers that remained after all had perished in the fire and to scatter the dust and ashes remaining in them. God makes clear that, despite the error of these men, these censers had been hallowed by the fire coming out from God and burning them.

entries.section: (4) Beating out the censers

paragraphs.text: Sinners against their own souls: that is, those who sinned and thereby brought punishment on themselves. God commanded Moses to beat out these censers for a covering of the altar of burnt offering, because they had been hallowed by being offered to God. It would be a sign to the children of Israel, a memorial never to be forgotten, of what the rebels, the leaders of the rebellion, had done and how their end came. Eleazar did exactly as Moses commanded him.

entries.section: (4) Beating out the censers

paragraphs.text: Stranger: one of the common people, but not of the descendants of Aaron, who was called to the priesthood.

God makes clear again here the purpose, that this covering of brass on the altar is to be a warning memorial for the children of Israel, that no stranger come near and dare to offer incense before the Lord, lest his end be like the end of Korah, to whom Moses spoke and who took no heed and did not listen to his words.

Remember your great sins into which you fell long ago and which God forgave you, so that you may humble yourself before Him, take care of your repentance every day, guard against these sins, and strive to acquire the virtues opposed to them.

entries.section: (5) The people's murmuring against Moses and Aaron and God's punishment of them

paragraphs.text: Despite the clear gravity of the sin of rebellion before the eyes of all the people, they fell into murmuring against Moses for the death of Korah and those with him, forgetting that this was the justice of God and their necessary recompense.

entries.section: (5) The people's murmuring against Moses and Aaron and God's punishment of them

paragraphs.text: Facing this new revolt, Moses and Aaron found no protection from the evil of the people except taking refuge in God and standing at the door of the tabernacle of the congregation. The glory of the Lord came down again, and the sign of this was that the tabernacle was covered with the cloud.

entries.section: (5) The people's murmuring against Moses and Aaron and God's punishment of them

paragraphs.text: The scene was repeated, with almost the same dialogue as in (vv. 21, 22). God asked Moses and Aaron to get away from the congregation until the murmurers were consumed, but we find Moses again prostrating himself before God with his brother Aaron, as a sign of submission on the one hand and an entreaty for divine pardon and forgiveness on the other.

entries.section: (5) The people's murmuring against Moses and Aaron and God's punishment of them

paragraphs.text: Moses knew that God's judgment on the disobedient of His people this time was a deadly, destructive plague that leaves a man only dead. With the same fatherly heart that has pity on the folly of his people, he quickly asked Aaron to take holy fire from the altar and go out with it to all the people and pass among them between their tents, and offer atonement for the people so that God would remove His wrath and stop the plague. Indeed Aaron did exactly as Moses commanded him, put on incense, and prayed an atoning prayer for the people. The word “ran” shows how hasty Aaron was in carrying out the command to stop the plague.

entries.section: (5) The people's murmuring against Moses and Aaron and God's punishment of them

paragraphs.text: When Aaron went down among the people, he stopped the spread of the plague, so that the sick who were dying were on one side and the living, whom Aaron protected, on the other. Aaron stood with his censer between the dead and the living, in a beautiful picture that makes his priesthood, his prayer and his incense a barrier that prevents the evil of the punishment of sin from reaching the rest of his people. We see that God answered this priestly, intercessory work, so the plague stopped and spread no further, and there appeared before all the people the greatness of the priesthood and its effectiveness in protecting from death, this priesthood confined to Aaron and his sons. So they honored the priesthood and feared God, Moses and Aaron.

entries.section: (5) The people's murmuring against Moses and Aaron and God's punishment of them

paragraphs.text: The price of sin was heavy and the loss great, for the number who died in the plague because of the second murmuring was fourteen thousand and seven hundred, while those who died in the first punishment were Korah, the two hundred and fifty, and the households of Dathan and Abiram.

entries.section: (5) The people's murmuring against Moses and Aaron and God's punishment of them

paragraphs.text: This chapter ends by declaring the end of the sad events and the return of things to their first state after the plague was lifted and Aaron returned to Moses, who had remained standing, awaiting the mercies of God, at the door of the tabernacle.

My beloved brother... how evil it is for a man not to accept God's warnings and punishment, but to persist in his disobedience and murmuring, and so bring on himself a punishment worse and graver than the first. So be quick to return and repent, and go to your father the priest in repentance to receive God's mercies and pardon, instead of continuing in evil, lest there come upon you a divine wrath that you cannot bear.

Introduction to Aaron's rod and the rods of the tribes: After the events of the preceding rebellion and God's punishment of the murmurers, God wished to give a sign to His people by which to prove the distinction of Aaron and his priesthood from the rest of the tribes.

entries.section: (1) The choosing of the rods and their placing in the Holy of Holies

paragraphs.text: The Lord gave Moses, in speaking with him, a new command, for a reason He will explain to us in (v. 5). This command was to take a rod from each tribe, so that the total of the rods of the tribes was twelve rods. God also commanded that the name of the head of each house, representing his tribe, be written on his rod. It was known that each tribe had a head like those heads who helped in numbering and counting the people, as mentioned in the first chapters of the book.

Each of the heads carried a rod as a sign of his headship of the tribe, in addition to using it to lean on. Most likely the rod of Aaron was a branch of an almond tree, as was the custom. Note: the tribes were twelve tribes apart from the tribe of Levi, and so there are two opinions on this matter, which we thought it honest to present:
The first opinion: that twelve rods were gathered from the tribes, and the rod of Aaron was the thirteenth for them.
The second opinion: that the twelve rods also included the rod of Aaron, and that the tribes of Manasseh and Ephraim shared one rod on which the name of their father Joseph was written.

entries.section: (1) The choosing of the rods and their placing in the Holy of Holies

paragraphs.text: God affirms that Aaron, through his priesthood, became the head and prince of the tribe of Levi, and therefore his name is written on the rod that represents his tribe.

entries.section: (1) The choosing of the rods and their placing in the Holy of Holies

paragraphs.text: God then commanded that all the rods be placed in the Holy of Holies before the ark of the covenant, which contains the two tables of the testimony on which the Ten Commandments are written.
Where I will meet with you: that is, in the place before which Moses stands when God speaks to him as a representative of all the people.

entries.section: (1) The choosing of the rods and their placing in the Holy of Holies

paragraphs.text: What God wanted by all this was that He would declare His choice by a miraculous act and a sign at which all would marvel, namely that one rod out of all the rods presented before God would blossom and put forth green leaves or fruit like any living branch not cut from a tree, which is impossible for a dry rod.
The rod that budded, in which life stirred after death, would belong to the man whom God chooses, apart from all others, to have the priesthood, he and his descendants alone.
I will make to cease from me: I will stop, prevent and nullify the murmurings of the children of Israel.

God regarded the murmurings of the people against Moses and Aaron as murmurings against His own blessed person, so He once said “from me” and also said “against you.” God makes clear here that He is a partner with His faithful servant in everything, and in divine humility God regards every insult directed at His servants and priests as directed at His divine self.

entries.section: (1) The choosing of the rods and their placing in the Holy of Holies

paragraphs.text: The heads of the tribes responded to God's request and gave their rods to Moses after their names were engraved on them, and the rod of Aaron joined them. Moses laid all the rods before the Lord as commanded, awaiting what the Lord would declare of His choice of the man set apart for the service of the priesthood.

God intervenes to support His children in difficult situations with many kinds of support. He declares His responsibility for the service of His children, to encourage them to serve Him faithfully while He completes what they lack. So be zealous, my brother, for the service of God, that you may experience His work in you and rejoice in His fellowship.

entries.section: (2) The budding of Aaron's rod

paragraphs.text: Buds: small shoots that grew from the buds.

On the very next day Moses went in before the Lord to find himself before a wonderful miracle, for the rod of Aaron had put forth buds and full blossoms and ripened almonds. Moses took all the rods and went out to the heads of the tribes gathered at the door of the tabernacle, and each of them took his own rod, which he knew, with his name engraved on it.
In the budding of Aaron's rod many miracles appear:
1- A dry rod cannot give blossoms and fruit, for it is dead and cannot give life after its death.
2- The rod gave branches, buds, blossoms and fruit, which are the different stages of a plant that do not come together at one time but in stages.
3- The choosing of one rod, the rod of Aaron, apart from the rest of the rods.

entries.section: (2) The budding of Aaron's rod

paragraphs.text: Because Aaron's rod became a symbol of God's miraculous work and a clear sign of His choice of Aaron, Aaron did not take back his rod, but God commanded Moses to keep it in the Holy of Holies, so he placed it inside the ark of the covenant (Heb 9:4), that it might be a permanent sign and testimony before the eyes of the rebellious people, so that they would not return again to their former murmurings or transgressions, and these murmurings would not become a new cause of their destruction.

God in His fatherhood to His people and His care for them, despite their many murmurings, wished to give them a memorial so that they would not return to their evil and He would be compelled to punish them... Do you too keep memorials of God's works in your life, so that you do not forget His kindnesses and give thanks for them?... How evil it is for a man to forget and murmur, so that his punishment is great. And remember, my brother, that a man's pride and constant discontent are behind the sin of murmuring and what it brings upon him.

entries.section: (2) The budding of Aaron's rod

paragraphs.text: Moses carried out the Lord's command and left Aaron's rod in the Holy of Holies.

entries.section: (2) The budding of Aaron's rod

paragraphs.text: Feelings of fear mingled with grief and regret among the people, and the people spoke, broken before the death and destruction that had come on Korah, Dathan and Abiram, those who followed them in the rebellion, and those whom the plague destroyed afterward. They offered repentance before God and said that they had learned a hard lesson, the price of which was that we were all exposed to perishing, and this lesson is that we should not stand again before the house of the Lord, for everyone who comes near this tabernacle with boldness and rebellion, like Korah and the two hundred and fifty men, perishes utterly. The people said this in grief and brokenness, but what they uttered was also far from the reality, because destruction did not come on one who wished to stand before the house of the Lord, but on the few who murmured against God and His priesthood and wanted the priesthood to belong to all, thereby breaking what God Himself had ordained. As this chapter ends, we wish to pause a little before the miracle of Aaron's rod, for the meanings and symbols it carries:

1- The Incarnation: Aaron's rod first signifies Christ, for He is the life that came out of the dry ground (the Jewish people), as Isaiah prophesied and said, “For he shall grow up before him as a tender plant, and as a root out of a dry ground”
(Isa 53:2), that is, the Incarnation of Christ and the appearing of God from the midst of humanity condemned to death.
2- The Cross: for the Cross is the dry wood that gives life to everyone who holds fast to it, since in it is the power of the crucified Redeemer.
3- The Resurrection of Christ: where Christ rose alive from the dead like the budding of the dead rod.
4- The coming forth of life from the dry wood is an indication of the Gentiles' acceptance of the faith, for the living faith came forth from dead idolatry.

5- Aaron's rod also signifies the Virgin Lady, who without any human planting, sowing or watering conceived and bore the Son of God, the Word incarnate, and for this reason we pray in the Midnight Praise and say, “What is the rod but Mary, for she is the type of her virginity..”

6- The coming forth of life from death fills our hearts with hope when facing difficult and distant souls, for how many souls were dry and refusing and became believers, even fruitful servants in the Church of God.

Introduction to the obligations and rights of the priests and Levites: This chapter moves us to the priests and the Levites. It speaks in general about their responsibilities in guarding the tabernacle, that is, the house of God, then speaks about the material rights of the priests and Levites, and the obligation to pay the tithes of the Levites and the priests.

entries.section: (1) The duties of the priests and Levites

paragraphs.text: Shall bear the iniquity: you will bear the results of your faults before Me and their consequences.

This time God spoke with Aaron directly, as high priest, because all the speech concerns him and the Levites with him. The beginning of the speech with him was decisive, for God reminds him of his basic and important responsibility. He and all his descendants after him have become responsible directly before Him for two things:

First: the sanctuary. This means their responsibility to oversee all the affairs of the service in the house, inside and outside, such as cleanliness and order, preventing anyone of the people from touching the holy things, and also keeping all the ordinances and rites as the Lord delivered them to Moses and Aaron.

Second: your priesthood. The responsibility also includes their keeping watch over their conduct and being careful in all they do, so that no stumbling block comes to the people from their shepherds and leaders. The expression “shall bear the iniquity of your priesthood” is an expression that carries the form of a warning more than the form of counsel or guidance.
In sum, they are responsible for:
1- Guarding all the contents of the house of the Lord.
2- Being careful in offering worship according to the commands of the Law.
3- Guiding the people and preventing them from wrong against the house of the Lord.
4- The good conduct of the priests, that they may be an example to the people in their relationship with God and in their whole life.

entries.section: (1) The duties of the priests and Levites

paragraphs.text: God also charges Aaron, who represents the priesthood, not to be proud toward the rest of the Levites of his tribe, who signify the deacons, but that the relationship between them be a relationship of connection, support and completeness. For the service in the end is one service in its two parts, whether the priesthood or the service of keeping and carrying. This teaches us that in the service, regardless of the difference of our positions, each of us needs the other.

entries.section: (1) The duties of the priests and Levites

paragraphs.text: The Levites likewise are to be a guard and protection for Aaron in his own person and for his priestly descendants after him against any assault or attack by the people, and they also guard the whole tabernacle against any intrusion or damage. But they must also know their limits and not transgress them by entering the sanctuary or the Holy of Holies or touching any of the vessels of the service, lest both Levites and priests be exposed to the penalty of death for transgressing what God ordained for the affairs of the service and the determination of duties within the tabernacle.

entries.section: (1) The duties of the priests and Levites

paragraphs.text: The stranger: that is, anyone of the common people other than the tribe of Levi.

God repeats and affirms to Aaron what He had said before, to show all the seriousness of the matter. He adds here that one of the tasks of the Levites is also that no individual of the people other than the tribe of Levi come near the tabernacle, otherwise the divine wrath would include the whole people of the children of Israel. God also repeats that the care and service of the outer and the inner altar belong to the priests alone.

entries.section: (1) The duties of the priests and Levites

paragraphs.text: God repeats for the third time what He had said, which increases the awe of this matter on the soul, but this time He adds something new and shows us a new spiritual concept, that God is the One who chooses His servants by His grace and calls them to serve His vineyard, that is, His Church. So the Levites gained a special honor and a distinguished position. Because of the distinction and majesty of the priestly service, God gave the Levites to the priests as helpers, but the priests must also care for the dignity of the grace they have received, “keep your priesthood,” and this means:
a) Caring for the ritual worship as God delivered it to them.
b) Caring for their own life and general conduct, for they are an example to all the people.
c) That no one other than the priests enter the sanctuary, and no one other than the high priest enter the Holy of Holies, which is beyond the veil.

My beloved brother, you may be a servant or a deacon whom God has called to serve His house. Do you realize the measure of this honor and this calling? Do you also care for your service and not neglect or treat it lightly? Do you keep all that God ordained or the Church established of rites and order of worship? You are responsible before God, so do not forget this!!!

entries.section: (2) The priests' rights from the offerings of the people

paragraphs.text: The charge of mine heave offerings: a portion of the sacrifices offered to My name, for the heave offering is the sacrifice lifted up to God.
By reason of the anointing: that is, as a wage and portion for the service of the priesthood.

God speaks here with Aaron and shows His care for every servant who serves Him. He says to him: I have given and granted you, that is, all the priests, portions of the sacrifices offered to Me and to My name from all the offerings of the children of Israel, whether vows or sacrifices required to be offered. It is as if God wished to say to the priests: in return for your service and your consecration to Me, you have become partners of My table and you eat from My portion that is offered to Me.

entries.section: (2) The priests' rights from the offerings of the people

paragraphs.text: This shall be thine of the most holy things: an expression meaning that what you will receive is considered most holy, since you will eat of what is offered to the Lord Himself.

Heave offerings: everything lifted up from the sacrifice to be offered to God, which is the breast and the right shoulder (Ex 29:28). The right of the anointing: the right of the anointing of the priesthood, that is, the rights of the priests.

The priests have a portion of all the offerings presented to the fire of the altar, whether sin offerings or trespass offerings offered to God, and it becomes a holy portion and due for them and for all their generations. The details of this came in the book of Leviticus (ch. 4-7).

entries.section: (2) The priests' rights from the offerings of the people

paragraphs.text: In the most holy place shalt thou eat it: of course what is meant here is not the place of the Holy of Holies, which it is forbidden to enter except once a year on the Day of Atonement and by the high priest alone, but eating it in a clean and holy place. The usual place where the priests ate of the sacrifices was the outer court of the house of the Lord, and those who ate of these sacrifices were the priests and their male children only.
It shall be holy unto thee: that is, it shall become a portion for you.

entries.section: (2) The priests' rights from the offerings of the people

paragraphs.text: From the sacrifices there were other portions that the priests took to their homes for their women to eat, which are some parts of the peace offerings, such as the shoulder of the sacrifice or its breast, which were offered by “waving” before the Lord. The divine inspiration added the words “by a statute for ever” to be sure that this applied to the whole line of the priesthood throughout the days, as long as the Levitical priesthood stood, and was not limited to Aaron and his family.

entries.section: (2) The priests' rights from the offerings of the people

paragraphs.text: Wine: the wine.
Wheat: the grain.

The portions of the priests also included “all the best,” that is, the best of what is offered of oil, wine or grains of wheat from the firstfruits of the people. Everyone who offered his firstfruits to the Lord, the Lord gave them to His priests. These firstfruits also included the fruits and produce of the land, which the priest takes to his house to eat with his family.

entries.section: (2) The priests' rights from the offerings of the people

paragraphs.text: Every thing devoted in Israel: the devoted thing is what a man forbade to himself and gave to the Lord in the form of a vow or property or the like, and every devoted thing becomes the portion of the priests.

entries.section: (2) The priests' rights from the offerings of the people

paragraphs.text: The firstborn of man and of animals were offered to God, as is stated in (Ex 13). God replaced the firstborn of men with the tribe of the Levites and chose them for service and consecration. If the number of the firstborn exceeded the number of the Levites, the firstborn was redeemed with a sum of money of five shekels of silver, or a hundred gerahs, because the shekel is 20 gerahs (see ch. 3:46). The firstborn of all clean animals was given to the priests, while the firstborn of unclean animals, such as the ass, had its blood not brought to the altar, but its offering was replaced with another offering, such as a sheep, and if it was not redeemed it had to be killed.

entries.section: (2) The priests' rights from the offerings of the people

paragraphs.text: But the firstborn of clean animals, such as cattle, sheep or goats, must be offered, and nothing can be offered in place of them, because they are set apart and chosen by the Lord, that is, He set them apart and hallowed them for Himself, so they cannot be replaced, but their blood and fat must be offered on the altar for a sweet savour as the Lord commanded, while the flesh belongs to the priests. This is like what happens with the portions that God had previously fixed for them, such as the heave shoulder and the wave breast, which were spoken of before.

If God cared for the priests and the details of their material needs because they consecrated their lives to His service, be sure that you too, if you are bound to Christ and His service, He will care for all your needs and will not forsake you.

entries.section: (2) The priests' rights from the offerings of the people

paragraphs.text: A covenant of salt: that is, an everlasting covenant.
To thee and to thy seed: that is, to the priests and their descendants.

As a final review of all that preceded, God repeats to Aaron and his sons that all the portions, vows, offerings and sacrifices, except the burnt offering, that are offered to the Lord, the Lord in turn gives to the priests after the sprinkling of the blood around the altar and after the burning of their fat, and the priests eat them with their households all the days.

entries.section: (2) The priests' rights from the offerings of the people

paragraphs.text: God affirms to Aaron that he will have no fixed portion in the land like the rest of the tribes, because God will be his portion and in place of everything. The beautiful spiritual meaning is that whoever leaves anything for the sake of God possesses everything in return, since the Lord has become his portion, as St. Paul mentioned and said, “as having nothing, and yet possessing all things” (2 Cor 6:10).

entries.section: (3) The rights of the Levites

paragraphs.text: After God spoke about the portions of the priests from the offerings and sacrifices, His speech turned to the Levites also, the servants of the tabernacle of the congregation, and God established for them the tithes of the income of all the people, from their produce and the profits of their trade, after they dwell in the land. If the priests take the firstfruits, the Levites take the tithes.

entries.section: (3) The rights of the Levites

paragraphs.text: They shall bear their iniquity: they bear their responsibility and the results of any failure in it.

God warns all the people not to come near the tabernacle of the congregation and touch anything of its contents, otherwise they will be exposed to death. Those allowed to serve the house of God are only the Levites, because they know how to fulfill the Law of God, and any breach of it brings God's punishment on them. This service is assigned to the Levites throughout the generations until Christ comes. The Levites possess no inheritance in the Promised Land, because God is their inheritance, like the priests.

entries.section: (3) The rights of the Levites

paragraphs.text: Heave offering: lifted up and offered to the Lord.
This verse comes as a confirmation and review of what was said before in verses 21-23, the sum of which is that the tithes the people give to the Levites are offered to God Himself.

Know that everything you have is a gift from God, so before you use it, may you receive God's blessing by offering a part of it, which is the tithe, and be sure that the rest, by God's blessing, will be enough for your needs, however narrow your financial circumstances. “The blessing of the LORD, it maketh rich, and he addeth no sorrow with it” (Prov 10:22).

entries.section: (4) The tithes of the Levites

paragraphs.text: Ye shall offer up: you shall present.

God's speech here is to the Levites also, telling them through Moses that just as they received tithes from the people and their houses were filled with good things, so they too must offer to the Lord their tithes. The Levites are not excepted from the tithes here, for God wishes to teach them that He gives to all and is the maker of good things, and that as a man rejoiced in receiving, so he must rejoice in giving.

entries.section: (4) The tithes of the Levites

paragraphs.text: Your heave offering: your offering.
Wheat: the grain.
The threshingfloor: the floor, which is the place where the grain is separated from the husk and stored.
The fulness: what fills the vessel to its brim.

As the people offer from their tithes the grain that is in the threshingfloor and the oil and wine that are in the winepress, so also the Levites offer a tenth of what they took from the people and give it to the priests in the person of Aaron. That is, if the Levites receive the tenth, the priests take 1/100 of the produce of the people.

entries.section: (4) The tithes of the Levites

paragraphs.text: The best thereof, the hallowed part: the best of the good things and offerings.

God affirms what He said before and asks the Levites that the tithes they will offer must be of the best that can be offered, because the offering is offered to God Himself and He gives it to His priests.

entries.section: (4) The tithes of the Levites

paragraphs.text: He asks Moses to tell them that when they do this and offer the best they have, God regards it as the fruit of their labors, and this is a repetition of what came in (v. 27), so God blesses the remaining nine tenths with the Levites.

entries.section: (4) The tithes of the Levites

paragraphs.text: The speech here is about the nine tenths remaining with the Levites, for God blesses them for them and wishes them to enjoy them with their families, since He fully appreciates their labor in the service of the tabernacle, in taking it down, carrying it and setting it up.

entries.section: (4) The tithes of the Levites

paragraphs.text: Holy things: offerings.

When you offer the tithe, “the best thereof,” from your portion, you will be justified before God and will bear no sin or guilt, for if you do otherwise you defile the offerings of the children of Israel offered to My own self, and thus expose your souls to punishment and death.

My beloved brother... it is not enough to give tithes to God, but you must also give the best that you have and not the least or most despised of it. For what you give to any man you give to God Himself in the person of this man... Would God, then, be given the lesser, the worse and the stale!!!

Introduction to the law of the red heifer: This chapter is connected with what came in the book of Leviticus (ch. 11, ch. 21). If the book of Leviticus spoke of the uncleanness of one who touches the dead and the necessity of his purification before dealing with or touching anyone, the book of Numbers in this chapter presents the law of purification through the sacrifice of the red heifer, whose law we shall come to know in detail.

entries.section: (1) Slaughtering the heifer and gathering its ashes

paragraphs.text: An ordinance of the law: that is, a rite and order that must be followed in what is to come.

A red heifer: that is, the color of its whole skin is red, with no spot on it, nor even a hair of any other color. By red is meant the light brown that is the well-known color of cattle, as Esau said to Jacob about the color of the lentils (light brown), "Feed me with that same red pottage" (Gen 25:30). The Lord commanded Moses and Aaron that the offering that would be set apart for the sacrifice of purification must be a heifer of red color, which the children of Israel were to seek out and bring to the Lord. The second condition, besides its color, is that it be perfect and without blemish, so it is not sick, nor does it have a visible defect or any other color. The third condition here is that it not have been used for plowing or field work, nor have had anything carried on its back.

entries.section: (1) Slaughtering the heifer and gathering its ashes

paragraphs.text: Eleazar the priest takes the heifer, and it is slaughtered by him or under his eyes outside the camp. Then he takes some of the heifer's blood and looks toward the door of the tabernacle, while outside the camp, and sprinkles the blood seven times. The blood, of course, points to the atonement for the sins of all the people, and the seven times to the perfection of this purification. The red heifer is slaughtered outside the camp because it is a symbol of the uncleanness of sin.

entries.section: (1) Slaughtering the heifer and gathering its ashes

paragraphs.text: Her dung: this is the remains of food in her bowels.
The Lord then commanded that the heifer be burned entirely, like the burnt offering or the sin offering, but outside the camp and not on the altar of burnt offering.

entries.section: (1) Slaughtering the heifer and gathering its ashes

paragraphs.text: The priest, whether Eleazar or those who follow him in the later generations, takes three things that carry symbolic meanings and casts them also on the fire that consumes the slaughtered heifer. These things are:
1- Cedar wood: it signifies incorruption, since it is not subject to decay.
2- Hyssop: this is the herbal plant that signifies purification: "Purge me with hyssop, and I shall be clean."
3- Scarlet: it signifies sin and forgiveness at the same time.
a- Sin: "though your sins be as scarlet" (Isa 1:18).
b- Forgiveness: because in its redness it signifies the blood of Christ who forgives the sins of the world.

entries.section: (1) Slaughtering the heifer and gathering its ashes

paragraphs.text: As for the priest and the one who helped him in slaughtering and burning the red heifer, one law applies to both of them, namely:
a) He washes his clothes that were defiled by the blood of the sacrifice.
b) He also washes his body of the traces of the blood.
c) The two become unclean, so the priest may not approach the tabernacle or the service, nor may the person who helped him touch any other person until the evening of the same day of the slaughter.

entries.section: (1) Slaughtering the heifer and gathering its ashes

paragraphs.text: A third person comes, after the priest and the one who helped him have departed and after the fire that consumed the whole heifer has gone out, and gathers the ashes remaining after the burning of the heifer. Jewish tradition teaches us that these ashes were ground fine and afterward kept in a safe place outside the bounds of the people's dwelling, that is, outside the camp, so that the people might use them through the priests when needed, that is, when one of them became unclean by touching a dead person, for example.

Kept for the water of separation: that is, the ashes are kept dry, but when they are used, some of them is mixed with water to be sprinkled on the unclean person. This water is called the water of uncleanness, although it is used for purification.
A purification for sin: the heifer is considered here a sin offering because it was used for purification from sin.

entries.section: (1) Slaughtering the heifer and gathering its ashes

paragraphs.text: The man who helped in gathering the ashes also becomes unclean until the evening.

These ashes are a law and an ordinance that continues always, because of man's constant need for purification, whether for the Jew by origin or the proselyte from among the strangers who are not of the tribes.
The red heifer as a symbol of Christ:

There is no sin that does not need atonement or purification, and the sin of touching the dead came to signify the transmission of sin by contagion or association; in every case there was a need for purification. Here the law of the red heifer came, carrying many meanings, the most beautiful of which is that it is a direct symbol of the atoning work of Christ in cleansing sins.

1- It is red: pure red is rare and distinctive among cattle, like Christ, who, although He resembled us in kind through the Incarnation, has no equal in the purity of His red blood, which did not bear our original sin.
2- Without blemish: this is also a condition of the burnt offering, and Christ alone, of all the sons of men, is the one to whom this applies.
3- Never yoked: that is, like Christ, who did not bear the yoke of sin, but bore on the Cross all our sins.
4- It was burned entirely: in this is an indication of the perfection of Christ's sacrifice and of His complete sufferings.

5- The cedar wood was added: the addition of cedar wood, which does not decay, is a clear reference to the Lord Christ, of whom David prophesied and said, "Neither wilt thou suffer thine Holy One to see corruption" (Ps 16:10).
6- The priest was the one who offered the sacrifice of the red heifer and slaughtered it himself, and Christ offered Himself as a sacrifice on the Cross for the whole world.
7- The red heifer was slaughtered outside the camp, and Christ also was crucified outside Jerusalem.

8- The priest sprinkled the blood of the red heifer's sacrifice toward the house of the Lord, and Christ was hung on the Cross and they lifted Him up toward heaven to satisfy the Father and reconcile us with Him.

9- The ashes of the heifer were mixed with water to purify the unclean, and Christ by His death on the Cross gave us the water of Baptism to save us from the evil nature and cleanse us from every sin.
10- The ashes of the heifer lasted a long time, and the sacrifice of Christ also lasts forever, so He gives His Body and Blood to all generations.
11- A little of the heifer's ashes purified every unclean person, and the smallest part of Christ's sacrifice, that is, His Body and Blood, purifies and satisfies every believer in Him.

If Christ suffered outside the camp to cleanse us from our sins, do not be troubled if others neglect you, or wrong you, or drive you away from them, for they did all this to your Lord Christ. Endure, confident of God's help that upholds you, and you will also experience His presence with you, and He will comfort your heart.

entries.section: (2) Purifying one made unclean by touching the dead

paragraphs.text: The dead body of a man: this is mentioned here to distinguish it from touching the dead body of an animal.

Whoever touched a dead animal was unclean until the evening, but here whoever touches a dead human being becomes unclean for seven days; the continuation of uncleanness for seven days is an indication of the seriousness of sin and the necessity of being cleansed from it.

entries.section: (2) Purifying one made unclean by touching the dead

paragraphs.text: For this person the law of his purification must begin with the priest sprinkling on him some of the water of purification, which is called the water of uncleanness, on the third day ... and he repeats this action on the seventh day also (v. 19). But if he is negligent and does not come forward for purification on the third day, the seventh day comes upon him while he is still unclean. The spiritual meaning is that the seven days here signify the fullness of man's lifetime: time, however long, does not blot out man's iniquity, but repentance and the blood of Christ in the sacrament of the Eucharist alone blot out iniquity, which the purification on the third day signifies, in addition to the fact that the number three signifies the Resurrection of Christ and the seven days the seven sacraments of the Church.

entries.section: (2) Purifying one made unclean by touching the dead

paragraphs.text: Defiles the tabernacle of the Lord: that is, he defiles the camp in which God dwells in the midst of His people.

But if a person treats the law of his purification lightly and remains unclean, he is considered to be despising and scorning the house of the Lord and the whole purity of the people. The spiritual meaning is that the person who sins and does not come forward with repentance and the sacrament of confession before God becomes a transgressor not only against himself but against the whole Church, so his sin is multiplied many times over. Therefore the punishment in this verse is severe, as the sentence against him is that he be cut off from his people, that is, put outside the people, so that he is deprived of his membership in the people of God, and the judges may sentence him to death by stoning.

Beloved, if God in His mercies is longsuffering toward sinners until they return by repentance to His embrace, this does not mean laxity and indifference. The merciful God is not lax about the price of sin either, because continuing in laxity means, sadly, making light of the sacrifice of His only-begotten Son, our Lord Jesus Christ.

entries.section: (2) Purifying one made unclean by touching the dead

paragraphs.text: In these three verses is an enumeration and definition of the ways in which a person may become unclean by touching the dead, and the obligation of his purification. They can be listed as follows:

1- Everyone who was in the tent of the dead, or entered it, or touched anything in it, and indeed every open or uncovered vessel, that is, without a cover, also becomes unclean; this is a symbol of the senses that are not disciplined and not closed against evil.
2- Even if a person is in the desert or in the open field and touches one slain, or an ordinary dead person, or the remains of a human bone, or touches a grave, he becomes unclean.

The law of uncleanness is applied to the unclean person as mentioned in (v. 11): seven days, and of course the purification begins on the third day as explained before. Whatever the cause of the dead person's death, whether in a tent, that is, sin working in him gradually, or slain with a sword, that is, sin working in him suddenly, or a man's bone, that is, an old sin. For death is unclean because sin is its cause.

entries.section: (3) The law and steps of purification

paragraphs.text: The steps of purification for one who has touched a dead person can be summarized in the following steps:

1- This work must be done by a clean man, for it is not reasonable that one who is unclean should perform the purification, since the blind cannot lead the blind. In this is a beautiful teaching for all servants of the Church and its leaders: the one who teaches and guides must be pure in conduct and clean in conscience, so that he may be able to lead others.

2- The clean man, who may be the priest himself, takes a little of the ashes of the burnt red heifer in a vessel and puts water on it, and also takes a bunch of the hyssop plant and dips it in this water and sprinkles the tent and all the furnishings, the bedding and the vessels that are in it.
3- The sprinkling includes also all the dwellers of the tent who were present at the time of the death, and whoever touched the dead, or touched a dead man's bone, or a grave (v. 16).
4- This sprinkling is done twice, on the third day and on the seventh.
5- On the seventh day, after the sprinkling, the one who was unclean comes and washes his clothes and bathes, and becomes clean at the evening of the seventh day.

entries.section: (3) The law and steps of purification

paragraphs.text: In this verse is a repetition of what came in (v. 13): whoever makes light of this law and the water of uncleanness, that is, the water of purification, is not sprinkled on him becomes a cause of uncleanness for the whole people, and therefore his punishment is severe, for this person is taken outside the camp and sentenced to death by stoning.

entries.section: (3) The law and steps of purification

paragraphs.text: A perpetual statute: a permanent ordinance and a continuing law.

As for the one who was clean and sprinkled the water of uncleanness on the unclean person, he himself is considered unclean until the evening, and at evening he must also bathe and wash his clothes. In this is a beautiful reflection for our spiritual life: the servant, the guide and the priest who hears the sins and troubles of his people may be affected, even a little, and "become unclean" by what he heard, so he too must lift up his heart in prayer for his own sins and the sins of the one he heard, or for the sins of his people if he is a priest.

entries.section: (3) The law and steps of purification

paragraphs.text: God affirms that sin is like a contagious disease, quick to spread and reach another. Everyone who was unclean because of touching a dead person and then touched another passes the uncleanness to him, and he in turn needs the water of purification. The spiritual meaning here is clear: a person must keep away from the wicked in order to preserve himself and his salvation, for being influenced is possible, and many people have lost their lives because of bad friends.

My beloved brother ... we must care for those who are far away and call them to Christ and the salvation of their souls, but set limits for yourself in mixing with their circles, lest you slip toward them instead of lifting them up to Christ. There is no one who is not affected by the surroundings around him, so beware lest evil enter your heart. The death of Miriam and Aaron and the water of Meribah

entries.section: (1) The death of Miriam and the people's murmuring over water

paragraphs.text: The wilderness of Zin: it is an extension of the wilderness of Paran toward the northeast, and lies south of Canaan. As for Kadesh-barnea, where the people stayed and set up the tabernacle, it is on the border between Paran and the wilderness of Zin (map 1). The congregation of the people moved according to the Lord's command to the northeast and settled in Kadesh. The omission of the year in this verse made some commentators believe that it was the first month of the third year, while others thought it was the first month of the fortieth year. And Miriam the prophetess died in that place, and it is known that she was the elder sister of Moses.

entries.section: (1) The death of Miriam and the people's murmuring over water

paragraphs.text: Water in desert regions is always scarce, even when rain falls, and the people were accustomed to drink from natural springs or from wells they dug. Perhaps because of the difficulty of the rocky ground in the region of Kadesh they were not able to dig, and therefore the people chided Moses, that is, they protested and murmured against him, saying that our death with our brethren who went before us and died in Sinai would be better than what we are in now.

entries.section: (1) The death of Miriam and the people's murmuring over water

paragraphs.text: After the words had been addressed to Moses, the people also pointed the finger of accusation at Aaron with him, saying that the two of them were the cause of the people's destruction because they had brought them to this place where water is scarce. The people forgot that Moses and Aaron did not move except by the Lord's command by means of the pillar of cloud and the pillar of fire.

entries.section: (1) The death of Miriam and the people's murmuring over water

paragraphs.text: The people continue their protest and accusation that they had been deceived by coming out of the land of Egypt, where there were the Nile, greenery, shade, and abundance of water and food, in comparison with this barren desert, especially since until now they had not seen the promised land, which flows with milk and honey and abundant good things.

entries.section: (1) The death of Miriam and the people's murmuring over water

paragraphs.text: As Moses and Aaron, the faithful servants, were accustomed to do when troubles increased, they took refuge in God, and went to His house, that is, the tabernacle of meeting, and bowed down, humbly declaring their inability to find a solution and apologizing to God for this murmuring.

entries.section: (1) The death of Miriam and the people's murmuring over water

paragraphs.text: The Lord commanded Moses to take his rod and go toward a rock, perhaps one fairly high and with a distinctive shape so that Moses would recognize it, and to gather with him all the congregation of the people and speak to the rock, and it would bring forth water ... This differs from God's earlier command to strike the rock that was in "Rephidim" (Ex 17).

entries.section: (1) The death of Miriam and the people's murmuring over water

paragraphs.text: Moses rose from the ground and took his rod and prepared to carry out what God had commanded him.

We learn from the life of Moses, the faithful servant, something important: when great troubles occur, and the storms that Satan stirs up, we have no way out except to bow down, pour ourselves out before God, and pray with persistence, confident that God does not send away empty those who seek Him, and He will solve all problems, for nothing is impossible with Him.

entries.section: (2) The water comes out and the punishment of Moses and Aaron

paragraphs.text: Rebels: the rebellious.

Despite Moses' great meekness before, and his endurance and breadth of heart, here we find him as if he had exhausted all his patience. He gathered the people before the appointed rock and addressed them angrily, saying to them, "Hear now, ye rebels," asking them whether water could come out of this rock?! Of course, by human logic, water cannot come out of rock, for it comes out of springs or wells, as is well known.

entries.section: (2) The water comes out and the punishment of Moses and Aaron

paragraphs.text: Moses lifted up his hand with the rod and struck the rock, while in the same state of anger, and thereby violated God's command, who had commanded him to speak to the rock and not to strike it. And because of the intensity of his anger, the divine inspiration shows us that Moses struck it twice and not once. Although this angry action was not according to God's goodness, God brought forth a large quantity of water so that all the people and also their livestock could drink from it.

entries.section: (2) The water comes out and the punishment of Moses and Aaron

paragraphs.text: God was angry at the disobedience of Moses and Aaron to His word, for He had wanted to perform a new miraculous work before the people, namely that merely speaking to the rock would bring water out of it ... But Moses' anger and his striking of the rock hindered the work of God, and this is what God expressed by His saying, "to sanctify me," that is, you prevented the people from sanctifying and glorifying My name by this action of yours. Therefore God's punishment of Moses and Aaron was severe and decisive, as He declared to them that they would be deprived of the land they had long yearned for and would not enter it with the rest of the people.

Moses' anger deprived him of entering the Promised Land, and the Holy Bible declares that "the wrath of man worketh not the righteousness of God" (Jas 1:20). So do not justify your anger, but offer repentance and apology for it, first to God and second to the one with whom you were angry, and God will have compassion on you and forgive you your sin.

entries.section: (2) The water comes out and the punishment of Moses and Aaron

paragraphs.text: Meribah: the testing.

As a conclusion to the preceding events, the divine inspiration declares that this was the story of the water of testing, when the children of Israel tested the Lord by their murmuring, their complaining, and their doubting of God's care for them; yet God showed His glory and His power when He brought water out of the rock and gave drink to all His people.

entries.section: (3) Moses' conversations with the king of Edom

paragraphs.text: Edom: this is the name of Esau by which he was known, and it was applied to his descendants, who increased and became a people with a king. The people of Edom dwelt in the mountains of Seir, which lie between the Dead Sea to the north and the Gulf of Aqaba to the south, that is, on the border dividing present-day Jordan and Palestine (map 3). Map (3) shows the route of the people during their journey beginning from Sinai, and Kadesh was west of the land of Edom, and therefore the people had to pass through it to reach the land of their inheritance. Therefore Moses sent some of his men to the king of Edom, saying to him, "Thy brother Israel," that is, we are the descendants of Jacob, the brother of Edom, and we ask you to allow us to pass through your land, especially since you know very well the hardships that befell us, whether in Egypt or after coming out of it.

entries.section: (3) Moses' conversations with the king of Edom

paragraphs.text: These three verses carry the summary of the message that Moses' messengers carried to the king of Edom, and its elements can be summarized in the following points:-
1- They began by presenting their earlier history and referred to the humiliation they suffered in the land of Egypt, in an attempt to move the heart of the king of Edom.

2- Making clear that God had not forgotten them but brought them out with a strong arm and a divine arrangement beyond human imagination, when their humiliation grew intense and they cried out to Him.
3- The request to pass through the land of Edom.

4- The promise that this passage would be a peaceful passage in which the people would not touch anything belonging to Edom: they would not eat anything of the fruit of their land, nor take even a little of the water, nor look with their eyes at anything on their right or left, but would go straight on their way to their promised land.

entries.section: (3) Moses' conversations with the king of Edom

paragraphs.text: The answer of the king of Edom came severe and harsh, for he refused the request of Moses and the people, and even added to that by threatening them that he might destroy them with the sword if they tried to pass.

entries.section: (3) Moses' conversations with the king of Edom

paragraphs.text: Moses did not despair, but returned a second time and addressed the king of Edom through his messengers in order to dispel his fears, saying to him, let us pass with our people, and we will even pay you the price of the water if we drink from your wells or your springs, for we want nothing but to pass on foot only.

entries.section: (3) Moses' conversations with the king of Edom

paragraphs.text: With rage and hardness of heart, the king of Edom refused a second time the request of Moses and his people to pass through his land, and added to that by gathering his people and his men and going out to the border between the land of Edom and Kadesh, prepared for war if they tried to pass through his land. In view of this, Moses and the people decided to keep away from evil and not confront it, especially since God had not commanded them to fight him.

Here we learn from Moses, the wise leader, that it is not wise in any way to meet evil with evil, but we must avoid confrontation with it as much as we are able, for meeting evil with evil usually brings nothing but a greater evil whose price everyone pays, and a person loses his peace and calm, which cannot be valued by any other gains.

entries.section: (4) The end of Aaron's service and life

paragraphs.text: Mount Hor: most probably it is the mountain known as Jabal Madurah, which is northeast of Kadesh (map 4). All the people journeyed in the northeast direction and pitched the tabernacle at Mount Hor on the border of the land of Edom, and there God spoke with Moses and Aaron, telling them that Aaron would not enter the land that God had given to the people because of his rebellion against the divine command at the incident of the rock and the water, but would be "gathered unto his people," that is, would die as his fathers.
Map (4)

entries.section: (4) The end of Aaron's service and life

paragraphs.text: God continues His speech with Moses and commands him to go up to the top of the mountain and take with him both Aaron and his son "Eleazar," and there Aaron takes off his garments, which represent the high priesthood, and Moses puts them on "Eleazar" his son, who would become high priest in place of his father, while Aaron's days come to their end and he follows his fathers in the hope of the redemption and coming of Christ. The taking off of the high priest's garments and the clothing of the new high priest with them became a Jewish tradition for many ages.

entries.section: (4) The end of Aaron's service and life

paragraphs.text: Moses did exactly what God commanded him, and indeed Aaron died after Moses clothed Eleazar in his father's garments. Perhaps the people saw this scene, and this means that Mount Hor was not a lofty or high mountain, and after Aaron's death Moses and Eleazar both came down to the people. Jewish tradition mentions that Aaron was buried on the same mountain on which he died.
And Aaron's death was on the first day of the fifth month in the fortieth year after their coming out of Egypt (ch. 33:38).

entries.section: (4) The end of Aaron's service and life

paragraphs.text: As for the people who saw this event and witnessed the death of their high priest, they grieved greatly and mourned for Aaron for a whole month, in recognition of his labor with them and his service to them.

Without doubt Moses and Eleazar were deeply affected by the death of Aaron ... who supported his brother first before Pharaoh of Egypt, second in the Exodus, and third in his priestly service. But Moses did not surrender to his sorrows because of his brother's death, for he still had work to complete before God and a mission not yet finished; and we too must grasp this lesson well and not let our sorrows disturb us .. but always lift up our hearts in times of hardship, asking God for help and support.

We also learn from the life of Aaron that however long a servant's life in his service, a day will come when he leaves everything, whatever his responsibilities; therefore the aware leader and faithful servant is the one who is concerned to teach, hand over, disciple and train others, so that the service does not stop or fall into confusion, and only the humble leader does this. The bronze serpent and the victory over many kings

entries.section: (1) The war with the king of Arad

paragraphs.text: Canaanite: that is, from the descendants of Canaan, son of Noah's son Ham, but the curse came upon him, so the Canaanites did not walk in God's statutes but became an example of evil.
Arad: a Canaanite city in the south of Palestine.
The south: what is meant is the south of Palestine.

The way of the spies: this is the road that the twelve spies had taken before to enter the land. The Canaanite king of the town of Arad heard of the matter of the people and that their aim was to pass through, and learned of their talk with the Edomites and the refusal of the king of the Edomites to let them pass (ch. 20). Because of this king's abundant evil, he attacked the peaceful people and took some of them as captives to be slaves for his people. Perhaps Arad's attack on the children of Israel was out of fear of their great number, so he rushed to attack them and took some of them captive to frighten them so that they would keep away from him (maps 2, 4).

entries.section: (1) The war with the king of Arad

paragraphs.text: The people took refuge in God, their leader and supreme governor, and prayed to Him, and vowed a vow to God that if He gave them victory over this wicked king and their captive brothers were freed, they would utterly destroy the cities of Arad, that is, destroy and wipe out the buildings of the city.

entries.section: (1) The war with the king of Arad

paragraphs.text: We see God's just answer, for He permitted His people this war and also gave them victory.

The expression "delivered up the Canaanites" means that God handed the enemies over to the people to do with them as they wished, and that the victory was fundamentally from the Lord and not by the hand of Israel. Indeed the people destroyed everything, and therefore the place was afterward called "Hormah," as a sign and allusion to what happened there.

May we not let our feelings or emotions lead us to act in any situation, but let us bring all our complaints and feelings to God in prayer, trusting and believing that God is able to solve all our problems or to guide us to what we ought to do.

entries.section: (2) The bronze serpent

paragraphs.text: When the king of Edom refused to let the people pass, Moses was compelled to go around the land of Edom, so they passed by Elath, at the head of the Gulf of Aqaba, then eastward at Mount "Hor," which lies south of Palestine and east of the Gulf of Aqaba, a difficult mountain road, which had a bad effect on the morale of the people, who became very discouraged.

entries.section: (2) The bronze serpent

paragraphs.text: In a new episode in the series of murmurings of the people of the children of Israel in the Book of Numbers, the people expressed their anger with words very wounding to the heart of God, for they murmured against God Himself and against Moses their leader, forgetting all God's earlier works of care and providence. Their murmuring included three things:
1- Their coming out of the land of Egypt, forgetting their former bondage and forced labor.
2- Complaining of the lack of water and bread, although God daily undertook to feed them.
3- Describing the "manna," the free divine food, as light bread, in clear contempt for the love and gift of God.

entries.section: (2) The bronze serpent

paragraphs.text: Fiery: very painful.

God's punishment of this ungrateful people was clear and severe, so He sent among them serpents whose bites were highly poisonous and very painful, and many of the people died as a result. It is to be noted that God had kept His people on their way from the fiery serpents hiding in the mountains, but when they murmured against Him they lost His protection, so the serpents attacked them and bit them and they died.

entries.section: (2) The bronze serpent

paragraphs.text: The scene is repeated, and Israel feels its error and that it had gone beyond every limit when it insulted its God. They confessed before Moses and God the greatness of the offense of their error and asked Moses for intercessory prayer on their behalf so that God would remove from them the punishment of the serpents. And because Moses was a loving shepherd and an intercessor beloved of God, he indeed lifted up his prayers to God for his people.

entries.section: (2) The bronze serpent

paragraphs.text: God intervened at once and answered the prayer of Moses and commanded him to make a serpent of bronze in the form of the fiery serpents that were biting the people, and to lift it up on a pole or a high column like a banner, so that everyone bitten by one of the serpents might see it and be saved from the poison by looking at this bronze serpent.

It is to be noted that the serpent made of bronze cannot heal from deadly poison, but God wanted to test the obedience of His people and their faith by their looking at this bronze serpent, and He healed them because He is the Healer, and He asks only obedience and faith from His children.

My beloved brother .. if you feel that you have sinned and that God in His love has allowed you to be disciplined, return at once with repentance and confession of your error, and ask the prayer of your father the priest at the altar, and God will answer you and remove His wrath from you.

entries.section: (2) The bronze serpent

paragraphs.text: Moses did as the Lord commanded him and set the bronze serpent on a raised pole and a high place, so that whenever any person bitten by a poisonous serpent looked at it with hope and faith, God healed him and he escaped death. The spiritual meanings in this lifted-up serpent are many, but the most important thing in this story is the very clear symbol between the lifted-up serpent and Christ, who was also lifted up on the wood of the Cross, and here, beloved, are some aspects of this likeness:
1- The serpents bit the people and they died, as the ancient serpent brought down Adam and he was sentenced to death.
2- The people cried out to God for deliverance, as humanity cried out for redemption from the sentence of death.
3- Moses made a likeness of the same kind, that is, a bronze serpent like the serpents, and thus God took a body like our bodies, but it did not carry poison (sin) but deliverance and life.
4- Moses lifted the bronze serpent high, and Christ was also lifted up on the Cross so that everyone who believes in Him might be saved from the bites of Satan and sin and have eternal life.

Sadly, when the people grew weak in their relationship with God, they worshiped the bronze serpent as they had worshiped the statues of the pagan gods, and they called the image of the serpent "Nehushtan," and therefore Hezekiah king of Judah crushed it to remove this pagan worship (2 Kgs 18:4).

Let us lift up our eyes in faith toward the Cross, seeking healing from our sins, remembering that He who went up on the Cross opened His arms and His bosom to hold us within it, if we ourselves wish it.

entries.section: (3) The people's continued journeying

paragraphs.text: Oboth: northeast of Elath.

The people journeyed to Oboth, and from Oboth northward to Ije-abarim, which has another name, "Iim," by which it is mentioned in ch. (33:45). The expression "before Moab, toward the sunrising" means east of Moab (map 3).

entries.section: (3) The people's continued journeying

paragraphs.text: The journey continued to a valley named "Zared," which took its name from a small river of the same name, "Zared," a river that flows into the Dead Sea and is considered the dividing boundary between Edom to the south and the land of Moab to the north.

entries.section: (3) The people's continued journeying

paragraphs.text: Israel also journeyed northward to a new river, the river "Arnon," which represents a new boundary between Moab to the south and the Amorites to the north. The expression in the wilderness "that cometh out of the coasts of the Amorites" means that this journeying was alongside the land of the Amorites, that is, the river Arnon was between the people and the Amorites.

entries.section: (3) The people's continued journeying

paragraphs.text: The book of the wars of the Lord: this is a historical book from the books of the people, written by Moses, and it is a record of God's work in the confrontations, wars and situations that the people met on their way and journeying. It is a historical book and not among the holy inspired Scriptures.
Suphah: the region around the Red Sea.
The brooks: the slope of the valley of Arnon.
Ar: the capital of the land of Moab.
Border: boundary.

Moses, "the writer of the Book of Numbers," matches the events of the journeying here and also confirms them by the fact that this was recorded in another book written in poetic form, describing the same events and places. And since the prophet Moses relied on the book of the wars of the Lord, this means that it was written before the Book of Numbers, and this book mentions that God was with His people Israel, and as He brought it through the Red Sea and gave it victory, so also He gave it victories at the river Arnon and it passed by the land of Moab.

entries.section: (3) The people's continued journeying

paragraphs.text: The people journeyed again from the valley of Arnon, and when their weariness increased, the Lord guided them to a place to dig a well there: "Gather the people together, and I will give them water."

entries.section: (3) The people's continued journeying

paragraphs.text: Because of the greatness of the Lord's work for the people, the children of Israel praised God with a new song, thanking Him by it for what He had done with them by helping them to dig this well through their princes, and He brought them through until they passed the borders of the land of Moab. The words of this song came as follows: Spring up, O well: rise up, O waters.
Sing ye unto it: sing and chant to it.

The well which the princes digged, the nobles of the people: that is, those who did the digging were those counted as princes and nobles of the people and not just any ordinary folk, in response to God's request.

By the direction of the lawgiver, with their staves: the scepter is the king's rod and symbolizes authority and majesty, and the staves symbolize hard work and striving, that is, the water came out by divine authority and the effort of the noble men. This meaning is very close to what the Church teaches, that salvation is in the first place a work of divine grace ("the scepter"), provided that man responds to grace through his spiritual striving ("the staves").

entries.section: (3) The people's continued journeying

paragraphs.text: Mattanah: a city on the border of Moab.

In these two verses is a continuation of the people's journey and journeying, and it mentions a series of places they passed through from the south of the Dead Sea going north alongside it until they reached a place called "the top of Pisgah," which is the head of a mountain that looks out over and overlooks the wilderness and lies east of the Dead Sea. This mountain was also called Mount "Nebo," and it is the place from which Moses saw the Promised Land and on which he also died.

entries.section: (4) The defeat of Sihon and Og

paragraphs.text: The Amorites: they are the descendants of Canaan the son of Ham the son of Noah, and their land was very wide east of the river Jordan.
The king's highway: the main public road within the kingdom.

As Moses did with the king of Edom (ch. 20) and asked his permission to pass through his land, so also he did here with Sihon king of the Amorites, and even repeated exactly what he had said before in the wording of the request, that they would not touch anything of the fruit of the land and would not take water from their wells, but all they wanted was permission to pass only, so that they might cross the border. Although this land of the Amorites is a land that God promised to Abraham as an inheritance for his people, Moses did not begin with war but resorted to peace, dialogue and asking permission.

entries.section: (4) The defeat of Sihon and Og

paragraphs.text: Jahaz: a Moabite city (map 5). Border: boundary.

Ashtaroth ● Edrei ● Dibon ● valley of Zared. Map (5). Sihon king of the Amorites was not content with refusal, but in pride and a display of strength without justification, he went out with his army into the wilderness to meet the people of God at a place called Jahaz, and the two parties met and the Lord gave victory to His people, and Israel prevailed by the edge of the sword, and the people took possession of all the cities of the Amorites, whose borders were from the river Arnon to the south to the river Jabbok to the north, and to the west was the river Jordan. The northern river Jabbok separated the border of the Amorites from the border of the children of Ammon, whom the Book describes as strong.

entries.section: (4) The defeat of Sihon and Og
