paragraphs.text: Heshbon: the largest city of the Amorites and their capital.

Israel possessed the land, which was the first land considered fit for dwelling after the long journey in the wilderness, and they settled in the capital of the Amorites, "Heshbon," and all the small villages around it.

entries.section: (4) The defeat of Sihon and Og

paragraphs.text: This verse presents an addition, namely that this land of the Moabites had been seized by Sihon from the former king of Moab, and he took all the land with all its borders. The meaning intended to be made clear here is that the usurper, however great his power, has a day of punishment laid up for him by God, and as He did to the one before, He does also to him, for often the recompense is from the same deed, and what a man sows, that he will reap.

entries.section: (4) The defeat of Sihon and Og

paragraphs.text: They that speak in proverbs: that is, the composers of the songs or ballads that record history and its events. The people sang of this victory and it became for them a beloved song commemorating this victory, and it included verses (27-30), and its first part spoke of the victory of Sihon king of the Amorites over the Moabites, and its second half (v. 30) spoke of the victory of the people of God over Sihon ... The meanings of the words of this poem were as follows:
Come into Heshbon: come to Heshbon, which had belonged to the Moabites.

The city of Sihon: that is, which after the victory of Sihon became the possession of him and his people the Amorites. A fire is gone out of Heshbon: fire and flame, that is, severe wars and battles, which Sihon waged from Heshbon on the rest of the cities of the Moabites until he occupied them all. As examples of these cities the singers mentioned the name of the city "Ar," and also the heights of Arnon.

Moab's great city: "great" meaning large, and the meaning is the great Moabite city, which is the capital, that is, Heshbon. The lords of the high places of Arnon: this means the princes or priests of the idols in the valley of Arnon.
Woe to thee, Moab: destruction has come to you, O cities of the Moabites.

O people of Chemosh: the speech is also about the destruction of the Moabites and the end of their pagan god Chemosh, for all his followers became either fugitives from before Sihon or slaves of the Amorites and their king Sihon.

entries.section: (4) The defeat of Sihon and Og

paragraphs.text: This verse is the last stanza of the poem, but it speaks of the victory of the people of God over Sihon and the Amorites, and its meaning is:
We have shot at them: that is, we struck them and hit them.

Heshbon even unto Dibon: we destroyed our enemies from Heshbon in the north to the town of Dibon in the south, and our victory reached all the cities and borders of the Amorites, such as Nophah toward Medeba.

entries.section: (4) The defeat of Sihon and Og

paragraphs.text: After the end of this song, which the singers and then the people sang, the people dwelt in all the land of the Moabites, and this victory had the greatest effect in raising their morale and began a series of other victories (map 5).
Do not fear the attack of the wicked upon you, because God is able to protect you from them and even to punish them for your sake. Only hold fast to God and ask His help at all times.

entries.section: (5) The victory over the king of Bashan

paragraphs.text: Jazer: one of the cities of the Amorites on the border of the Ammonites, and therefore it was a fortified and strong city.

The people did not take the fortified city of "Jazer" at first, but after a period of settling in Heshbon and its villages, Moses sent spies to the city of Jazer. We understand from the words that the people were able to take it and its villages also.

entries.section: (5) The victory over the king of Bashan

paragraphs.text: The people continued to advance northward alongside the eastern bank of the river Jordan, and the city of Bashan was in their way, and Moses did not think of storming it or fighting it, but the king of Bashan, perhaps because of his fear of what had happened to the Amorites, gathered his men of war to the city of "Edrei," the largest of their cities and their capital at that time, to meet Moses and fight him.

entries.section: (5) The victory over the king of Bashan

paragraphs.text: As for Moses, who did nothing without God's guidance or asking Him, the divine signal came to him to advance and not fear, for God informed him that he would triumph over Og king of Bashan, and that the people would possess all his land, as He had previously given him victory over Sihon and he possessed all his land.

entries.section: (5) The victory over the king of Bashan

paragraphs.text: Indeed Israel prevailed over Og and all his army and destroyed them completely and took possession of the land as the Lord had said.
None left him remaining: that is, none of his men escaped, but they all perished.
Consult God in all your decisions and do not undertake anything without His will, for if you submit your will to His will you will be successful in all the matters of your life.

The story of Balaam, an introduction: the next three chapters speak of the story of Balaam and his meeting with Balak king of the Moabites and his pronouncing blessing on the people instead of a curse.

entries.section: (1) Balaam's refusal to curse the people as Balak requested

paragraphs.text: The plains of Moab: the word "plain" (Arabah) means a waste or a place dominated by desert nature, and the word "plains" means an extended and desolate region, and it was applied to the whole region from the Gulf of Aqaba in the south to the Dead Sea in its middle and then the river Jordan to the north, and the expression "plains of Moab" means the region in which the tribes of the Moabites dwell (map 4). On this side Jordan by Jericho: the word "side" (ebar) means "the bank or shore of the river," and "on this side Jordan by Jericho" means the eastern bank of the Jordan opposite the city of Jericho.

After the victories of the children of Israel over the Amorites, they journeyed northward alongside the eastern bank, and when they were opposite Jericho, which lies on the western bank of the river Jordan, "Balak" king of Moab, whose lands extend alongside the Dead Sea to the south and the river Jordan to the north on the eastern side, saw them, and he was distressed and greatly terrified at the sight of the people and their great number on the one hand, and at what the people had done to "Sihon" and "Og" on the other.

entries.section: (1) Balaam's refusal to curse the people as Balak requested

paragraphs.text: Expressing his fear and dread, "Balak" gathered the chiefs of his people and his wise men of the Moabites and some elders of the Midianites who were pasturing their livestock in the lands of the Moabites, and said to them that this people is very numerous and that all the good things of our lands and our farms are not enough to feed them. The use of the expression "lick up" means that it will consume everything and there will be left for us no greenery or crops to eat after it, for it will leave the land bare.

entries.section: (1) Balaam's refusal to curse the people as Balak requested

paragraphs.text: Balaam the son of Beor: he is the same as Balaam the son of Bosor (2 Pet 2:15), and opinions differ about his person. Some regarded him as a diviner who followed Satan, because of the saying of Joshua the son of Nun, "Balaam also the son of Beor, the soothsayer" (Josh 13:22), but most commentators regarded him as a prophet of the Lord whom God used to deliver some messages to the peoples of the region, and this is confirmed by the following events in this chapter ... But although he was a prophet, the Holy Bible afterward describes him as betraying and allying with the enemies of the people for the sake of money, although he blessed the people with his mouth as God first commanded him (ch. 23). Pethor: the name of the village where Balaam lived, and it lies on the western bank of the river Euphrates. So Balaam was a prophet, but not of the children of Israel, but living among the Gentiles.
The land of the children of his people: that is, present-day Iraq.
A people come out from Egypt: that is, the people of Israel.

Balak sent messengers to Balaam at his place of residence, and they told him of his fears of the very numerous people of the children of Israel who had come out of Egypt and now stood in their full number before the borders of the Moabites.

entries.section: (1) Balaam's refusal to curse the people as Balak requested

paragraphs.text: The content of Balak's message was an invitation to Balaam to come and curse this numerous people, for Balak and the Amorites had no ability to fight it, but if Balaam cursed it, Balak would be able to defeat the children of Israel and drive them out of the whole region. And Balak adds in his message, as a kind of praise for Balaam, that it is known of him that whoever he blesses is blessed, and whoever he curses is cursed by God.

entries.section: (1) Balaam's refusal to curse the people as Balak requested

paragraphs.text: The rewards of divination: that is, a gift and reward in return for his divination or his cursing of the people, and its colloquial meaning, which some people still use, is "the sweets" given in return for good news. As for the word divination, its meaning by itself is knowledge of the unseen.

The delegates and messengers of Balak, from the elders of the Moabites and the Midianites, came with a valuable gift to Balaam and told him all that Balak had said before ... As for Balaam's reply to them, it was not hasty, but he asked them to lodge overnight so that he might pray to God and learn His opinion ... From this it appears that Balaam was wavering between obedience to God and love of money, which will appear afterward.
Would that you not hurry or give an answer about an opinion or counsel before you lift your heart to God in a quick prayer.

entries.section: (1) Balaam's refusal to curse the people as Balak requested

paragraphs.text: And God came unto Balaam: it may have been in a vision, or God sent him an angel.

Although God knew all the events, in His message to Balaam He asks him like one inquiring about something, "What men are these with thee?", in order to alert Balaam so that he would be on guard against the events to come.

entries.section: (1) Balaam's refusal to curse the people as Balak requested

paragraphs.text: Balaam's answer came as a faithful summary of what had come before in verses (5-7).

entries.section: (1) Balaam's refusal to curse the people as Balak requested

paragraphs.text: As for God's reply to Balaam's words, it was decisive and clear, for He told him plainly not to go with them and not to curse the people, and God made clear to him that it is a blessed people and that God Himself is the cause and secret of its blessing.

entries.section: (1) Balaam's refusal to curse the people as Balak requested

paragraphs.text: Balaam's answer to the messengers of Balak came exactly as the Lord had commanded him, for he refused to go to their lands, making clear that God had forbidden him, so the chiefs returned to Balak without Balaam and told him of his refusal to come with them.

It is to be noted that Balaam told the messengers of Balak all of God's words, which is His saying that the people of Israel is blessed by God, and perhaps he had become attached to Balak's gifts and wished that he would send to him again with new gifts.

entries.section: (2) The second delegation from Balak to Balaam

paragraphs.text: Balak did not despair at Balaam's first refusal, so he returned and sent him a delegation more numerous and of higher rank and standing, and the message of this delegation to Balaam was that he should come down with them to meet Balak and curse the people of the children of Israel. The delegation enticed him by saying that Balak would honor him very greatly, meaning of course gifts and monetary offerings, and that he would also carry out for him any wish or request.

entries.section: (2) The second delegation from Balak to Balaam

paragraphs.text: Balaam's answer was unexpected by the delegation sent to him, for he appeared decisive and clear and refused the offer and enticement, whatever was offered to him of money, gold or silver, and he declared his unwillingness to go against God's word to satisfy Balak's wish. This shows the good side in him, that is, his holding to obedience to God, if only outwardly, although he would afterward devise a way to disobey it.

entries.section: (2) The second delegation from Balak to Balaam

paragraphs.text: Despite Balaam's sound position in the preceding verse, it carried more pretense than sincerity, and here his heart began to expose him, for he knew already that it was God who had prevented him from cursing the people and from going with them. But this last offer from Balak swayed his heart, and therefore he proposed to the messengers that they stay with him overnight, perhaps that God would bring him something new other than what He had said to him before, that is, he was not decisive in refusing their new invitation and their gifts.

Very often this happens to us ... when God's will is perfectly clear in some matter, but because of our own wicked or self-serving will we argue with ourselves, hoping that God has another opinion, and perhaps we ask many people in roundabout ways until we get an answer that agrees with what we want and not what God wants... Reject enticement and weakness and listen to the voice of God within you.

entries.section: (2) The second delegation from Balak to Balaam

paragraphs.text: God spoke with Balaam by night and permitted him to go with the men, but He set him a condition that he speak only what God commanded him.
She ass: a female donkey.
Perhaps we ask why God permitted Balaam to go after he had refused at first?!!
First: because God knew well that what Balaam had uttered was not what was within him, for the lust for money had stirred in him.

Second: God had a plan through which He wanted to teach him a lesson, and we shall see that in the coming verses. Third: God's plan also included that Balaam bless the people instead of cursing them before Balak, so that Balak would be certain that this people is the people of God, who enjoys His protection.

entries.section: (2) The second delegation from Balak to Balaam

paragraphs.text: Balaam rose in the morning and saddled his donkey and set out with the messengers to meet Balak.

entries.section: (3) Balaam and his meeting with the angel of the Lord on the way

paragraphs.text: His two servants: two of his slaves.

Balaam took two of his slaves with him on the way to meet Balak, and while he was riding on his she ass, the angel of the Lord stood in his way and stopped before him, and the inspired Word indicates that God was angry at Balaam's conduct because his heart was attached to the love of money, and God had agreed to his going in order to test his heart. So the appearance of the angel and his rebuke of him was an opportunity for his repentance, as we explained before, and the time of the lesson had come here, and God's showing His displeasure.

entries.section: (3) Balaam and his meeting with the angel of the Lord on the way

paragraphs.text: The angel appeared in a fearful sight, for he carried a drawn sword in his hand, and the remarkable thing is that the one who saw him was the donkey and not Balaam the prophet. Of course this was by divine arrangement, that the angel should appear to the donkey without Balaam seeing him, in order that God might show us the blindness of the man whose eyes money and gold have shut, so that he does not see God nor hear His voice. And the she ass was disturbed by the fearful sight and left the road and turned aside into the field, and Balaam struck her to bring her back to the road.

entries.section: (3) Balaam and his meeting with the angel of the Lord on the way

paragraphs.text: A path of the vineyards: a narrow road or passage between two walls, roofed by a grape trellis.

During the journey the she ass passed through a narrow passage, and when she saw the angel and his sword again she was terrified and leaned toward one of the two walls, and as she leaned she pressed against the leg and foot of Balaam, who of course was angered at the conduct of the she ass and struck her a second time.

entries.section: (3) Balaam and his meeting with the angel of the Lord on the way

paragraphs.text: To turn: to draw back.
She fell down: she lay down.

In another place on the road, which was still narrower, the angel stood again before the she ass, in a place where she could not turn to the right or to the left, so she stopped walking altogether, and therefore Balaam was very angry and struck her a third time, and more violently.

entries.section: (3) Balaam and his meeting with the angel of the Lord on the way

paragraphs.text: Mocked: despised.

We now stand before a great divine miracle, for God by His power made the animal speak with Balaam, and the speech came in the form of a reproach, as the animal asked the man why he had struck her three times. We do not know Balaam's reaction when he heard the animal speak, but we believe it was a mixture of astonishment and fear, yet this did not prevent Balaam from speaking with the she ass and answering her that he struck her because she had disobeyed him three times in walking, and he added that he was very angry with her and that she deserved to be killed and not merely struck.

entries.section: (3) Balaam and his meeting with the angel of the Lord on the way

paragraphs.text: Continuing the dialogue, the she ass replies to Balaam again, trying to draw his attention to her constant obedience to him since he had owned her before this day, and she asked him whether she had ever rebelled against him before, and he answered no.

The message is clear to all of us through these events, by which God wants to rebuke Balaam, as if He were telling him that the dumb animal obeyed My will, but you, O man, since evil filled your heart, did not understand and did not see what the animal saw!!!!!!
May we, when we are exposed to afflictions, examine ourselves so as to repent of our sins and learn from the events of life and even from animals as well.

entries.section: (3) Balaam and his meeting with the angel of the Lord on the way

paragraphs.text: God opened Balaam's eyes, and he saw the angel and his drawn sword, and then he was so afraid that he got down from his donkey and bowed before the angel.

entries.section: (3) Balaam and his meeting with the angel of the Lord on the way

paragraphs.text: Thy way is perverse before me: the way is thorny and leads to destruction.
To withstand: to prevent, hinder and warn.

The angel spoke to Balaam, making clear to him that his appearing to him was to prevent him from going and cursing the people, and he makes clear that the hidden things of his heart, that is, his love of money, are exposed before God. He also rebukes him for striking his she ass three times without cause, and that the she ass was better than he spiritually, since she saw the angel whom he did not see because of his evil. And the angel adds, in his defense of the struck she ass, that if she had not done so, the angel of the Lord would have killed him and spared the she ass.

entries.section: (3) Balaam and his meeting with the angel of the Lord on the way

paragraphs.text: Balaam offered an immediate apology to the angel of the Lord, making clear to him that he had not seen him, otherwise he would not have struck the she ass three times, and, completing his apology, he declared his immediate readiness not to complete his journey to Balak and to return to his house; but the angel commanded him to complete his journey, though he must not say anything of his own but speak what the Spirit of God would tell him by means of the angel, and therefore Balaam completed his journey with the messengers of Balak.

Balaam carried many contradictions in his character, yet it must not escape us here to highlight his quick response of repentance and apology. For the word "I have sinned" that he said was the cause of his deliverance from punishment, while Adam did not utter it when he fell!!! May we all learn to apologize quickly for error and not justify ourselves, for the word "I have sinned" calms the anger of the one we have wronged and makes God have pity on our weakness.

entries.section: (4) Balak and Balaam

paragraphs.text: One of Balak's messengers went ahead of the procession and told him of Balaam's coming this time, and in his great joy at this news Balak went out quickly to receive Balaam at the farthest border of his country, as is done in receiving great men. He did not wait for him to enter the land of the Moabites but went out himself to the border, and at the first city of the Moabites, called "a city of Moab," which lies on the border at the small river Arnon, he received Balaam.

entries.section: (4) Balak and Balaam

paragraphs.text: Balak was first to greet Balaam and speak, and in a gentle reproach he asked him, did I not send for you before? Why then did you not come? And now that you have come, shall I not honor you and give you abundant reward?

entries.section: (4) Balak and Balaam

paragraphs.text: Balaam answered that he was here now and this was what mattered, and under the effect of his fear from the sight of the angel whom he had seen a little while before, he added to Balak that he would not be able to speak anything but what God says to him.

entries.section: (4) Balak and Balaam

paragraphs.text: Balaam went with Balak to a village named "Kirjath-huzoth," one of the cities of Moab and the first city fit to receive and honor Balaam and those with him, and it lies north of the river Arnon, and Balak was very generous, for he slaughtered for the feast in honor of Balaam many oxen and sheep, although the number of men was small, but he wanted to show Balaam the extent of his generosity as an indication of what Balaam would get of gifts and gold if he cursed the people, and it also shows the warmth of the reception of this great guest.

entries.section: (4) Balak and Balaam

paragraphs.text: The high places of Baal: the name of a high and elevated place, like a plateau, which was called "Baal."

Because they used to sacrifice to Baal on it, that is, they offered worship to Baal as one of the pagan worships (map 6). The chain of mountains of Abarim, Shittim. Map (6). After spending a night of honor and rest, Balak took Balaam in the early morning to a high place, the "high places of Baal," and showed him the people from there, and because the place was high Balaam was able to see all the people to the farthest point of their encampment.

The enticements of the world are many to distract you from God's commandments, but on the other hand God warns you so that you do not perish with this wicked world, as the angel warned Balaam, so hold fast to God's commandments, and do not run after the dazzling allurements of the world, for all of them are passing away, and if you have become preoccupied with them, hasten to return to God and set limits to your attachment to the world.
The discourses (parables) of Balaam, an introduction:

In this chapter and the one after it (ch. 24) we find four discourses that Balaam uttered about the people of Israel and then a prophecy about other peoples. This chapter includes the first and second of them, while the coming chapter includes the third and fourth.

entries.section: (1) Balaam's first discourse (parable)

paragraphs.text: Balaam asked Balak to build him seven altars on the high places of Baal, "here," and asked that a bull and a ram be sacrificed on each altar to offer to the Lord. We do not know why he asked for seven altars instead of one, but some see that he did so in honor of the Lord, who had not forgotten His angel with the drawn sword.

entries.section: (1) Balaam's first discourse (parable)

paragraphs.text: Because of Balak's confidence in Balaam and the power of his prophecy or the power of his sorcery, he responded at once and offered a bull and a ram on each altar, and Balak, as the priest for his people, took part in offering up these burnt offerings on the seven altars.

entries.section: (1) Balaam's first discourse (parable)

paragraphs.text: A bare height: a high place.

Balaam asked Balak to remain beside his altars and his sacrifices, while he would go alone to a high place, perhaps the Lord would answer and speak with him, and Balaam promised Balak that he would tell him all that the Lord said to him or showed him.

entries.section: (1) Balaam's first discourse (parable)

paragraphs.text: We do not know how the Lord came to Balaam, whether it was a vision or He sent him an angel, but we find Balaam speaking with God of all that he had done in building the altars and offering burnt offerings on them, and perhaps by this saying he wanted to appease God with these seven altars.

entries.section: (1) Balaam's first discourse (parable)

paragraphs.text: God spoke with Balaam and put a word in his mouth and commanded him to return to Balak and to speak this word. And indeed Balaam returned to Balak and found him standing by his altars and his burnt offerings, with the chiefs and great men of his people.

entries.section: (1) Balaam's first discourse (parable)

paragraphs.text: He took up his parable: the four discourses of Balaam were called parables, perhaps because of the wisdom they contain and because they were spoken in a measured prose form that approached poetry.
Aram: highlands between the rivers Tigris and Euphrates, that is, present-day Iraq.

Balaam said at the beginning of his discourse, "Balak the king of Moab hath brought me from Aram, out of the mountains of the east," saying, "Come, curse me Jacob, and come, defy Israel." It is to be noted in this that Balaam pronounced the old name Jacob and his new title Israel, which confirms that what he spoke was a spirit of prophecy from God.

entries.section: (1) Balaam's first discourse (parable)

paragraphs.text: Balaam rejects answering Balak's request and declares clearly that he cannot curse or revile what God has not cursed. He continues his discourse that he sees this people with its abundant number from his high place on which he stands, that is, "the top of the rocks," and describes the people of God as follows:
1- A people dwelling alone: that is, it is an independent people that does not share with the pagan peoples in their evils or their pagan sacrifices, but has its own divine laws.
2- Not reckoned among the nations: that is, God distinguished it from the rest of the peoples and considered it a chosen people and a firstborn son to Him.
The fourth part: a dwelling or tents.

entries.section: (1) Balaam's first discourse (parable)

paragraphs.text: Who can count this great people, in whose number God gave blessing so that it became like the sand of the earth and its dust (Gen 22:17), indeed who can even count the number of the tents of this people, as an allusion to the abundance of number and strength. And after Balaam uttered this speech that the Lord put in his mouth, he turned his speech to something else, for he wished for himself that his life on earth might end having received a blessing like that which God reserved for His people Israel, so that his soul would die like these righteous ones and he would have a share in the eternity that God prepared for them.

It is to be noted that this speech is the word of God on the tongue of Balaam and not the feelings of his heart, as is proved by the fact that he afterward devised a plot to destroy the children of Israel (ch. 25).

entries.section: (1) Balaam's first discourse (parable)

paragraphs.text: Balak was distressed by Balaam's words, so Balak reproached him, saying to him, I brought you and honored you to curse this people, and behold you bless them instead of cursing them. Balaam answered him that he had done nothing except utter what the Lord had declared to him, and he can do nothing else.
May your wishes for life with God become real action through earnest striving, and be confident that God will support you to enjoy fellowship with Him and then to rejoice in eternal life with Him.

entries.section: (2) Balaam's second discourse

paragraphs.text: The utmost part of them: its far extremities.

The field of Zophim, to the top of Pisgah: the top of Pisgah is one of the peaks of the chain of mountains of Abarim that extends northeast of the Dead Sea, and the field of Zophim was on this peak, and from the top of Pisgah Moses saw the land of Canaan before he died (Deut 34:1) (map 6). Balak thought that when Balaam saw this people in its abundant number from his place, the high places of Baal, he was terrified by the greatness of the number and therefore did not curse the people, and so he invited him to accompany him to another place, also high, which is the top of one of the hills. Balak's aim in this new place was that Balaam should see only a part or an edge of the people, that is, a small part, so that his soul might be reassured and he could curse the people. And Balak did as Balaam had asked at first, for he built seven altars and offered a bull and a ram on each altar.

entries.section: (2) Balaam's second discourse

paragraphs.text: These three verses are a similar repetition of what came in verses (3-5) of the same chapter.

entries.section: (2) Balaam's second discourse

paragraphs.text: After Balaam returned from his second retreat and Balak's anxious question about what the Lord had spoken with him, Balaam began to speak, addressing Balak, saying to him, rise up and listen well and prepare yourself for the word that God has sent you, for God is the God of truth and not like man, who is liable to lie, and not like the sons of men who issue judgments and then repent of them and withdraw what they have spoken. Is it reasonable that God should say something and not do it (God forbid), or give a promise and not be able to fulfill it?! For God has promised His people blessing, and He must fulfill His promise.

Sometimes it is mentioned in the Holy Bible that God repents of a decision He issued, as happened with the people of Nineveh in the days of Jonah, and what is meant is an expression that human beings understand, namely repentance, but the truth is that God is compassionate and forgives men if they repent; the change comes from men, and it is repentance, and so God forgives them.

entries.section: (2) Balaam's second discourse

paragraphs.text: I, Balaam, was commanded earlier and now by God to bless this people and not curse them, and God has indeed blessed this people, so who am I that I should oppose or annul His blessing?

entries.section: (2) Balaam's second discourse

paragraphs.text: The shout of a king: they used to sound trumpets at the feasts to glorify God their King.

We cannot forget the people's earlier errors and their murmurings and God's punishment of them, but with all this, God in His love and mercy sees no fault in His people so long as they repent and are sorry for their evil. Though He punishes them, He is a Father who pities the weaknesses of men. He called His people to come out of Egypt knowing all that would come from them, and He even declares that He saw in His people no fault or sin for which they deserve a curse, for the Lord their God is with them and dwells in their midst as their King, and they sing and praise His holy name.

And the people of God are distinguished from the rest of the Gentile peoples by their faith in God, and their errors toward God they quickly turn back from, so He means the relative perfection of His people.

entries.section: (2) Balaam's second discourse

paragraphs.text: The unicorn (reem): one of the swift kinds of gazelles (the antelope).
Enchantment: sorcery.
Divination: astrology.

Balaam continues his discourse and says, is this not the people that its God brought out with the right hand of His power from the land of Egypt, and it went out of it with the speed of the gazelle and no harm from Pharaoh and his soldiers overtook it? Therefore nothing of the works of sorcerers will afflict this people, whether sorcery or astrology, for it is a people that shelters in its great God, and a time will come (after the people's settling) when it will be told among the nations what God has done with His people from their going out of Egypt until their victory over the nations and their possessing the land.

entries.section: (2) Balaam's second discourse

paragraphs.text: It is a people that rises to attack its enemies with the strength of the lioness (the female lion), which is famous for hunting, seizing prey and speed more than the male lions, and it lifts itself up among the nations like the lion, which has more authority than the rest of the animals, and God has given this people victory, for it does not rest nor sleep until it finishes off all its enemies among the nations and destroys them.

My beloved brother ... how beautiful is the heart of God, who forgives His people and does not forsake them before their enemies ... The prodigal son sinned, and yet his compassionate father received him on his return (Lk 15). So take courage, and encourage others also to repent, for Christ receives everyone in tenderness when they repent and confess, for He does not desire the death of the sinner so much as that he return and live.. and He keeps His promises and covenants to all His people.

entries.section: (3) Balak's third attempt

paragraphs.text: Balak was greatly distressed and enraged by Balaam's discourse, and therefore we find him asking Balaam that if he was not able to curse the people, then at least he should not bless them, but Balaam's answer to Balak came that he had already informed him that he would not speak anything of his own, but everything the Lord speaks he would tell to Balak.

entries.section: (3) Balak's third attempt

paragraphs.text: In a new attempt and an unjustified insistence, Balak proposed to Balaam to take him to another place, in the hope that the Lord would change His mind and, with the new sacrifices, permit the cursing of His people.

In this third attempt of Balak we discover the stubbornness and stupidity of the wicked man in understanding God or His purposes. King Balak did not despair of trying to bribe God with sacrifices or to bribe Balaam himself, who in his third obedience to Balak also reveals the evil lust of his heart to obtain Balak's material blessings, as if God changes His mind, though he knew well that God is not a man that He should change His mind or turn back from what He promised (v. 19).

entries.section: (3) Balak's third attempt

paragraphs.text: The top of Peor: one of the mountain peaks overlooking the wilderness, on which the pagan Baal "Peor" was worshiped, and it is the northern peak of the mountains of Abarim (map 6). Balak took Balaam to the holiest of the hills to him and his people, for they sacrifice there to the god "Peor," and he thought that this place had a special standing and an awesome holiness that might make God change His thought and heart if the burnt offerings were offered from this place... And this place was high, so it overlooks the whole wilderness in which Israel pitches its tents.

entries.section: (3) Balak's third attempt

paragraphs.text: And as he had done before, Balaam asked that seven altars be built and burnt offerings be offered on them, consisting of seven bulls and seven rams. And Balak also did what Balaam asked of him, for he was thirsty to curse the people whatever the price or cost.

If God proclaims His voice to you to repent of your sins, return to Him and do not persist in your snare, taking advantage of God's longsuffering, for His mercy is upon you if you benefit from it, but your making light of His mercies will in the end bring His wrath upon you and you will perish.
The third and fourth discourses of Balaam

entries.section: (1) Balaam's third discourse

paragraphs.text: The wilderness: the wilderness of Moab adjoining the Dead Sea, in which the children of Israel pitched their tents, that is, Balaam looked toward the people of the children of Israel.

In the two previous times Balaam would leave the altars and go far away into retreat to receive the divine revelation, but this time, as he was sure that the Lord wanted to bless the people and not curse them, he thought it good to remain in his place, looking toward the wilderness toward the people and waiting for God's revelation to come upon him.
To meet with enchantments: that is, to receive a revelation or a divine message.

entries.section: (1) Balaam's third discourse

paragraphs.text: Balaam looked at the people abiding in the camp around the tent of meeting with all its twelve tribes, and the Spirit of God came upon him, so he prophesied and spoke before Balak that what he uttered was not his own word but a revelation from God, a revelation to a man whose eyes are open, that is, it was granted him by God to see and hear what God wanted to convey to Balak.

entries.section: (1) Balaam's third discourse

paragraphs.text: He declares and confirms again that he speaks what he hears from God, and that he sees a heavenly vision, majestic and fearful, that makes him fall to the ground in fear and reverence for it. The expression "having his eyes open" means that it is a true vision and not a dream about which people may differ.

entries.section: (1) Balaam's third discourse

paragraphs.text: Balaam uttered sweet words about the people of Israel, describing the beauty of its tents around the tent of meeting with its order and the banners of its tribes, and he also describes it as having an abundance of number extending like gardens and orchards and like the trees of lign aloes, fragrant, which God blessed and planted and tended, and its tents are also likened to the tall cedar trees, famous for the high price of their wood and their greenness throughout the year ... and all these similes point to the standing of this people in the heart of God.

entries.section: (1) Balaam's third discourse

paragraphs.text: His buckets: the plural of bucket, that is, a vessel with which they fill water.
Agag: a title that was given to the kings of the people of Amalek, as the title Pharaoh was given to the kings of Egypt.

Balaam continued describing the people and praising them, using poetry and symbol, and he says that this people in its descendants and multiplication will be like the water overflowing from a full bucket when it is carried, and he repeats the meaning again in a new form using the expression "many waters," while its kingdom will be a great and exalted kingdom, and its kings will be higher than the kings of the Amalekites, who bear the title Agag.

entries.section: (1) Balaam's third discourse

paragraphs.text: Break their bones: breaks and grinds the bones with his teeth.
His arrows: that is, the arrows of Agag, the strongest of the kings in the region.

God enveloped it in His love and care, so He brought it out with a strong arm from Egypt, and the people became like the gazelle in its speed (ch. 23:22), and God gave it strength to triumph over all the nations that oppress it and destroy them, and "break their arrows," meaning "Agag," that is, take away from its enemies their strength and their honor.

entries.section: (1) Balaam's third discourse

paragraphs.text: He couched: he sat.
He lay down: he sat and settled on the ground.

This people sat in its place in a state of alertness and readiness to leap and seize its enemies, like the lion and the lioness, which no one can move, and everyone who blesses this people and does good to it, God blesses him, and everyone who curses this people or stands before it, God curses him.
This verse also signifies Christ, who rested on the Cross and by His death bound Satan and all his soldiers, for He is the Lion that came out of the tribe of Judah to save those who believe in Him.

entries.section: (1) Balaam's third discourse

paragraphs.text: Balaam ended his discourse and his third parable, and the result and Balak's reaction was rage and anger at Balaam, so he smote his hands together in astonishment and declared his distress, saying, I brought you and honored your hospitality to curse and revile my enemies, that is, the people of Israel, and behold, instead you have blessed them three times.

entries.section: (1) Balaam's third discourse

paragraphs.text: Also in anger Balak commanded Balaam to leave his land at once, "flee," and added that he had wanted to honor him if he cursed this people, but by these words of his he would receive no honor, for the Lord, Balaam's God, had kept him back from this honor.

entries.section: (1) Balaam's third discourse

paragraphs.text: Balaam defends himself by saying that he deceived no one, and clarified his earlier position, that he had promised nothing, and he reminds Balak of what he had told his messengers from the first, that he would not utter anything other than what God declares to him even if the enticement were all Balak's wealth). (ch. 23:18).

entries.section: (1) Balaam's third discourse

paragraphs.text: Balaam announces the end of his journey and mission and his return to his people, but he adds, addressing Balak, that before his going he will declare a last prophecy of what the people of the children of Israel will do to his people, and of course Balaam did not declare anything of his own but what the Lord declared to him also, and this prophecy was Balaam's fourth discourse, as we shall see.

If God is with you He blesses you, and the whole world cannot stand before you. So do not be shaken however much those who wrong you increase, for God protects you from their rage and their threats and establishes your peace.

entries.section: (2) Balaam's fourth discourse and parable

paragraphs.text: Balaam began his fourth discourse with what he had said at the beginning of his third discourse in (vv. 3, 4).

entries.section: (2) Balaam's fourth discourse and parable

paragraphs.text: The corners of Moab: that is, its strength, because a people fortifies its borders with its military strength, and what is meant is the breaking of its strength.
Tumult (sons of Sheth): war, and what is meant is the destruction of everyone who fights him.
Balaam began his fourth discourse with a speech that may seem obscure, for he speaks of some person and not of the people of Israel, and describes this person as follows:
1- He is a man, but the time of his coming is not the present time but he will come in the distant future.
2- He will be a star in his brightness and shining, a clear indication of his purity and righteousness.
3- He carries a scepter in his hands, for he is a king and has absolute authority and sovereignty.
4- He smites the corners of Moab, that is, by his coming he declares the end of the pagan worships, which Moab symbolizes.
5- He destroys the sons of tumult: that is, he rules over and destroys the wicked by the authority of his everlasting kingdom.

It is clear that all the speech here has no relation to Balak and the people of Israel, but the divine inspiration used Balaam to utter a prophecy that applies to none of mankind except the Lord Christ, God incarnate, who alone has authority, kingship and glory. And Christ is the One who will come from the people of the children of Israel and break the power of the wicked, which Moab symbolizes.

entries.section: (2) Balaam's fourth discourse and parable

paragraphs.text: Edom: they are the descendants of Esau.
Seir: the mountains of Seir are the regions in which the Edomites lived.

And among the attributes of Christ also is that He reigns over the neighboring peoples and subdues them to Himself, so the Gentiles believe in Him and He reigns over the hearts of those who are symbolized by the people of Edom, that is, Christianity spreads among the Gentiles.

entries.section: (2) Balaam's fourth discourse and parable

paragraphs.text: And the authority of Christ will be over every city, that is, the whole world, but those who did not accept Him as King over them, that is, the wanderers, their end is destruction.

entries.section: (2) Balaam's fourth discourse and parable

paragraphs.text: Amalek: they are the descendants of Eliphaz, firstborn of Esau (Gen 36:13, 14), and their land was south of Canaan.

Balaam saw another sight in his vision and declared it concerning the people of Amalek, who always represented the wicked peoples that resisted the people of God (Ex 17:8), so he says that Amalek was the first of the nations to fight the people of God and resist it and was also the strongest of the peoples at this time, but look at his end, for God destroyed him; God may permit the wicked to exist for a while or for some time, but their end is always destruction.

entries.section: (2) Balaam's fourth discourse and parable

paragraphs.text: The Kenite: they are the descendants of a man called "Cain" who lived in the regions where the Edomites lived.
Thy dwellingplace ... thy nest: the place of your residence.

These two verses point to some tribes who lived in the mountains and caves, descended from Cain, and who thought that they were immune from evil and destruction, but the time of the Assyrian state will come and it will take possession, that is, take captive, these tribes.

entries.section: (2) Balaam's fourth discourse and parable

paragraphs.text: Balaam completes his speech and says, but who shall live and survive until all these future events happen? No one of the present generation, and what is meant is that this prophecy relates to the relatively distant future.

entries.section: (2) Balaam's fourth discourse and parable

paragraphs.text: Chittim: a name that was given to the island of Cyprus and was also given to the European kingdoms, which include the Greek and Roman kingdoms.

Ships will come from beyond the sea, whether carrying the Greeks led by Alexander the Great first and then followed by the Romans second, and these new nations will subdue the kingdoms before them such as Babylon and Assyria, and also Eber, that is, the Jewish kingdom, who are the Hebrews, the descendants of Eber, and the whole region of the East and the Mediterranean basin. And he also shall perish for ever: what is meant here is the new invader, that is, the Greeks and the Romans, for even the new powerful kingdoms, with all their philosophy or power, will not stand before the great Star that comes out of Jacob, that is, Christ (v. 17). With these messianic prophecies concerning Christ Balaam ended his fourth and last discourse.

entries.section: (2) Balaam's fourth discourse and parable

paragraphs.text: The end of the meeting was in parting, so Balaam and Balak each went to the way of his return and the place from which he had come.

The kingdoms of the world fluctuate and all its powers change, so do not be troubled by them or attached to them, but stand firm in your faith in Christ, who protects you in this world and gives you to enjoy bliss forever.
The fornication of Israel and the zeal of Phinehas

entries.section: (1) Israel's fornication and fall into idolatry

paragraphs.text: Shittim: the word Shittim means acacia trees, and this word was applied to the place where the people camped because of the availability of a large number of acacia trees in this place (map 5). Although the people were very near the Promised Land and nothing separated them from it but the river Jordan, they fell into a great evil, for they fell into fornication with the pagan daughters of Moab and thereby violated all the divine covenants and commandments. The Book of Revelation mentions that behind this terrible stumbling block that brought the people down was Balaam, for he is the one who suggested this to Balak out of greed for money, since he failed to obtain Balak's gifts because God commanded him to bless the people and not curse them, so he resorted to this stratagem to obtain Balak's gifts and told him that if the people of Israel committed fornication and worshiped idols, their God would forsake them (see Rev 2:14), making it easy for Balak to fight and defeat them. And this is what actually happened, for the women of the Moabites whom Balak sent seduced the men of Israel.

entries.section: (1) Israel's fornication and fall into idolatry

paragraphs.text: And because sin drags another sin behind it, and lust, when it possesses a man, takes away his will and his insight, the people fell into the next sin, which is the sin of idolatry and bowing down and offering incense to idols, in open defiance of God, their Savior and Redeemer and the One who brought them out of the land of Egypt. For the Moabite women lured the men of the children of Israel just as happened with King Solomon (1 Kgs 11), and as a kind of courtesy and participation the men bowed down and worshiped the idols.

entries.section: (1) Israel's fornication and fall into idolatry

paragraphs.text: The matter developed from mere bowing down to something more, for it became faith and love toward the god of the Moabites, and the people replaced their God with an image and an idol to which they sacrifice, from which they ask, and in whose powers they trust, namely the god Peor, so God's anger was kindled against His ungrateful people, who insulted Him and insulted His holy name and His glory and honor.

entries.section: (1) Israel's fornication and fall into idolatry

paragraphs.text: The Lord spoke with Moses and commanded him to take "the heads of the people" and to hang them on a tree after killing them, and that their bodies be left "before the sun," that is, before the eyes of all the people, so that they might be a lesson to the rest of the people and the sin might stop and God's anger against them also stop, so that they would not be exposed to the greater punishment. So Moses gathered the judges of the people and commanded them to kill "every one his men," that is, everyone of his tribe who had worshiped Baal-peor and seduced others to worship him.

Sin is exceedingly sinful, and a man sinks into it gradually, and when he makes light of God's kindness and patience and does not repent after his fall, the punishment is great and severe. For God does not tolerate evil, so beware, my brother, of being careless, and do not say that this sin is small and that one is great, for the first leads to the second, and the wages of both is death.

entries.section: (2) The zeal of Phinehas the son of Eleazar

paragraphs.text: The people took refuge at the tent of meeting, as they were deeply affected by God's anger and the killing and hanging of some of their men, and also in seeking His mercies, since God, besides the killing of those fornicators and worshipers of Baal, struck the people with the plague, which took thousands of them (v. 9). And while the people were weeping over their sin and asking for pardon, a man of the tribe of Simeon appeared with a Midianite woman, in open defiance of Moses and all the feelings of the people, and to add a new provocation to God by his carelessness and his insolence against the holiness of the house of God, for he passed before it in pride and arrogance.

entries.section: (2) The zeal of Phinehas the son of Eleazar

paragraphs.text: Phinehas the son of Eleazar the son of Aaron was a priest, and his father Eleazar was high priest after the death of Aaron, and when Phinehas saw the sight of this Israelite man with the woman, he was jealous with great zeal for the house of the Lord and the glory of the name of the God of Israel, and took a spear, most likely from one of the men around him, and went in after the man into the tent, "the pavilion," and thrust both the man and the woman through the belly with the spear and killed them, and when God saw what Phinehas had done, He lifted the plague from Israel.

entries.section: (2) The zeal of Phinehas the son of Eleazar

paragraphs.text: The number of those who died in the plague was twenty-four thousand, and we notice that St. Paul mentioned this very incident in (1 Cor 10:8) with a difference in the number, for he said that they were twenty-three thousand ... so is there a difference ...?! In answer to this difference we say:

a) The first opinion: that the total number of those killed was twenty-four thousand, of whom twenty-three thousand were in one day, as St. Paul mentioned in the text of the verse, and therefore the following thousand could have been on another day.

b) The second opinion: that the true number who died in the plague is a figure between twenty-three thousand and twenty-four thousand, and that the Book of Numbers used rounding up and St. Paul used rounding down to the lower whole number.

entries.section: (2) The zeal of Phinehas the son of Eleazar

paragraphs.text: Perhaps some felt that this conduct of Phinehas was excessive, but the situation was a contempt on the part of the Israelite man, the companion of the Midianite woman, that would stir up laxity among the people, so God declared His pleasure and delight in what His priest Phinehas did, and declared this to Moses. And He makes clear that this conduct of Phinehas represents what God wanted, for he was jealous with a jealousy like that of the heart of God and acted according to His pleasure, and God declares to Moses that because of this conduct the rest of the people were not consumed, and therefore He commanded Moses to tell Phinehas that God gives him a special blessing and a covenant of peace. And the expression "covenant of peace" means a firm covenant for his peace.

entries.section: (2) The zeal of Phinehas the son of Eleazar

paragraphs.text: As a reward for Phinehas, God gives His promise and blessing to him and to his descendants after him that his priesthood would be an everlasting priesthood, in return for what he did and how he removed God's wrath from His people by punishing the sinner.

And the expression "everlasting priesthood" means so long as the Levitical priesthood remains, which would of course end with the coming of Christ and the cessation of animal sacrifices. And every covenant to which the inspired Word applied the description everlasting means a covenant that remains in force as long as man is careful to keep it, but if man sins and neglects his life, he by this conduct annuls this covenant and even deserves punishment. And the verse in its spiritual meaning also makes clear to us that God never forgets the labor, or the true witness, or the zeal of a man offered for the glory of His name, for God keeps His covenant and His kindnesses to those who love His holy name.

entries.section: (2) The zeal of Phinehas the son of Eleazar

paragraphs.text: In these two verses the name of the Hebrew man and the Midianite woman is mentioned, so as Phinehas was honored and his name and his work mentioned, so also God mentions the name of the one who sinned and was killed, and the remarkable thing is that the sinful man was a chief of one of the clans of the Simeonites and had a high standing among his tribe, but God and His priest, who was responsible for carrying out His commandments, wants to teach us that there is no partiality in the execution of His judgment. It is to be noted that the woman was also the daughter of a chief of one of the clans of the Midianites, who was like a ruler or a mayor, for example. And this shows Phinehas' courage in his obedience to God's command, not fearing the position of the man or the woman.

Beware of laxity or sin even if you are a servant or a deacon or a leader, because no person is above error, and although God forgives all sinners when they repent, He punishes the careless and the one who treats sin as permissible.

entries.section: (2) The zeal of Phinehas the son of Eleazar

paragraphs.text: After the end of the plague, God commands Moses to fight the Midianites, and God makes clear the reason for the war against them: they are the authors of the plot and the snare that they set for the people of the children of Israel, and of their being brought down into fornication and bowing down to Baal-peor, and among them was the fornicating woman "Cozbi," the daughter of one of the chiefs of their clans, whom Phinehas the priest killed when he was jealous with zeal for the Lord. And indeed Israel fought Midian and prevailed over them, and the details of that are in (ch. 31). It is to be noted here that there was an alliance of the Midianites, among whom was "Cozbi," with the Moabites, who sent daughters to cause the children of Israel to stumble and fall into fornication, for some tribes of the Midianites lived beside the Moabites, and therefore God commanded Moses to fight the Midianites, in addition to the fact that He had fought the Moabites also.
The second numbering of the people and the numbering of the Levites

entries.section: (1) The numbering of the people

paragraphs.text: After the incident of the plague and the death of about twenty-four thousand, God commanded Moses, together with Eleazar the priest, to take the sum and number of all the males of the people of the children of Israel who were more than twenty years old, who are those able to bear arms and go to war. And the expression "after the house of their fathers" means according to their tribes and clans, except the tribe of Levi, because it is set apart for the service of the house of God.

This is the second numbering of the people, while the first was 38 years before, at the beginning of their going out to the wilderness of Sinai, and it is the one mentioned in (Ex 30:11, 38:36, and also ch. 1).

entries.section: (1) The numbering of the people

paragraphs.text: The plains of Moab: the place where the people were settled at that time, which is the plain extending east of the river Jordan opposite Jericho, which lies across on the western side of the Jordan (map 5). Moses and Eleazar spoke with the people of what God had commanded them, as He had commanded them 38 years before in the first numbering after their coming out of the land of Egypt and their encamping in the wilderness.

entries.section: (1) The numbering of the people

paragraphs.text: In verses (5-51) is a listing of each tribe and the number of its males, and so that the dear reader may not be wearied, we shall summarize all that came in these verses in a table that shows the figure and also shows the difference in the numbers between the first numbering (ch. 2) and this second count, but we must note the following observations:

1- The command was to number all the tribes except the tribe of Levi, whom God chose for guarding the tabernacle, and therefore its men do not enter the wars but devote themselves to the important spiritual task to which God appointed them.
2- This numbering was a psychological preparation of the people for the series of wars they would enter, as we say now, a kind of military mobilization.
3- Knowing the number of each tribe also helps in dividing the lands in a way that suits each tribe.

4- An affirmation of God's true promise, for despite the destruction of most of the generation that came out of the land of Egypt and the hardship of life in the wilderness, God blessed their number, and they became almost as they had been, apart from a slight decrease.

5- In (v. 9) the name "Dathan and Abiram" of the tribe of Reuben is mentioned, and God indicated that they are the ones who took part in the rebellion and murmuring of Korah, an indication that a deed is usually tied to its doer and disgraces him if it is a bad deed, and the reputation of this person remains tied to his error; and likewise in (v. 10) he mentions the rebellion and its punishment and the number of those who died in it.

6- In (v. 51) he mentions the total number of the people after the numbering, and it was (601,730), six hundred thousand, one thousand, seven hundred and thirty, and this number is less than the first numbering by one thousand eight hundred and twenty (1,820), which is a very small difference.

Name of the tribe, first count, second count, sign of increase or decrease. Reuben 46500 43730 - Simeon 59300 22200 - Gad 45650 40500 - Judah 74600 76500 + Issachar 54400 64300 + Zebulun 57400 60500 + Ephraim 40500 32500 - Manasseh 32200 52700 + Benjamin 35400 45600 + Dan 62700 64400 + Asher 41500 53400 + Naphtali 53400 45400 -

If it was necessary to number the conscripts for war before invading the land of Canaan, then you should prepare yourself for spiritual warfare, and discipline your senses and arm yourself with the weapons of the Spirit, which are prayer and the Holy Bible, relying on the sacraments of the Church, which guarantee you victory however much Satan schemes to destroy you.

entries.section: (2) The way of dividing the land

paragraphs.text: Although Moses himself would not divide the land but his successor and disciple Joshua, God directs His speech to Moses because he was still the leader of the people. As for the manner of division that God explained to Moses, that the division be according to numbers, that is, the tribe that has the greater number of males, as in the count, possesses a larger share, and the reverse is true. And the wisdom of God in that is to be noted, so that each individual in the end takes an equal share.

entries.section: (2) The way of dividing the land

paragraphs.text: So that no disputes might occur among the tribes, God commanded Moses that the land be divided into twelve parts and lots be cast to determine for each tribe a part of the land. And after the land is determined, the survey division of the land is made according to the number of males in each tribe.. so if the number of the tribe is less than the land it took, a part is cut from it and given to the tribe whose number exceeds the land it possessed. It is to be noted that the actual division among the tribes was carried out by Joshua (Josh 15-19).

God is just in dividing the land so that every person takes an equal share with the rest. So imitate Him and be just in your judgments with others, and do not show partiality to anyone because you were swayed by his manner of speech or out of fear of him or for any personal purposes that benefit you. And know that the just God looks upon you in all your works and words.

entries.section: (3) The numbering of the Levites

paragraphs.text: As God did before, He does here also, and the Levites are numbered alone, separately, and not with the count of the people. First he mentions the heads of the great clans of the Levites, who are the sons of Levi, to whom the subsidiary clans afterward are ascribed, as we shall see, and the three great clans were the Gershonites, the Kohathites and the Merarites" (ch. 2).

entries.section: (3) The numbering of the Levites

paragraphs.text: The three great clans branched into other clans, and he mentions their names also.
a) The Libnites: named for Libni the son of Gershon.
b) The Hebronites: named for Hebron the son of Kohath.
c) The Mahlites: named for Mahli the son of Merari.

d) The Mushites: named for Mushi (Ex 6:19). e) The Korathites: named for Korah the son of Izhar the son of Kohath (Ex 6:18, 21). It is to be noted that the other names of the sons of Levi mentioned in (Ex 6:16-25) are not mentioned here because they were joined to the clans of their brothers because of their small numbers.

entries.section: (3) The numbering of the Levites

paragraphs.text: The inspired Word mentions the name "Amram" and his wife "Jochebed" of the whole tribe of Levi because of their importance, since they were the parents of Moses and Aaron and Miriam.

entries.section: (3) The numbering of the Levites

paragraphs.text: Likewise the inspired Word is concerned to mention Aaron and his descendants because to him alone belongs the priesthood, so it mentions the names of his four sons, who are "Nadab," "Abihu," "Eleazar," and "Ithamar," and it also mentions that none of his sons remained a priest except Eleazar and Ithamar, and the reason for that is the death of both Nadab and Abihu by the wrath of the Lord when they dared to offer strange fire on the altar (Lev 10).

entries.section: (3) The numbering of the Levites

paragraphs.text: As for the total number of the Levites counted, it was twenty-three thousand from the age of a month old, and not like the rest of the tribes whose numbering began from the age of war, which is twenty years, and we notice two things:
1- That their number increased by one thousand males over the first count in the wilderness.
2- That God reminds them that they do not possess land, for the land is for the tribes, but the tithes are theirs.

entries.section: (3) The numbering of the Levites

paragraphs.text: After mentioning the number of the Levites, the discourse concludes that this is the total number of the people and the Levites that was counted before the people entered the land and took possession of their portions.

entries.section: (3) The numbering of the Levites

paragraphs.text: God repeats to us His true word, for He said that because of their much murmuring and their fear of entering the land (ch. 14), none of them would enter the new land. And the verse comes here to confirm to us that what God said indeed happened and the punishment was carried out, so none would enter the land except Joshua the son of Nun and Caleb the son of Jephunneh, who encouraged the people and praised the Lord and the right hand of His power (see ch. 14).

God's promises are true, for when He promised that the sons would enter and the fathers who rebelled against Him and refused to enter the Promised Land would die, now He fulfills His promise and the sons enter. So be assured that God fulfills His promises to you and keeps you as long as you are obedient to His commandments.
The daughters of Zelophehad and Joshua as successor to Moses

entries.section: (1) The daughters of Zelophehad and the laws of inheritance

paragraphs.text: When the people learned, after the census, that one of the purposes of this census was to divide the land among the clans of the tribes, five sisters (v. 33) came forward to Moses. They were the daughters of a man named Hepher, of the tribe of "Manasseh", and they had no brother to carry their father's name. They brought their complaint to Moses the leader of the people, to Eleazar the priest, and to the leaders and judges of the people, before the tabernacle of meeting.

entries.section: (1) The daughters of Zelophehad and the laws of inheritance

paragraphs.text: The substance of the complaint was that their father had died and left them without brothers, so why should their father have no inheritance like the other men of his clan? In defense of their father they mentioned that he was not among the men of the rebellion of Korah and his company, who angered the Lord so that He destroyed them, but was an ordinary man who died like the rest of the people.

He died in his own sin: by this expression they meant that their father was like the rest of the people who died, either by the ancestral sin which all inherited from Adam .. or that he died like the others who murmured against entering the land, which was their sin, or that he was among those who died in the last plague, which took twenty-four thousand of the people.

entries.section: (1) The daughters of Zelophehad and the laws of inheritance

paragraphs.text: This was a new matter for Moses, the man of God, so he did not make a decision on his own, but returned to God "before the Holy of Holies" to ask Him about this matter.

entries.section: (1) The daughters of Zelophehad and the laws of inheritance

paragraphs.text: The Lord's answer to Moses came in favor of the five daughters. He commanded him that their father should have a portion like the rest of his brothers, and that they should inherit this portion from their father.

Here we learn two important things. The first is that Moses the servant returned to God when he met a matter that was new to him, and did not rely on himself or his own opinion in it ... May you too do likewise and return to God in all your affairs.

The second matter is the complaint of the daughters themselves. They came to the man of God to ask about their right to the land. May we learn from them this conduct, and go to the Church, according to the commandment of Christ, seeking guidance or arbitration when there is a dispute, instead of going to the courts or elsewhere.

entries.section: (1) The daughters of Zelophehad and the laws of inheritance

paragraphs.text: God used this situation, the question of the daughters of Zelophehad, to establish some laws used in inheritance. They were as follows:
1- If a man dies who has no sons, his inheritance passes in full to his daughter.
2- If a man dies who has no offspring at all, his brothers inherit his land and possessions.
3- If there are no brothers or sons, the land returns to the paternal uncles and is distributed among them.
4- If there is none of the above, the land and the inheritance are distributed among his kinsmen (his cousins) who bear the name of the man's grandfather.
These laws were observed by all the people of Israel all the days of their lives.

entries.section: (2) The death of Moses and Joshua's succession

paragraphs.text: Mount Abarim: a range of mountains east of the Jordan. The word Abarim means "beyond the Jordan" or opposite the river, and these are the mountains on which Balaam and Balak king of Moab went up (chs. 23, 24) (Map 6). In this verse God calls Moses to go up to the top of a mountain or high hill, one of the hills of the mountain lying east of the river Jordan, and asks him to look well at the land that God had promised His people. We also learn that the name of this hill was "Nebo", which is the summit of the headland of Pisgah, lying north of the Dead Sea. It is noticed that God said to Moses, "Behold the land which I have given", although He had not yet given it; but since God has promised, His word is sure, and the people are considered to have already possessed it.

entries.section: (2) The death of Moses and Joshua's succession

paragraphs.text: Although God had punished Moses by not allowing him to enter the land (v. 14), yet in His tenderness He is gentle toward him and makes him go up and look at the land, the inheritance of his people, so that his soul rejoices in the work of God and His fulfillment of His promises. God also tells him that this would be the last thing he would do in his life before his departure and death.

entries.section: (2) The death of Moses and Joshua's succession

paragraphs.text: God reminds Moses of the reason for the punishment and for his not entering the land. These are the events recounted in detail in (ch. 20). In summary, the people murmured because of the lack of water, and God commanded him to speak to the rock, but when he fell into anger he struck the rock, and even rebuked the people. God considered this a sin of disobedience, and its punishment was that Moses would not enter the land.

entries.section: (2) The death of Moses and Joshua's succession

paragraphs.text: Moses asked nothing for himself, but accepted what the Lord announced to him in submission and surrender, and was content to see the land from every side (Deut 3:27). But with the heart of a father who is not concerned for his own life so much as for the future of his children, he asked God, the Creator of all mankind, to choose a man after him to take over the leadership of all the people.

entries.section: (2) The death of Moses and Joshua's succession

paragraphs.text: The task of this new leader would be to lead and guide the multitudes of this people: to bring them out of their present place, bring them into the new land, and divide it among the tribes and clans. These words show Moses' concern for his people to the last moments of his life, for he did not want the people to be scattered like a flock of sheep that has no shepherd.

entries.section: (2) The death of Moses and Joshua's succession

paragraphs.text: In whom is the Spirit: that is, a man who has heart, zeal and fervor.

God chose "Joshua", the closest disciple of Moses, and the Lord states the reason for choosing him, namely that he possessed the spirit of leadership and love for the people. He commands Moses to lay his hand on him, as a clear sign before the people that "Joshua" was taking over the leadership.
Note: the laying on of hands is an ancient custom that was known among the nations. Jacob laid his hands on "Ephraim and Manasseh" for blessing. The laying on of hands here means:
1- The appointment and installation of Joshua before the people.
2- A sign to the people that the days of Moses were drawing to a close, so that they might prepare themselves psychologically for it.

3- The expression of the laying on of hands was taken up by the Church in her New Covenant as a sign of the giving of the Holy Spirit to the faithful through the pure Apostles, and after them the Fathers the bishops (Acts 19:6), and it also came about through the anointing with the Holy Myron for the Fathers the priests.

4- The expression of the laying on of hands is also used of the one who receives the sacrament of the priesthood in the holy Church of God, for the bishop lays his hand on the head of the candidate and declares his ordination and his rank as well, whether a consecrated deacon or a priest.
God chose Joshua to lead the people because of his distinction in many spiritual situations, which are:

1- He was the servant of Moses, clinging to him, and he was discipled at his hands. When Moses spoke with God in a tent outside the camp of Israel and the glory of God appeared to him, and then left the tent, Joshua remained standing before the tent until Moses returned (Ex 33:11).
2- He led the people in their war with Amalek and defeated them, the first war that the children of Israel faced after their exodus from Egypt (Ex 17).

3- He was the only one who accompanied Moses when he went up the mountain, and he continued waiting for him on the mountain forty days until he received the commandments and the Law and the design of the tabernacle of meeting.

4- He spied out the Promised Land with his companions, and returned with Caleb glorifying God and encouraging the people to enter the Promised Land, despite the murmuring of the ten fellow spies, which made the people rebel against God (ch. 14).

entries.section: (2) The death of Moses and Joshua's succession

paragraphs.text: To complete the choice and installation of Joshua, God also asks Moses to take Joshua before all the people and before Eleazar the priest and to charge him in their presence, so that the priest and the people would be the witnesses. Moses also surrounds him with awe and respect and commands the people to obey and submit to the new leader, so that Joshua would have the place of Moses in the hearts of the people.

entries.section: (2) The death of Moses and Joshua's succession

paragraphs.text: The Urim: the Urim and Thummim were two stones that the high priest placed on his breast. Through these two stones the answer of the Lord came to the questions and requests of the people, by their shining or not, so that the high priest knew the mind of God, whether it was affirmative or negative.

Although Joshua was the leader of his people, God commands him not to bring anything from himself, but just as Moses used to return to God in every matter, so Joshua must also return in every matter to the high priest (Eleazar or his successor), so that God's mind in everything might be made clear. The means by which God made known His will was the two stones, the Urim and Thummim. Consequently Joshua himself would be subject to all the divine commands.

entries.section: (2) The death of Moses and Joshua's succession

paragraphs.text: As God spoke, Moses did exactly what God had commanded him in the preceding verses, and Joshua was installed as the successor of Moses by the laying on of hands and by his acceptance of all the commandments.
It is noticed that Moses had sons, but he did not think of appointing one of them as leader over the people. Instead he appointed the one whom God chose, who was the best spiritually and personally.
In the last moments of Moses' life, and in his last conversation with God, Moses thought of nothing but a successor for his people, for the good of this people ...

So if you are a person in charge, or a leader, or even a father at the level of your family, take care to teach leadership to others and involve others with you, so that the work may continue and the good may continue. Many people's projects ended with the end of their lives because they did not care to involve others and took the front in everything themselves.
Offerings and burnt offerings

entries.section: (1) The daily offerings and burnt offerings

paragraphs.text: God first commanded Moses concerning the presentation of offerings at the beginning of the second year after their exodus from Egypt (Ex 40:2), (Lev 1..). Before their entry into the new land He reminds them once again, especially since the first generation that came out of Egypt had all perished.

entries.section: (1) The daily offerings and burnt offerings

paragraphs.text: My offering: that is, the sacrifices and gifts with which a person draws near to God.
My bread: a figurative expression meaning that what a person offers to God is considered a feast to honor Him. And made by fire: that is, what was kindled and burned on the altar.
A sweet savor: that is, God was pleased with them and accepted them with satisfaction and love from His children.

God's commandment to Moses was that the people should not neglect the divine offerings which He had already mentioned many times. The expression "in their due season" means care and watchfulness for the honor of God, for nothing that concerns God should be postponed, because this postponement is a kind of slackness in respecting the name of the holy God.

My beloved brother, these words apply even more to us. You must not delay your tithes, your vows or your offerings, for it is not right to neglect God in His rights, when He is the giver of all good things.

entries.section: (1) The daily offerings and burnt offerings

paragraphs.text: In the following verses (3-8) is an explanation of the offering of the continual burnt offering, whose provisions included the following:
1- A lamb in the morning, one year old (a yearling), without blemish or disease, burned completely on the altar of burnt offering every morning.

2- Another exactly like it, which was offered in the evening. The expression "between the two evenings" means after the afternoon (the first evening) and at the end of the sunset (the second evening).

entries.section: (1) The daily offerings and burnt offerings

paragraphs.text: Mingled: kneaded.

3- There was also offered with each sacrifice separately fine flour mingled with pure olive oil beaten out, that is, the fruit was beaten so that the oil flowed from it. As for the quantities, they were about (2.29) liters for the flour, with half a liter of oil, by present measures and volumes.

This offering, that is, the burnt offering, was daily and continual. God reminds them that they had offered it in Sinai, so they must offer it also in the land of Canaan and not make light of it after their rest in the new land.

entries.section: (1) The daily offerings and burnt offerings

paragraphs.text: Strong wine: that is, good, aged wine.
A drink offering of good wine, in the amount of half a liter, was also offered with each lamb and the flour mingled with oil (see ch. 15:5).
