entries.section: (1) The daily offerings and burnt offerings

paragraphs.text: God again emphasizes to Moses that just as he did in the morning offering, he must repeat all of it, with the same offerings, with the evening sacrifice, which was offered between the afternoon and sunset.

entries.section: (2) The offerings and burnt offerings of the Sabbath day

paragraphs.text: Because of the importance of the Sabbath day and its standing, and its being considered the most important day of worship in the week, the offering is doubled. A lamb is offered in the morning and another in the evening, besides the daily offering, and all this also includes the flour and the poured wine, as a type and in the same amount as is offered in the daily sacrifice.

Note: the morning and evening sacrifices, as well as the additional Sabbath sacrifices, are burnt offerings offered entirely to God, and the priest eats nothing of them. As for the offerings of flour mingled with oil, the priest would take from them a handful and burn it on the altar, while the rest of it the priests would take as their portion.

May the Lord's day be honored in your eyes, so that you offer in it more worship than usual, and love and service to others, remembering that your life was renewed on this day by the Resurrection of Christ, so that you care for spiritual things more than material things.

entries.section: (3) The offerings of the beginnings of the months

paragraphs.text: The Jewish year was a lunar year, and the month began with the observation of the appearance of the crescent moon. The first day of the month was a spiritual as well as a social celebration. God commanded Moses that there should be a special offering for the beginnings of the months, and this offering consisted of:
1- Two bulls 2- A mature male sheep (a ram) 3- Seven lambs one year old. God commanded the keeping of a feast at the beginnings of the months for the following reasons:
1- That they might know that God is the Creator of the universe and the ruler of time, so that in every period of time, which is a month, they offer Him worship.

2- The pagans used to offer acts of worship at the beginnings of the months, so God wanted to occupy them with His worship rather than with idols, and gave them the keeping of a feast at the beginnings of the months in place of the customs of the pagans.

entries.section: (3) The offerings of the beginnings of the months

paragraphs.text: As usual, these sacrifices or burnt offerings were not offered alone, but the flour mingled with oil and the drink offering of wine had to be offered with them. It is to be observed that the quantities and measures which God set with each offering were proportionate to the size of the animal slaughtered, whether more or less, and this was already discussed in (ch. 15). The meaning we draw from all this is that God does not want us to forget Him in our celebrations, our feasts and our joys, for He alone is the source of our delight and joy, and we must not be preoccupied with material joys and with eating and drinking, but make God a partner with us in everything, so that we taste the meaning of the true joy that God gives to His children.

entries.section: (3) The offerings of the beginnings of the months

paragraphs.text: The burnt offerings that were offered at the feasts of the beginnings of the months were also accompanied by the offering of a male goat as a sin offering, so that God might take away the sins of His people. God reminds Moses and his people that all these offerings particular to the beginning of the month do not cancel the morning and evening burnt offering, nor do they take its place, but are additions to it.

It is good that you remember God on all occasions, not only every year but every month, every week and every day, so that you sit and account for your sins, and think of God's kindnesses to you, to thank Him and to contemplate His love.

entries.section: (4) The feast of the Passover and of Unleavened Bread

paragraphs.text: Because of the utmost importance of the feast of the Passover, and the remembrance of God's work of redemption in the salvation of the people of the children of Israel and their exodus from the land of Egypt and the redemption of their firstborn by the blood of the Passover lamb, God reviews with His people what He had said to them before in (Ex 12), (Lev 23) and also (Deut 16), about the duty of celebrating the feast of the Passover at its usual time, which is the fourteenth day of the month of Abib (Nisan) every year; and this was a type of what Christ did for us.

After the eating of the Passover, beginning from the fifteenth day of the month and for 7 days, nothing is eaten but unleavened bread, that is, bread without leaven. The feast of Unleavened Bread is from the fifteenth day to the twenty-first day of the month of Abib, in addition to the eating of unleavened bread at the feast of the Passover, which is the fourteenth day.

entries.section: (4) The feast of the Passover and of Unleavened Bread

paragraphs.text: It is stated in this verse, as it will also be stated in (v. 25), that both the first day and the seventh day of Unleavened Bread are considered holy convocations to the Lord, so that on them a person may not do any work, exactly like the law of the Sabbath day. This emphasis from God is so that His people might reflect and remember the spiritual meanings in the feasts and occasions, that they are works of salvation, and we should not be too busy to remember them and reflect on them.

entries.section: (4) The feast of the Passover and of Unleavened Bread

paragraphs.text: These verses include an explanation of the offerings that were offered every day throughout the seven days, from the day after the feast of the Passover for seven days. Their details were as follows:

1- Daily burnt offerings of two bulls, one ram and seven lambs one year old, and all these are offered with the flour mingled with oil and the drink offering of wine in the proportions explained previously.

2- A he-goat, that is, a male goat, is also offered as a sin offering to make atonement for the sins of the people. God reminds His people that all these offerings are offered every day throughout the week of Unleavened Bread, and this is in addition to the daily offering, that is, the morning burnt offering and the evening burnt offering.

entries.section: (4) The feast of the Passover and of Unleavened Bread

paragraphs.text: A confirmation of what is stated in (v. 18), that the seventh day is like the first day of Unleavened Bread, so that the two days are considered feasts on which no work is done.

My beloved brother, God cared greatly about public worship, so much that He repeated it again and again to emphasize it!! ... If this was so in the days of animal sacrifices, how much more with the sacrifice of His only Son our Lord Jesus Christ ... Take care, beloved, about the prayer of the Liturgy, and do not be slack or postpone attending it, for it is a holy convocation to the Lord which God made for your salvation and deliverance. Do you truly understand and feel this?!

entries.section: (5) The feast of the Firstfruits

paragraphs.text: The discussion of this feast came in more detail in (Lev 23:15-21). The day of the firstfruits: the feast of harvest or the feast of Pentecost (the fiftieth day), on which the firstfruits of the produce were offered to God on the occasion of the wheat harvest. This is distinct from the first feast of firstfruits on the first Sunday after the Passover (in the view of the Sadducees), which was called the feast of the wave offering (Lev 23:9-14). When you bring a new meat offering to the Lord in your weeks: the day of firstfruits came 7 weeks after the feast of the waving of the barley before the Lord, "that is, the first feast of firstfruits", and therefore what is meant is the feast of harvest and not the feast of firstfruits which comes on the first Sunday after the feast of the Passover. At the feast of Pentecost a person offered the firstfruits of his land of wheat to God in the form of two loaves of new wheat with their appointed sacrifices (Lev 23:17). And God commanded His people to do no work in their celebration of this day, like the rest of the holy convocations of the Lord.

entries.section: (5) The feast of the Firstfruits

paragraphs.text: A repetition of what God had already explained in the preceding verses of the same chapter: the offering of two bulls and a ram as burnt offerings and a goat as a sin offering, with all their offerings of flour and the drink offering, and all this besides the daily burnt offerings represented by the morning sacrifice and the evening sacrifice as well. They shall be unto you without blemish: that is, all the sacrifices offered to God are to be free from defects.

How beautiful it is to offer the firstfruits to God, so that you feel His blessing in everything you have, and God becomes a partner in your life, so that you are at ease and rejoice. And know that His blessing is far greater than your gifts, but keep Him always before you, with His hand stretched out, so that He takes before you take, and your whole life is for Him.
The feasts of the seventh month, an introduction: the Jews had two calendars, one civil and the other religious, and both had the same names for the months of the year!! How was this?

When the people kept the Passover for the first time in Egypt, it was in the seventh month of the ordinary Jewish year. Because of the importance of this feast and this occasion, God commanded that this month also (with the same name) be the head and first of the months of the new religious calendar, and consequently the eighth month in the civil calendar (with the same name) became the second month in the Jewish religious year ... And this chapter speaks of the seventh month in the Jewish religious calendar, which therefore corresponds to the first month of the civil year, the month of "Tishrin the First", or its Hebrew name "Ethanim".

entries.section: (1) The feast of trumpets

paragraphs.text: This feast was the first of the feasts of the seventh month and came on its first day, that is, it was the first day or head of the Jewish civil year. For this reason its celebration was great among the people. The celebration began with the priests blowing the trumpets to announce the beginning of the religious celebration, and it was forbidden to the people to do any work on it, for this day became a holy convocation to which the law of the Sabbath and its rest applied fully (Lev 23:23). God commanded this feast for many reasons, the most important of which are:
1- It is a preparation for the great feasts of the seventh month, which are the feast of Atonement and the feast of Tabernacles.
2- The beginning of the season of agriculture.
3- The trumpets recall God's promises to His people.

entries.section: (1) The feast of trumpets

paragraphs.text: These verses mention the sacrifices offered at the feast. Taken as a whole, they are almost similar to the sacrifices of the previous feasts mentioned in (ch. 28..), and they can be summarized as follows:
1- The day begins with the daily morning sacrifice, which is the burnt offering, and ends also with the evening burnt offering, and these are the two continual burnt offerings.
2- The burnt offerings of the feast are offered, consisting of a bull, a ram and seven lambs one year old.
3- The burnt offerings are accompanied by the usual offerings of flour mingled with oil and a drink offering in the same proportions as before.
4- A he-goat is offered as a sin offering to make atonement for the sins of the people.
5- A burnt offering is also offered on the occasion of the beginning of the month, apart from the burnt offering of the feast.
6- Another sin offering particular to the beginning of the month is offered, consisting of another he-goat apart from the sin offering of the feast.
Remember God's promises to you every day, so that your heart may be at peace whatever problems you meet or fears war against you in the future, for your God loves you and never leaves you.

entries.section: (2) The feast of Atonement

paragraphs.text: Nine days after the feast of trumpets, on the tenth day, comes the feast of Atonement, which was known for fasting, prayer and contrition ("ye shall afflict your souls"). For this reason one of the names of this feast was also "the feast of Forgiveness". Like the other feasts, the people were forbidden on it to do any work, in order to be free for worship and fasting. This feast was explained in detail in (Lev 16, 23) with all its ceremonies and steps, and here God again reminds the people of the importance of the spiritual meaning of this feast and affirms the meaning of forgiveness through blood. This feast carries in the substance of its rites the idea of redemption (see the explanation of Leviticus 16).

entries.section: (2) The feast of Atonement

paragraphs.text: Like the preceding ones, these verses describe what was required to be offered of burnt offerings particular to this feast and the offerings accompanying them, besides the continual morning and evening burnt offerings.

Contemplate the love of Christ in His redeeming you on the Cross, so that you feel His surpassing love, and your heart rejoices, and on the other hand you refuse every sin, because it is the cause of His sufferings and His death on the Cross.

entries.section: (3) The feast of Tabernacles and the freewill offerings

paragraphs.text: This feast was also mentioned in detail in (Lev 23:33-36), and here we review some of its meanings:

1- The first spiritual meaning of this feast is that Israel, after entering and dwelling in the land, should remember the days of their earlier sojourn in the wilderness and God's provision for them, and also that the idea of man's being a stranger to the whole earth, and that he has another homeland, which is heaven, might be made firm.
2- The period of the celebration was seven days, which they spent away from their houses and around the house of the Lord, in booths made of palm branches.
3- This feast had another name, the feast of Ingathering and Thanksgiving, since it came after the people had finished gathering all the crops and the fruit of the trees.

4- The first day of the feast, that is, the fifteenth of the seventh month, and the eighth day, that is, the twenty-second day, or the end of the feast, were holy religious convocations on which the people did no work.

entries.section: (3) The feast of Tabernacles and the freewill offerings

paragraphs.text: In these verses God specifies the offering of each day separately during the seven days of the feast.

The offerings of all the days, in their general structure, are like the rest of the offerings and sacrifices of the feasts, but in the feast of Tabernacles there was one difference: the offering of the first day was thirteen bulls of the burnt offering, and every day God reduced it by one bull, until, when the seventh day came, the number of bulls was seven. With every daily offering God affirmed the continuation of offering the continual daily sacrifices, morning and evening, and this is of course besides the offerings of flour mingled with oil and the drink offering of wine.
We note here that the total of the sacrifices offered during the seven days of the feast amounted to the following: 70 bulls, fourteen rams, ninety-eight lambs, and seven he-goats.

The purpose of all this was that God might teach His people the virtue of thanksgiving at the end of the agricultural season, and that, just as God helped them and blessed them in everything, they too should give generously and not grudgingly.
The reduction in the number of bulls, one bull each day, signifies:
1- God's commandments, which seem hard at first, but with time a person grows used to them and delights in them.
2- The commandments of the Law gradually dwindle, and the need for Christ the Redeemer appears in the fullness of time.

My brother and my friend .. perhaps this subject touches us too, so let us ask ourselves a question .. Do we give to God generously, and do we give with joy, expressing to Him our thanks .. When your children succeed, or you succeed, do you remember to bring God an offering of thanksgiving by which you express your love for God!!?!

entries.section: (3) The feast of Tabernacles and the freewill offerings

paragraphs.text: The eighth day was called the great day, and it points symbolically to eternity and its hoped-for rest. God asked them on this day to make it a day of retreat ("seclusion") for worship and praise, and to do no work on it (Lev 23:3, 23:36).

entries.section: (3) The feast of Tabernacles and the freewill offerings

paragraphs.text: As for the burnt offerings and offerings of the eighth day, they were like the offering of any feast, consisting of a bull, a ram and seven lambs, and a sin offering is added to the burnt offerings, consisting of one he-goat, with all that accompanies that of offering and drink offering as usual.

entries.section: (3) The feast of Tabernacles and the freewill offerings

paragraphs.text: These things ye shall do unto the Lord: that is, all that has been required of you to offer.
In your set feasts: that is, in the three preceding feasts which the seventh month of the religious year included.

The vow: the offering that a person pledges to God, which he must fulfill whatever the circumstances. The freewill offering: an optional offering not tied to a specific petition like the vow, but if it is lost before it is offered to God, God does not require the person to replace it.

At the end of the Lord's speech with Moses He emphasizes to him the necessity of offering all the preceding sacrifices for the feasts and seasons of the seventh month, and this ordinance does not cancel what people were accustomed to offer of vows and of other optional and additional offerings, such as the sacrifices and offerings of thanksgiving and peace, or any vows that a person pledges to God.

The communal worship that the Church offers is very like the offerings of the seasons that God appointed, but this does not cancel your own spiritual rule in your chamber, of prayers, readings and the like, for it is like the private offerings that God also asks of you.

entries.section: (3) The feast of Tabernacles and the freewill offerings

paragraphs.text: As God spoke with Moses, so also the faithful servant told his people all that God had said to him. The following appears from these sacrifices:
1- The necessity of the shedding of blood to obtain salvation: "without shedding of blood is no remission" (Heb 9:22).

2- The sacrifice of the Cross has very many results and effects, which are made clear by these many kinds of sacrifices that signify it, for the sacrifice of Christ carries all the meanings found in the different Jewish sacrifices. Vows, an introduction: vows were discussed before in other places such as (Lev 7, 22, Num 6:2), but the focus here is on the obligation to keep them, and on some kinds of vows that require the consent of the husband or father, as we shall see.

entries.section: (1) First: the vow of a man

paragraphs.text: We understand from the text that in an earlier conversation between God and Moses, Moses was told by God what the law of vows should be and how far a person is bound by them. Accordingly Moses gathered the heads of the people and the representatives of its tribes to tell them what God had commanded.
It is noted that a vow is one of these things:
1- A certain act 2- An offering 3- Abstaining from something such as food.
The following is required of vows:
1- That they be within the limits of God's commandments and not conflict with them, for Jephthah's offering of his daughter was a wrong vow (Judg 11:31).
2- That they be within the limits of a person's capacity and means.
3- That the vow be specific so that it can be fulfilled; one should not say "I offer the love of God", but "I offer such-and-such a thing".
4- A person does not vow on behalf of another, as in a father's vow on behalf of his son or his wife.
5- Whoever does not fulfill his vow is not punished by the priests and judges, but he is in the wrong toward the Lord and God is angry with him.
6- A girl asks her father's permission, or a wife her husband's, when she vows.
7- Not postponing the fulfillment of the vow, because in that is ingratitude toward God, and it exposes a person to forgetting the vow and not fulfilling it.
8- It is preferable to write down the vow and keep the writing in a known place, to avoid forgetting it.

entries.section: (1) First: the vow of a man

paragraphs.text: A bond: that is, the matter he has pronounced and is bound by, which is the subject of the vow.

The man, unlike the woman, who depended wholly on her husband or father for her support, and because the man is the source of income, there is nothing to nullify what he has pronounced with his mouth. Rather, if he vows and pledges an offering to God, he must keep it fully and fulfill it, and there is no one who can lift it from him or excuse him from it (Eccl 5:2-5).

entries.section: (2) The vow of a girl before her marriage

paragraphs.text: These verses deal with two cases. The first is the case of the girl who has passed childhood and lives in her father's house, and the ruling on her vow is as follows: if she pronounces her vow and her father hears it and does not comment or object to what she said .. her vow becomes binding on her. But because her father has the right of guardianship over her and oversight of her upbringing, and is responsible for and manages all the material aspects, God gave him the right of refusal or objection. If he refuses or objects, the girl is as though she had vowed nothing, and God forgives her and requires nothing of her.

entries.section: (2) The vow of a girl before her marriage

paragraphs.text: The second case is that of the same girl who was in her father's house and was under a previous vow she had not yet fulfilled, and who married and became another man's, not her father's. God gives her husband the same right that her father had, meaning that if he consents to the vow, with express consent or with consent by not objecting .. the vow she vowed in her father's house remains in force and binding ... But if he objects to her vow and prevents her from it, God does not require it of her but excuses her from it.

It is good for the girl to submit to her parents and not rush after her own thoughts and feelings, but to pray and consult her parents in every important matter. Better still, let there be a friendly relationship and understanding within the family, cared for by all parties, so that we secure a psychological stability that helps the growth of the spiritual life.

entries.section: (3) The vow of the widow, the divorced woman and the married woman

paragraphs.text: The third case for a woman is that she is divorced or a widow. This is the case of a free woman who is not under the authority of a man or of anyone who has jurisdiction over her, so in everything she has pronounced and vowed she is bound to fulfill it.

entries.section: (3) The vow of the widow, the divorced woman and the married woman

paragraphs.text: The fourth and last case in the vow of a woman is that of the wife who made a binding vow while in her husband's house. The same preceding rule applies to her as regards the necessity of the husband's consent. But if the husband objects to the vow on the day he hears of it, this vow is void, and God does not require it of her.

entries.section: (3) The vow of the widow, the divorced woman and the married woman

paragraphs.text: These two verses are a review of what came in (vv. 10-12), the gist of which is the necessity of the husband's consent to his wife's vow, and in the case of his silence and not objecting, the vow remains in force and the woman is not excused from it.

entries.section: (3) The vow of the widow, the divorced woman and the married woman

paragraphs.text: Finally God gives a warning to the man that if he postpones his objection, on hearing the vow, to a later time, and then wants afterward to object, he has become the guilty one and the transgressor of God's commandment, and God considers him the breaker of the vow and not his wife: "he shall bear her iniquity".

entries.section: (3) The vow of the widow, the divorced woman and the married woman

paragraphs.text: At the end of the chapter comes this verse, making clear the purpose of the whole chapter, which is:
First: the duty of fulfilling vows, on the one hand.
Second: the conditions for carrying out the vow, and the relation of that to the girl's father if she is still in his house, or to her husband when she moves to his house.
How beautiful it is to offer love to God, but what matters is to follow up what I pronounce, that I may keep it and enjoy offering the love of God and receive His blessings.
The war against the Midianites

entries.section: (1) The victory over the Midianites

paragraphs.text: Here God charges "Moses" with his last task before his death and his departure from this world to his fathers who went before him, and we note here several things:

First: the Lord asks this of Moses when he is a hundred and twenty years old and his days have drawn very near. The spiritual meaning here is that spiritual striving knows no time to stop or rest, so a person must continue in service and giving until the last days of his life, as long as he is able. Second: this war was just, for it was a war on a kingdom of evil and not on a particular people, since the Midianites were those who united with the Moabites against the people of God and put a stumbling block before them (ch. 25), and the woman "Cozbi the daughter of Zur", whom Phinehas the priest killed, was also a Midianite.

Third: the third and important meaning is that before you possess your inheritance, you must fight for it. The Promised Land is a type of the Kingdom of Heaven, and the Midianites are the enemies of God and the kingdom of Satan, and the rule is that there is no inheritance without victory and no victory without fighting, and it is a spiritual fight of course.

entries.section: (1) The victory over the Midianites

paragraphs.text: Armed: prepared for war, bearing their weapons.

Moses spoke to his people what God had spoken with him, and as a commander planning a battle he began to prepare his men, "his army". He asked them to choose men from all the tribes, a thousand men from each tribe, able to fight and bear arms. The wisdom of Moses here was the participation of the whole people in the war, so that no tribe might boast over another, on the one hand; and from the spiritual standpoint the meaning is that spiritual fighting and striving belong to all, and no one is exempt from it.

entries.section: (1) The victory over the Midianites

paragraphs.text: The presence of God in the midst of His people during the war was important, for the war was the Lord's and at His command, and the victory also came through Him. So that the people might understand this beautiful spiritual meaning, and also so that their hearts might be at ease in the first war they would fight for the new land, Moses sent with the people Phinehas the priest, the son of Eleazar, and with him also holy instruments from the furnishings of the tabernacle, which most commentators believe to be "the ark of the covenant". "Phinehas" also took the silver trumpets mentioned in (ch. 10), which were used in war to encourage the people and at the same time to glorify God.

entries.section: (1) The victory over the Midianites

paragraphs.text: Arm yourselves against Midian: that is, make war on Midian.

The people advanced and began the war against the Midianites, and the Lord gave them victory, and they killed all the males, who represented the greatest evil if they remained. The expression "every male" teaches us not to leave any amount of evil, even a small one, in our minds, because it will grow and return to war against us (Map 8).

entries.section: (1) The victory over the Midianites

paragraphs.text: The kings of Midian: that is, the heads of the great clans of the Midianites, as we now say "the mayor of the village".

This verse mentions the names of the five kings that Midian had, who were also killed with all the men, "the males". It also mentions here the killing by the sword of Balaam, the wicked prophet, who cast the stumbling block before the children of Israel. Although he had returned to his city (ch. 24:25), most commentators took his presence here with the Midianites as evidence against him that he went back and allied himself with them against the people of God, so that he deserved what befell him.

entries.section: (1) The victory over the Midianites

paragraphs.text: After the end of the war, the men of Israel burned all the cities of the Midianites with all their houses, but they kept for themselves the women, the little children and all the animals, and returned with all they had obtained to the place where the rest of the people were settled, east of the Jordan, opposite Jericho, in the place called "the plains of Moab" (Map 6).

entries.section: (1) The victory over the Midianites

paragraphs.text: Before they reached the place where the people dwelt, "the camp", the news of their victory reached everyone, so Moses went out, and with him Eleazar the high priest, to receive the victorious men of war, as an expression of their joy at the victory on the one hand, and as a kind of honor on the other.

Be careful to destroy evil and everything connected with it, so that the devil may not use it to make you fall again, and be confident that however great the power of sin, God is able to give you victory over it.

entries.section: (2) The anger of Moses and his decisions

paragraphs.text: The officers of the host: that is, the commanders of the army, who were chosen from the leaders of the tribes, that is, the captains of thousands and captains of hundreds.

When Moses saw his victorious army coming, and with it Midianite women after all the men had been killed, his anger grew fierce and he was jealous with a holy jealousy for the Lord, for he saw with the eye of a spiritual leader what the ordinary person did not see. He cried out to his commanders, displeased and reproachful, asking how they had brought the women of the Midianites with them. He began to explain to them the reason for his refusal of what they had brought, which was that these women had been the cause of the people's falling into fornication earlier when they mingled with them, and because of them they worshiped the pagan god "Baal-peor", so the vengeance of God on the people was the plague that destroyed twenty-four thousand ... There also appeared in the words of Moses a reference to Balaam, who was behind this wicked counsel which he gave to "Balak" and the kings of the Midianites (ch. 25).

Moses was truly a servant and a leader, for he had foresight beyond the rest of the army commanders, and saw well the danger that threatened his people through keeping the women alive. The joys of victory and the multitude of captives did not distract him from this danger, so he did not flatter but rebuked these commanders.

My beloved brother ... your spiritual father is the person who has been entrusted by God with the salvation of your soul, and God has granted him to see the evil surrounding you, so listen to him and obey his directions, and in this you receive the blessing of obedience and escape from evil.

entries.section: (2) The anger of Moses and his decisions

paragraphs.text: Moses firmly commanded the commanders of his army to kill all the male children, who, if they grew up, would become men resisting the people and might be affected by what happened to their fathers, and likewise all the women who were not virgins and who had defiled one another by seducing the children of Israel earlier, besides that they would carry a feeling of vengeance for the killing of their husbands, fathers and sons. As for the female children and the virgin girls, Moses spared them as captives and gifts for the men of his people. It is known that the women taken captive became Jewish and joined the people, and with time men married them, and such a woman was considered a wife and not a slave.

entries.section: (2) The anger of Moses and his decisions

paragraphs.text: Moses continued in his speech, not forgetting all that God had commanded earlier in the laws of purification. He commanded the men to go outside the camp for seven days and to carry out the law of purification on the third and the seventh day as the Lord commanded (Lev 19:26, ch. 5:1-4, 19:11-13). Purification included not only the one who killed or touched a dead body .. but the captives, the virgin women, were also purified, because they would become Jewish and so must be subject to the Law; and likewise every garment and every movable thing they had brought with them, whether wood or wool, because it was defiled by the touch of the pagans, or by their own touch, that is, the children of Israel, after they had been defiled by touching the slain. The meaning includes everything else.

entries.section: (3) The speech of Eleazar the priest

paragraphs.text: After Moses had finished his speech about the duty of purification, he left the speaking to Eleazar the priest, because by his priesthood he is responsible for applying the laws of the Lord, so he began to speak with the heads of the people, explaining to them how this purification was to be done.

entries.section: (3) The speech of Eleazar the priest

paragraphs.text: Eleazar divided the spoil that had been taken into two groups. The first was the metals, and their purification was by putting them in the fire without melting them, or more precisely passing them through the fire, and after that the water of purification, which was spoken of before (ch. 19), is sprinkled on these metals. As for other things, such as leather, wood or cloth, which burn in fire, their purification is by sprinkling water on them only.

entries.section: (3) The speech of Eleazar the priest

paragraphs.text: At the end of the time of purification, that is, the full week, the men wash their clothes and so complete their purification after their bathing too, and by this they are qualified to enter the camp and have fellowship with the people again.

Sin defiles us all, and repentance cleanses us from it, and the absolution that my father reads for me in confession restores me once again to fellowship with the Body of Christ .. So do not be slack and do not postpone .. but come forward and enjoy the purification and washing of your spirit.

entries.section: (4) The division of the spoil

paragraphs.text: After the men of war had completed their purification, and likewise the captives, God commanded Moses to count all the captives, the remaining virgins, as well as the living cattle and the goods. God associated with him in this work Eleazar the priest and the heads of the tribes, so that God might remove every suspicion from Moses, and also to teach us the necessity of collective work, of involving others, and of not holding authority alone.
The purpose of the counting was justice in dividing the spoil, to give a share to the fighters and also a share to those who did not take part in the war.

entries.section: (4) The division of the spoil

paragraphs.text: God commanded Moses to divide the spoil into two halves after the counting. The first half would be for the men of war who risked themselves for the people and exposed themselves to death, and the other half of the spoil would go to the whole people, because whoever did not go out to war was of unsuitable age, and so guarded the country and the houses of the fighters. Of course this carried justice on the one hand, and an incentive for the rest of the men to go out to war on the other.

Apart from the war of the children of Israel and the material spoil, the spiritual meaning here is that there is no heavenly reward except for the one who has conquered, and victory requires striving and fighting ... So be strong, my brother, and let no one take your crown.

entries.section: (4) The division of the spoil

paragraphs.text: Tribute: a necessary offering to God.

The command came here to the men of war to offer an offering from their half, and this offering is reckoned at one out of five hundred of the captives and of the beasts and the flocks. This tribute gives a portion to the priests, whom Eleazar represents, and God considered this offering as presented to Himself, "a heave offering of the Lord", because it is presented to His priests.

entries.section: (4) The division of the spoil

paragraphs.text: God did not forget the Levites either, so He commanded that a tribute also be taken from the other half of the spoil, which was given to the people, but the proportion would be one out of every fifty and not five hundred, because of course the number of the Levites is greater than the number of the priests. God also mentions here the necessity of honoring them and their obtaining a portion, since they are His servants and the keepers of the rites of His worship in His house.

entries.section: (4) The division of the spoil

paragraphs.text: And as the Lord commanded and ordered Moses, Moses the prophet and Eleazar did exactly as the Lord commanded.

entries.section: (4) The division of the spoil

paragraphs.text: In these coming verses is an explanatory detail of all that has been said before, and they are also considered a record in which the people wrote down the total of the spoil and the care taken to divide it exactly into two parts, and how from the first part came the share of the priests in the proportion God had set, and likewise from the second part, assigned to the people, came the share of the Levites in the proportion appointed for them. It is clear from these verses how abundant was the spoil the people obtained from this war, and the great blessing of God.

The idea of recording God's works and gifts is a spiritual idea practiced by many of the saints. For a person in times of distress may become prey to the enemy of good, who makes him doubt God's earlier works in his life; so what Moses and the people did here, in recording the numbers of the spoil and how it was distributed, is a testimony the people put on record against themselves, by their confession of God's wonderful work with them .. Would that we all did this, and remembered and recorded in our hearts and minds all that God has done with us. Indeed, some of us already write them down in their private meditations with God.

entries.section: (5) The freewill offering of the leaders

paragraphs.text: Verses (48-52) carry a wonderful scene, worthy of note, comment and contemplation. The captains of thousands and the captains of hundreds, and with them the commanders of the divisions of the army, that is, the officers, came forward to Moses to speak with him, of their own accord.

entries.section: (5) The freewill offering of the leaders

paragraphs.text: The beginning of this speech by the commanders and leaders was an acknowledgment of a tangible fact, namely their recognition of God's great work with them in this war, for they returned from it without a single man being lost, which is unusual and unheard of in any war. The inspired text records for us how humble these leaders were, for they spoke to Moses at the start of their speech saying "thy servants".

entries.section: (5) The freewill offering of the leaders

paragraphs.text: Ankle chains: anklets, which are worn on the lower leg of a woman above her foot.
Earrings: rings for the ear.
Bracelets: the necklace, or what is worn around the neck.

The subject of the speech was an offering of thanksgiving, consisting of the share of each one of them from the spoil of wrought gold, that is, worked gold, which they obtained from the adornment of the women, and they considered that this offering lifted up to God was an offering of atonement for their sins. The word atonement here also carries the meaning of "redemption" for them, and an acknowledgment that God redeemed them from death in this war.

entries.section: (5) The freewill offering of the leaders

paragraphs.text: Moses and Eleazar with him accepted this offering from them, since this offering was presented to God and the priest is God's steward, and consequently Eleazar is the one who received it. As for the amount of gold that was offered, it was very abundant, for by present weights its value was about two hundred kilograms of gold. This also shows how rich the people of the Midianites were, on the one hand, and the abundance of the shares which the leaders obtained, and consequently all the people.

entries.section: (5) The freewill offering of the leaders

paragraphs.text: Moses and Eleazar took the gold presented by the leaders and officers and brought it to the tabernacle and put it there, that is, presented it to the Lord, as a memorial for the children of Israel, meaning remembering the wonderful work of God in this victory, and that He is the only true God among the gods of the pagan nations and is able to crush His enemies. The word "memorial" before the Lord carries another meaning, which is that this offering was limited to the leaders only.

What the leaders of the people and its officers did is a beautiful and wonderful deed, expressing gratitude and how generous and kind their souls were, for they refused what was their right and offered it to God as a sacrifice of thanksgiving. This teaches us that it is fitting to offer to God from our surplus gains a sacrifice of thanksgiving which is more than the tithes, even by a little. If you cannot offer all that you have, will you offer some of it?
The tribes of Reuben and Gad and the half-tribe of Manasseh

entries.section: (1) The two tribes' request for the land and Moses' answer to them

paragraphs.text: The land of Jazer: one of the cities of the land of Gilead.

The land of Gilead: a region that included all the east of the river Jordan, famous for its trees and pastures that run through its mountains, for it is a mountainous region, and among its mountains some green plains were spread (Map 3). The leaders and heads of the tribes of Reuben and Gad looked toward the land east of the Jordan, part of which the Midianites had inhabited, and seeing that it was a land rich in valleys and fertile pastures, suitable for grazing cattle, they came to Moses the leader of the people and Eleazar the high priest with their request, mentioned in the following verses.

entries.section: (1) The two tribes' request for the land and Moses' answer to them

paragraphs.text: This verse includes the names of some cities and villages of the region of Gilead, the subject of the leaders' speech with Moses and Eleazar. The most important is the city of Heshbon, the capital of the land of the Amorites, and it and the rest of the lands mentioned lie east of the Dead Sea and southeast of the river Jordan.
Ataroth: it no longer exists today, and it is thought that it was between Heshbon, the capital of the Amorites, and the city of Dibon.

Dibon: it was one of the cities of the Moabites, and the Amorites took it, and then the children of Israel took it from them. Jazer: a city with some small villages belonging to it, lying west of Ammon, a city of the Amorites. Heshbon: the capital of Sihon king of the Amorites.
Shebam: a city considered adjoining and an extension of Heshbon on the north.
Elealeh: a city lying north of Heshbon also.
Nebo: a mountain city that took its name from Mount Nebo.
Beon: also called Meon, and also "Baal-meon".

entries.section: (1) The two tribes' request for the land and Moses' answer to them

paragraphs.text: As for the subject of the request and the speech, it is a petition from the tribes of Reuben and Gad to take this land as their portion and be content with it, and not cross the Jordan with the rest of the tribes. Their request to Moses was accompanied by an explanation that the number of the cattle of these two tribes was very great, and that these lands were the most suitable lands for them and their cattle. The expression "the country which the Lord smote before the congregation of Israel" is a gracious expression in which they ascribed the war and the victory to God and not to their own arm.

It is also noted that their request was presented in a humble and gentle form, for they said, "if we have found grace in thy sight", which is a courteous expression of asking leave in which they set aside their own will and declare their desire but leave the matter to Moses. Would that we too learned such a manner in the matters of our lives when we ask for something.

entries.section: (1) The two tribes' request for the land and Moses' answer to them

paragraphs.text: Moses held back from the request of the tribes of Reuben and Gad and told them what was within him with some disapproval!! .. Is it fitting that you take the land and settle with your cattle while the rest of the tribes go out to the wars of liberating the land and possessing it? Moses used the expression "your brethren" because of the shared responsibility it carries for all, since the work is one work, and also because this expression may embarrass the two tribes in their request. Moses put Gad before Reuben either because they were the owners of the idea, or because of their taking the lead in speaking about the sons of Reuben, besides the fact that Reuben lost the birthright and precedence over his brothers because of his sin with his father's wife.

entries.section: (1) The two tribes' request for the land and Moses' answer to them

paragraphs.text: Moses continues his speech and points out a new fault in this request, which is that if he allowed them to do so, they would be the cause of the remaining tribes' becoming slack. Why should the others fight while you are here at ease?!

entries.section: (1) The two tribes' request for the land and Moses' answer to them

paragraphs.text: In these verses Moses began a severe and decisive speech with the delegates and heads of the two tribes, and this speech can be summarized in the following points:

1- He reminds them that what they want to do here, "to possess the land", and its result in weakening the people's resolve, is the same as their fathers did when they spied out the land, as if history were repeating itself.
2- He recalls to them what bears on the matter of spying out the land, and how, when the spies returned, they discouraged and disheartened the people from going forward to take the land.
3- He also reminds them that this earlier cowardly stand led to God's anger against His people and His oath that none of them should enter the land (chs. 13-14).
4- The result of this anger was the people's wandering for forty years in the wilderness and the perishing of the whole wicked generation that doubted God's power and feared the peoples of the land.

5- Moses did not fail to add a parenthetical remark that this punishment did not include Joshua the son of Nun and Caleb the son of Jephunneh, the two faithful men who took a position different from the rest of the spies (v. 12).

entries.section: (1) The two tribes' request for the land and Moses' answer to them

paragraphs.text: Moses increases the sharpness of his manner and tone in speaking with the leaders. He begins by rebuking them for this very selfish idea, and adds that he sees them as he saw their fathers of old, and describes them as sinners, "an increase of sinful men", and that by such a request they will bring the anger of God upon the people once again, as happened of old, so that this whole people will perish because of them.

Leadership, whatever its level, even at the level of the family, requires the leader at times to take decisive positions in order to protect others. Decisiveness is not a fault in itself as long as love and counsel accompany it. Rather, slackness and lack of decisiveness is considered sin if a person neglects a wrong and is lax about it, especially if he is in charge.

entries.section: (2) The second speech of the two tribes and Moses' conditional agreement

paragraphs.text: Folds: pens.

After listening to Moses' rebuke, the heads of the two tribes did not leave, but continued speaking with Moses, presenting their point of view, which was as follows: allow us to build here folds for our cattle, and to build houses in fenced cities so that they may be strong, and to put in them our little ones and our wives. When this is done we shall be the first men to go forward, ready and ahead of the others, to war for our people Israel, so that they too may possess their portions of the land west of the river Jordan.

entries.section: (2) The second speech of the two tribes and Moses' conditional agreement

paragraphs.text: "And we will not return to our homes which you have given us until we are fully assured that every tribe has received by lot what God has apportioned to it, and we shall not possess anything with them in the new land west of the river Jordan, but shall be content with what we have taken of the land east of it."

entries.section: (2) The second speech of the two tribes and Moses' conditional agreement

paragraphs.text: As for Moses, after hearing their new idea, his answer was this: if you hold to all these words and fulfill your covenant, to prepare for fighting and war and even to go ahead of the rest of the tribes in advancing to war, and when God calls you to take part with your brethren in liberating the land you cross the Jordan with all your men armed for war, until the complete victory is achieved and God subdues all the peoples dwelling west of the Jordan to His people, then this land will be your possession as you wished, and keeping your promise will clear you of God's anger and vengeance. Note: the expression "before the Lord" (v. 20) means that these two tribes should take their position in the wars in the front ranks before the ark of the covenant, which represents the divine presence, and which the people took with them in most of their wars.

entries.section: (2) The second speech of the two tribes and Moses' conditional agreement

paragraphs.text: The rest of Moses' speech was also a warning to them of what would befall them if they did not fulfill their covenant, and were slack and did not take part with the people in the fighting, for this would be a shameful act on their part and would expose them to God's anger and vengeance, because this covenant and this promise were before God and He is the witness to it. We note here that Moses, before giving them permission and his agreement (v. 24), repeats his previous warning (vv. 10-11) so as to make their promise firm upon them and make them afraid of going back, and at the same time to clear himself of responsibility for the consequence of their going back on fulfilling their covenant, which would expose them to the wrath of God.

entries.section: (2) The second speech of the two tribes and Moses' conditional agreement

paragraphs.text: These were the words of Moses' agreement and his permission to them to build folds for the cattle and to build cities for the dwelling of their wives and children.

entries.section: (2) The second speech of the two tribes and Moses' conditional agreement

paragraphs.text: As a kind of thanks, and very humbly, the heads of the tribes of Gad and Reuben gave thanks to Moses and pledged to do all that they had promised and all that Moses had permitted them.

entries.section: (2) The second speech of the two tribes and Moses' conditional agreement

paragraphs.text: Likewise, for the last time, they renewed their covenants to number all the men prepared for war and keep them in a state of constant readiness, and to leave their wives and cattle in the cities of Gilead, that is, the lands of the Moabites and Midianites.

entries.section: (2) The second speech of the two tribes and Moses' conditional agreement

paragraphs.text: After the agreement had become final, Moses directed his words to the leaders of the people and the representatives: Eleazar the high priest, Joshua the son of Nun the supreme commander, and the heads of the tribes, who were the representatives of all the people. Moses' words to all carried a review of all the preceding speech, and made clear to them that his consent was a conditional consent, that all were witnesses to what the heads of the two tribes had pronounced, and that all also had authority over this agreement as to its validity or its annulment, and all this depended on how far the two tribes kept to what they had said and promised. If they took part in the fighting and crossed the Jordan with their men of war, and all the tribes took possession of their portions, this land would be theirs, that is, the tribes of Gad and Reuben's. But if they broke their promise, this land would not be given to them but taken from them, and they would share by lot with the rest of the tribes the land that is west of the Jordan.

entries.section: (2) The second speech of the two tribes and Moses' conditional agreement

paragraphs.text: These two verses carry the same as what the heads of the two tribes had pledged before, and its repetition here is to confirm their commitment to it. Joshua reminded them of their promise after the death of Moses, and they crossed and fought with their brethren, and after the end of the war he thanked them for keeping their promise, and then they returned to their lands east of the Jordan (Josh 1:12-18, 22:1-9).

entries.section: (2) The second speech of the two tribes and Moses' conditional agreement

paragraphs.text: The cities of the country round about: that is, the cities and the borders extending around them.

Although the tribe of Manasseh did not take part in all the preceding dialogue and asked nothing of Moses, we find that when Moses granted the land to the tribes of Gad and Reuben, he associated with them in this land half the tribe of Manasseh, perhaps because he found this land too large to belong to the two tribes alone. We also understand from the context the agreement of the heads of the clans of the tribe of Manasseh to this, since half of the tribe did in fact possess land east of the Jordan.

As for the land that was the subject of all the discussion, it was, as already explained, the land of the kingdom of Sihon king of the Amorites and Og king of Bashan, the land extending along the east of the river Jordan from its north to its south.

We must not fail to mention here that although Moses agreed with the two tribes on their choice, this does not free the two tribes from the suspicion of selfishness, for they set themselves apart and chose the land by their own will and did not wait for the Lord's choice or His lot. In any case, these two tribes paid the price of their haste and greed .. for they were relatively cut off from the rest of the people because of the river Jordan (the natural divide) and became exposed to harassment by many of the peoples of the region throughout their history ..
Would that you not be hasty, nor greedy, nor go ahead of your brethren in choosing, but wait for the portion the Lord has for you.

entries.section: (3) The rebuilding of the land after obtaining it

paragraphs.text: The books also carry a historical and geographical record of the people of God, and for this reason we find that the coming verses are all a record of the names of the cities that the two tribes and half the tribe of Manasseh rebuilt and built. However, honesty requires us to say that after research we found that most of these "villages", which are called here "cities", either disappeared, were changed or were annexed.

Also, given the lack of precise maps showing the reader the location of these very small cities, and the resort of the most careful commentators to the expressions "perhaps it is" or "perhaps it has now become", we content ourselves here with a general reference to these cities, mentioning in detail only what is certain.
Verses (34-36) include the cities that the tribe of Gad rebuilt and took, which were originally cities (villages) of the Amorites, and they were:

1- Dibon: it was taken from the Amorites and was afterward called "Dibon-gad" after the tribe of Gad. But Joshua afterward gave it to the tribe of Reuben (Josh 13), and it is in ruins now and does not exist.
2- Ataroth: it was spoken of in (v. 3), and it too has disappeared and does not exist now.
3- Aroer: also called Ararir. After having been the portion of the tribe of Gad, it was afterward taken by the king of Aram and then the king of Moab (2 Kgs 10-32), (Jer 48:19).
4- Atroth-shophan: it lay in the plain of Moab.
5- Jazer: it belonged to the tribe of Gad, and Joshua afterward gave it as a portion to the sons of Merari (the Levites).
6- Jogbehah: it is thought to be the present village of Jubeihat, which lies northwest of Amman.
7- Beth-nimrah: it lies north of the Dead Sea.

8- Beth-haran: it is now known as Tell er-Rameh .. and it faces Jericho, which lies west of the Jordan. These cities, after being rebuilt by the tribe of Gad, became fortified cities, and folds were also built for their cattle and sheep.

entries.section: (3) The rebuilding of the land after obtaining it

paragraphs.text: The tribe of Reuben did as their brethren of the tribe of "Gad" had done, and they rebuilt and built the cities that became their portion. They kept the names of some of them as they were, and changed others to names they gave them ... These cities were:
1- Heshbon: the most famous of all their cities, for it was the largest of them, and it was the capital of the Amorites.
2- Elealeh: it remained Reuben's until the Moabites afterward took it, as stated in (Isa 15:4, Jer 48:34).
3- Kirjathaim: after Reuben rebuilt it, it afterward fell into the hands of the Moabites.
4- Nebo: see (v. 3).
5- Baal-meon: it was also called "Meon" and "Beth-baal-meon".
6- Shibmah: also called "Shebam" or "Sibmah"; it is now a ruin, and in it are the remains of the stone winepresses for which it was famous.

entries.section: (3) The rebuilding of the land after obtaining it

paragraphs.text: After "Gad" and "Reuben" had each taken their portions of the land, it is mentioned here that the sons of "Machir", who was the firstborn son of Manasseh the son of Joseph, were able to cleanse some villages of the Amorites of the remnant of their inhabitants and drive them out, and for this reason Moses gave them these regions as a portion for them, that is, for the sons of Machir only.

entries.section: (3) The rebuilding of the land after obtaining it

paragraphs.text: The second portion, for the clans of the tribe of Manasseh, fell to Jair, who was originally of the tribe of Judah but joined the tribe of Manasseh by marrying a woman of the descendants of Machir the son of Manasseh. This was a strange and unusual situation in the sequence of the genealogy of the tribes, since it was usual for a woman to be reckoned to her husband's tribe, and not as happened here.
This portion that Jair had was lands famous for farms, so he took it and gave it his name, and called these farms "Havoth-jair", that is, the villages of Jair.

entries.section: (3) The rebuilding of the land after obtaining it

paragraphs.text: Nobah, also a father of clans of the tribe of Manasseh, took and seized the city of Kenath and some villages around it, and to perpetuate his name and his clans after him he gave it his name.

As the tribes of Reuben and Gad and half the tribe of Manasseh rebuilt cities for the dwelling of their children and wives, you should build up your life with many virtues, so that you can live with your thoughts and senses at ease, and even growing, in a pure life with God. And in proportion to how much you toil and God sees your love in your striving, He gives you many virtues.
The journeys of the children of Israel from Egypt to the east of the Jordan

entries.section: (1) The first stage: from Rameses to the wilderness of Sinai

paragraphs.text: With their armies: that is, they went out with all their men numbered for war.

This is the opening of the whole chapter: "These are the journeys of the children of Israel". It adds that this historical record is from the day of their departure from the land of Egypt with all their men numbered for war, everyone aged 20 years and above. The expression "under the hand of Moses and Aaron" means under the supervision and direction of the civil leader "Moses" and the spiritual leader "Aaron" the priest.

entries.section: (1) The first stage: from Rameses to the wilderness of Sinai

paragraphs.text: Their goings out: that is, the places from which the people began to move or set out.

It was God, by His providence, who commanded Moses to write this historical record for his people, so that he might review with them all the places they had passed through, their pleasant and painful events, and His work with them. So we are before a spiritual, historical and geographical record that summarizes and reviews for the people God's being with them on a journey that took 40 years. Verses (1, 2) are considered the introduction of this chapter, which is a comprehensive historical record of all the movements of the children of Israel until their arrival at the east of the Jordan.

entries.section: (1) The first stage: from Rameses to the wilderness of Sinai

paragraphs.text: The first station of departure was "Rameses", now known as the area of "San el-Hagar"

in Sharqia (Ex 12:37), where the people ate the Passover on the evening of the fourteenth day of the month of Nisan, which God made the first of the months of the religious year (ch. 28:16). On the second day after eating the Passover, the fifteenth of the month, all the people moved, leaving the place. The expression "with an high hand" points to God's mighty work with the people in the ten plagues, especially the last plague of the firstborn. This departure was before the eyes of all the Egyptians, who did not prevent the people of the children of Israel from leaving and quitting the city (Maps 7, 8).

entries.section: (1) The first stage: from Rameses to the wilderness of Sinai

paragraphs.text: This verse shows the Egyptians' preoccupation and their great grief for their firstborn who had died, and that they were busy burying them. The people were pained in all this, looking to their God, who "executed judgments" upon their gods, that is, that the Lord by His work and His high arm declared that He is the only true God, while the rest of the gods are vain and the work of human hands and cannot do anything before Him. They did not protect the Egyptian people from the plagues, and were not able to prevent the people of the children of Israel from leaving the land of Egypt.
The Exodus and the first stages in the wilderness, Map (7) Map (8)

entries.section: (1) The first stage: from Rameses to the wilderness of Sinai

paragraphs.text: If "Rameses" was the first point of departure, "Succoth" was likewise the first resting station after the people moved. Succoth means "booths", and it lies between present-day Ismailia and Suez, but a little toward the west.

entries.section: (1) The first stage: from Rameses to the wilderness of Sinai

paragraphs.text: The next rest was at "Etham", which is south of the Bitter Lakes and northwest of the Gulf of Suez. From there they saw the desert of Sinai before them, but they had not yet crossed (meaning that if the Suez Canal had existed in that time, they were still west of it.)

entries.section: (1) The first stage: from Rameses to the wilderness of Sinai

paragraphs.text: The people went down south instead of going north as far as "Pi-hahiroth", which lies west of the Gulf of Suez at its northern end, so the waters of the sea were before them, and at this point Migdol and Pi-hahiroth were to their north, while Baal-zephon lay to their south. From this point the people crossed the Red Sea after Moses stretched out his rod and touched its waters with it (Ex 14:15-30), and they went three days in "the wilderness of Etham", which is the one mentioned in (v. 6). We know from this that Etham was a wilderness extending west and east ("which the canal now divides"), south of Ismailia and north of Suez, and "Marah" was the first station of encampment after the crossing, where the people found bitter water and murmured, and when Moses cast a tree into it, it became sweet (Ex 15:23-25). It is noted that God led them away from the usual road for reaching Palestine from Egypt, which runs alongside the Mediterranean, that is, the direction of El-Arish and Rafah, because of the many Egyptian garrisons there that would have stopped their march, and He guided them with the pillar of cloud and the pillar of fire southward to the Gulf of Suez, where nothing would hinder them, and He parted the Red Sea before them, that is, the Gulf of Suez, and they crossed into the wilderness of Sinai.

entries.section: (1) The first stage: from Rameses to the wilderness of Sinai

paragraphs.text: Then the direction was downward alongside the Gulf of Suez, so they left "Marah" for "Elim", and there they found water for rest (Ex 15:27), twelve springs of water and seventy palm trees, and after staying a while in Elim they camped for a period alongside the Red Sea. Note the correspondence between this number and the number of the Fathers the Apostles, the pure twelve disciples, as well as the seventy apostles whom the Lord Christ sent to the regions of the world, who became water of refreshment and spiritual satisfaction for the whole world.(

entries.section: (1) The first stage: from Rameses to the wilderness of Sinai

paragraphs.text: The wilderness of Sin: it lies southwest of the wilderness of Sinai alongside the Gulf of Suez in the direction of the present city of El-Tor, and it is the place where the people murmured against God for food (Ex 16) (Map 2), and the Lord gave them manna in it. From the wilderness of Sin, in the direction north toward Rephidim, they stopped at two successive places, "Dophkah and Alush", and these two sites are not mentioned in the book of Exodus because of their smallness.

entries.section: (1) The first stage: from Rameses to the wilderness of Sinai

paragraphs.text: Rephidim was one of the famous stations in the people's journey, because in it the people murmured for water, and because of this murmuring this place was also given the name "Massah and Meribah", that is, "temptation and murmuring". In this place Moses met his father-in-law Jethro (Ex 18), and in it also the people were victorious in their war against Amalek.

entries.section: (1) The first stage: from Rameses to the wilderness of Sinai

paragraphs.text: The people reached the wilderness of Sinai, which lies northeast of the wilderness of Sin, and stayed in it for nearly a year, for all the preceding journeys took between two and three months. The wilderness of Sinai witnessed many events, the most important of which were:
1- The seeing of the glory of the Lord and the receiving of the Ten Commandments (Ex 19, 20).
2- The building of the tabernacle of meeting (Ex 40:1, 2 - 16:17).
3- The receiving of the laws of the Levites (Ex 21-24).
4- The first numbering of the people by Moses, Aaron and the heads of the people (ch. 1).

God led His people in the wilderness of Sinai with the pillar of cloud and the pillar of fire, but the people murmured at every problem instead of turning to God in prayer. Be confident that your God loves you and arranges good for you, and you will enjoy this care if you rely on Him. If you find any difficulties, ask for His help to support you, so that you fulfill His will and rejoice in His ordering of your life.

entries.section: (2) The second stage: arrival at Kadesh-barnea

paragraphs.text: The inspired text mentions here arrival at "Kibroth-hattaavah" immediately after the wilderness of Sinai, but we know from (ch. 11:3) that a short rest preceded "Kibroth-hattaavah", in the place called "Taberah", which means "burning", because the fire was kindled in their tents as a result of their murmuring. As for "Kibroth-hattaavah", it was spoken of before in (ch. 11:34), and we remind the dear reader here that its meaning is the graves of lust, where the people ate the quails greedily! ... And God punished them for their lust, and many of the people died.

entries.section: (2) The second stage: arrival at Kadesh-barnea

paragraphs.text: Hazeroth: a name meaning enclosures or settlements.

It is the station following Kibroth-hattaavah, and it is the place where Miriam, the sister of Moses, was punished by being put out of the camp for seven days, stricken with leprosy, when she spoke evil of Moses (ch. 11:35, ch. 12).

entries.section: (2) The second stage: arrival at Kadesh-barnea

paragraphs.text: Rithmah: a place considered to belong to Kadesh-barnea, and it was so named for a kind of tree in it called "broom trees".
The people were stationed for a considerable time at Kadesh-barnea, and it witnessed events, the most important of which were:
1- The sending of the spies and the story that followed it, of God's anger against the people for their fear and murmuring (chs. 13, 14).
2- The murmuring of Korah, Dathan and Abiram because of the priesthood of Aaron and what happened afterward (ch. 16).
3- From Kadesh began the journey of the people's wandering, according to the Lord's command, for about 38 years.

The people moved about in many places in the wilderness of Sinai, and this signifies the need for spiritual striving in our life on earth. Would that you, my brother, persevere in your striving throughout the stages of your life, and know that God looks with care on every toil you offer for His sake, and He is able to support you and reward you for all your labors.

entries.section: (3) The journey of wandering and the return to Kadesh-barnea

paragraphs.text: Rithmah, or Kadesh-barnea, was in the wilderness of Zin (v. 36), and when God commanded them to begin moving on the journey of wandering, they headed to the wilderness of "Paran" and toward the Red Sea again, and they passed through many of the places mentioned in the following verses.
Rimmon-parez: its meaning is the pomegranate of breaking forth.
Libnah: its meaning is whiteness.
Rissah: a place lying northwest of Libnah.
Kehelathah: its meaning is an assembly.
Mount Shapher: the mount of beauty.
Haradah: its meaning is fear.
Makheloth: means assemblies.
Tahath: its meaning is the lower place or the bottom.
Tarah: its meaning is the ibex, one of the animals of the desert, resembling gazelles.
Mithcah: its meaning is sweetness.
Hashmonah: its meaning is the fertile valley.
Moseroth: its meaning is bonds, and it is the place of the burial of Aaron, and consequently we conclude that it was near Mount Hor, on which he died.
Bene-jaakan: it lies north of the Gulf of Suez.
Hor-hagidgad: it lies northeast of the Gulf of Suez.

Jotbathah: it is said to be the original name of the present Taba, which is at the head of the Gulf of Aqaba. Some think that it is between the wilderness of Sinai and the wilderness of Paran, near the Gulf of Suez on the east.
Ebronah: a passage, meaning a way, and it is a low oasis between "Jotbathah" and "Ezion-gaber".

Ezion-gaber: it is the last station in the journey of wandering, and it is at the head of the Gulf of Aqaba on the western side, near the present port of Eilat. It is a city well known in the history of the people, since the First Book of Kings (ch. 9:26, 10:32) mentions that King Solomon built a fleet of ships there.

entries.section: (3) The journey of wandering and the return to Kadesh-barnea

paragraphs.text: They pitched: they settled.

From the starting point of the wandering the people returned once again to the wilderness of Zin, which is north of the wilderness of Sinai on the side of the Gulf of Aqaba, and then they were stationed again in its most famous city, Kadesh-barnea. There Miriam, the sister of Moses and Aaron, died (ch. 20:1), and there also Moses erred when he struck the rock contrary to what God had commanded him (ch. 20). So they moved from Kadesh-barnea after their murmuring against God and their refusal to enter the Promised Land, and God made them wander in the desert, and they went in different lines in all directions, and finally they returned from north of the Gulf of Suez to north of the Gulf of Aqaba and then to Kadesh-barnea again.

When you meet troubles in your life and do not reach your material goals quickly, do not be disturbed, for God keeps you away from evil, and when you submit to Him and believe in Him, He brings you back again to achieve your goals, but with a pure heart that relies on Him alone and not on the world.

entries.section: (4) From Kadesh to the east of the Jordan

paragraphs.text: Mount Hor: it lies between the north of the Gulf of Aqaba and the south of the Dead Sea.
The people moved, leaving Kadesh-barnea for the last time, and their first stop was at Mount "Hor".

entries.section: (4) From Kadesh to the east of the Jordan

paragraphs.text: These two verses are a brief review of what was explained in detail in (ch. 20:

22-29) of God's calling of Aaron, His telling Moses of his death, and his son Eleazar's taking over the headship of the priesthood, but here the age of Aaron at his death is stated specifically, which was (123 years.)

entries.section: (4) From Kadesh to the east of the Jordan

paragraphs.text: And king Arad the Canaanite heard: also a brief reference to what the chapter (21:1-3) had spoken of before, that this king, when he learned of the people's departure, went out against them and fought them, but God finally gave the victory to His people, who made a vow to God for the sake of this victory.
After that the fiery serpents attacked the people of God because of their murmuring, and then God healed them by means of the bronze serpent (ch. 21:5-9).

entries.section: (4) From Kadesh to the east of the Jordan

paragraphs.text: Mount Hor lies west of the Gulf of Aqaba, and had the Edomites allowed the people to pass, that would have saved much, but that did not happen, so the people were forced to go around Edom, which was the land of the descendants of Esau. The first station after Mount "Hor" was "Zalmonah", whose meaning is "the shade", and it is considered an extension of Mount Hor or one of its peaks. After it "Punon" is mentioned as the next station, which lies northwest of "Ezion-gaber" (v. 35), and after it was "Oboth", which lies north of the port of Eilat, and its meaning "near the water" expressed its location.

entries.section: (4) From Kadesh to the east of the Jordan

paragraphs.text: Iye-abarim: it lies southeast of Moab and is sometimes called Iim because it lies next to it, and some consider it a part of it.
With the people's arrival at "Abarim" they were on the border of the Moabites, east of the river Jordan (ch. 21:13).

entries.section: (4) From Kadesh to the east of the Jordan

paragraphs.text: "Dibon" was one of the cities of the Amorites, over whom and over their king "Sihon" the people were victorious. Its meaning was ruin, and the tribe of Gad asked for it as land for its cattle, and after Moses' agreement the land came to bear their name, "Dibon-gad"; see (ch. 32:2-5).

entries.section: (4) From Kadesh to the east of the Jordan

paragraphs.text: Then the journey was northward alongside the Jordan, and they took all the lands of the Midianites in the direction of the kingdom of Bashan, over which they were also victorious. In this northward journey the stations of the people's encampment and departure are mentioned, such as "Almon-diblathaim" and "the mountains of Abarim" (ch. 21:16-35). There they were victorious over Sihon king of the Amorites and Og king of Bashan.

entries.section: (4) From Kadesh to the east of the Jordan

paragraphs.text: Then came their complete settlement in "the plains of Moab", east of the Jordan and opposite the city of Jericho, which lies on the opposite west bank. (v. 49) came to draw the boundaries of the people's settlement on the east of the Jordan in the plains of Moab. Its southern boundary was "Beth-jesimoth", lying north of the Dead Sea where the river Jordan flows into it, while the northern boundary was "Abel-shittim", lying on the river Jordan itself opposite Jericho.
It is observed that when the people encamped here, all the events from (ch. 22 to ch. 32) took place, the most important of which were:
a- The story of Balak and Balaam (chs. 22-24).
b- The people's falling into fornication with the Moabite women and God's striking the people with the plague (ch. 25).
c- The second numbering of the people (ch. 26).
d- The laws of the division of the land, its portions and proportions (ch. 26).
e- Moses' appointing Joshua as successor and leader of the people after seeing the land from Mount Abarim (ch. 27).
f- The laws of offerings and vows (chs. 28-30).
g- The fighting of the Midianites and the victory over them, and the request of Reuben and Gad to obtain land for their cattle (chs. 31, 32).

God preserved His people in all their movements because He was their leader by the pillar of cloud and the pillar of fire, and whoever tried to oppose them, they were victorious over. Let God be a leader to you in your life, and you will be at ease, and even if some oppose you and try to trouble you, be confident that your God is with you, preserving you and bringing you through the troubles, and giving you victory over your enemies the demons, so that He keeps you pure at all times.

entries.section: (5) Warnings concerning the possession of the new land

paragraphs.text: As the people settled after 40 years of wandering, and the land of Canaan lay opposite them, God tells them that they will cross into the land and possess it, and He reviews with them some last matters in the form of warnings, so that the people might avoid the dangers into which they might fall, as we shall see.

entries.section: (5) Warnings concerning the possession of the new land

paragraphs.text: The first divine command and warning came as follows:

1- Driving out all the inhabitants of the land: God knows the weakness of human nature, and knows too that any person is liable to be influenced by those around him, and for this reason He completely forbade the people to mingle with the other peoples whose land they would take. They must drive them out, because keeping them would mean the people's falling into fornication and idol worship, as happened before (ch. 25).

2- Destroy all their pictures: that is, all the memorials, drawings and works of the molten idols and images which these peoples worshiped. The people of God had to destroy them utterly, for the same purpose as before.
3- Pluck down their high places: the high places are elevated places such as hills, on which the pagan peoples set up their altars. God's command was that they be destroyed completely.

What God commanded His people here is a general commandment for us all, and the sum of what God said is: keep away from evil and all its traces, and do not keep anything of it around you or within you, so that Satan may find no way to remind you of what went before in order to make you fall again. Let us understand this and all pray with the Church, asking for God's help and crying out to Him with the words of the Divine Liturgy: "Every thought that does not please Your goodness, O God, lover of mankind, let it be far from us."

entries.section: (5) Warnings concerning the possession of the new land
